1 · Requirements

Functional. Show each user a ranked list of suggested people on several surfaces (a panel in the feed, a full page, onboarding, after accepting a request), each with a short reason where safe ("12 mutual friends", "also studied at X"); let users send a request, dismiss a suggestion, or opt out of being suggested; react within minutes to new connections (after you connect with someone, their friends appear). Out of scope, said aloud: the feed itself (hd11), messaging, and follow suggestions for public figures, which behave like content recommendation.

Quality targets. Increase accepted connections that lead to interaction within 30 days; keep the ignore-and-report rate per request received below a set ceiling; every new user with at least one connection sees at least 10 credible suggestions within a minute of joining.

Latency targets. p99 of 100 ms for the online ranking request; new-connection-triggered candidates available within 5 minutes; precomputed candidates refreshed at least daily for daily active users.

Privacy and safety targets. Never suggest across a block in either direction; honour opt-outs within minutes; no adult-stranger suggestions to minors; no reasons that disclose another user's private data; no suggestions based on sensitive signals such as precise location co-presence or health-related affiliations.

Clarifying questions. "Mutual connections or follows?" "How many users and what is the degree distribution, including the largest accounts?" "Do we have contact uploads, and under what consent?" "Are there minors on the platform?" "What does success mean for the business: retention of new users, network density, engagement?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

The graph. 500 million monthly users, 200 million daily. Average degree 200, heavy-tailed: most users have tens of connections, some thousands, and a few organisational or celebrity accounts hundreds of thousands or more. Undirected edges: 500 million × 200 / 2 = 50 billion. Stored as adjacency lists, each edge appears twice: 100 billion entries. With 64-bit user IDs, 8 bytes each: 800 GB raw, before offsets, edge metadata (creation time, a tie-strength weight) and replication. Twitter's WTF paper (2012 numbers) is a useful contrast: over 20 billion edges among active users, held in memory on single servers with 144 GB of RAM at about five bytes per edge. Our graph is several times larger and carries metadata, so it is sharded by user ID across in-memory graph servers, a few dozen machines with three replicas.

Friends-of-friends fan-out for one user. The number of two-hop paths from user u is the sum of their friends' degrees. You might guess 200 × 200 = 40,000, but friends are not average users: well-connected people appear in many friend lists, so the average degree of a friend is higher than the average degree of a user. This is the friendship paradox, and its size is E[d²] / E[d]. With a heavy-tailed distribution, suppose friends average 600. Then a typical user has about 200 × 600 = 120,000 two-hop paths; with overlaps (many friends share friends), perhaps 50,000 to 60,000 distinct friends-of-friends. A user with 5,000 connections has millions.

Fan-out for the whole graph. Counting mutual friends for every pair is computing A² for the adjacency matrix A, and the cost is the number of two-paths: each node w contributes deg(w)² ordered pairs (every pair of its neighbours). The total is N × E[d²]. Since E[d²] = 600 × 200 = 120,000, the total is 500 million × 120,000 = 6 × 10¹³. A single hub with a million connections contributes 10¹² by itself. Even at a billion pair-updates a second, a full daily recomputation would take 17 hours of a large cluster just for counting. This is the number that forces the design: caps, sampling, hub handling and incremental computation (section 5).

Serving traffic. 200 million daily users see PYMK on about three surfaces a day: 600 million requests, about 7,000 a second on average and 20,000 at peak. Each request ranks about 500 candidates: 10 million model scorings a second at peak. A gradient-boosted tree model at about 5 microseconds per candidate per core is 50 core-seconds per second, plus feature fetching, which dominates. A modest CPU fleet, sized by feature-store reads more than by the model.

Precomputed candidates. For 200 million active users, 1,000 candidates each with an ID and a few precomputed scores (about 16 bytes): 3.2 TB in a key-value store, refreshed daily and patched incrementally.

The insight to say out loud. Storage fits in a few dozen machines; serving is ordinary ranking at 20,000 requests a second. The hard number is the two-hop fan-out, the sum of squared degrees, which the heavy tail of the degree distribution makes enormous.

3 · API and data

GET  /v1/pymk?surface=feed_panel&limit=20
  -> [{ "user_id": "u_83...", "reason": {"type": "mutual", "count": 12},
        "token": "imp_7f..." }, ...]
POST /v1/pymk/feedback { "token": "imp_7f...", "action": "send_request" | "dismiss" }
POST /v1/settings/pymk { "suggest_me": false }        # opt out of being suggested

Data. Graph: adjacency lists sharded by user, each edge with creation time and tie-strength (interaction count); pending requests; blocks and dismissals. Affiliations: user to school, employer, group, coarse city, with visibility settings. Contacts: hashed phone numbers and emails uploaded with consent, matched to accounts, kept separately with strict access. Embeddings: per user, from a model trained on accepted connections. Candidate store: per user, top candidates with source and offline scores. Impressions and outcomes: who was shown whom, where, in what position, and what happened (send, accept, ignore, report, later interaction), the training data for ranking.

4 · High-level design

Offline. A daily graph snapshot feeds the friends-of-friends job, which for each active user enumerates two-hop candidates under fan-out caps and computes mutual-friend count, Adamic-Adar and Jaccard. An affiliation join produces candidates sharing a school, employer or group (bounded per affiliation: a 100,000-person employer is not 100,000 candidates). Contact matching produces candidates from consented uploads. The embedding model's nearest-neighbour index produces candidates beyond two hops. The union, de-duplicated and pre-scored by a cheap model, is truncated to the top 1,000 per user and written to the candidate store.

Streaming. New edges, blocks, dismissals and opt-outs arrive as events. A new connection u–v triggers incremental candidate generation: v's friends become u's candidates (and u's friends become v's), scored and merged into the candidate lists within minutes. Blocks and opt-outs update filter sets immediately.

Online. A request loads the user's candidate list and any real-time additions, applies hard filters against fresh state (connections, pending requests, blocks, opt-outs, safety rules), fetches features for the top 500 by offline score, ranks them, re-ranks the top for diversity and exposure caps, attaches privacy-safe reasons, logs the impression, and returns 20.

5 · Deep dive: candidate generation and the fan-out maths

Mutual friends are triangles. If u and v share a friend w, the path u–w–v exists; suggesting u–v would close the triangle u, v, w. Graphs of human relationships are full of triangles (your friends tend to know each other), which is why mutual friends predict future edges so well. The common-neighbours score is the number of such w. Two refinements matter. Jaccard divides by the size of the union of both friend lists, so two users with 10 mutual friends out of 30 each score higher than two with 10 out of 3,000. Adamic-Adar sums 1 / log(deg(w)) over mutual friends w, so a mutual friend with 40 connections (1 / log 40 ≈ 0.27) counts about twice as much as one with 2,000 (1 / log 2,000 ≈ 0.13), and a celebrity hub with a million counts 0.07. In Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg's comparison of link-prediction scores on co-authorship networks, Adamic-Adar was among the strongest simple predictors.

Controlling fan-out. Four techniques, used together. Cap per friend: from each friend, take at most 100 neighbours, preferring strong ties (recent interaction) or sampling; a user's work is then at most 200 × 100 = 20,000 paths. Skip or down-weight hubs: friends with degree above a threshold (say 5,000) contribute no friends-of-friends; their Adamic-Adar weight is tiny anyway. Compute only for active users, daily for daily users and weekly for others. Incremental updates: when edge u–v is added, only u's and v's candidate lists change materially (each gains the other's friends), which costs reading two adjacency lists instead of recomputing anything. With caps, the daily job for 200 million active users is at most 200 million × 20,000 = 4 × 10¹² path visits in the worst case and far fewer in practice (most users have fewer than 200 friends), a large but ordinary batch job.

Random walks as an alternative. Instead of enumerating two hops, run short random walks from u that restart at u with some probability (personalised PageRank) and count visits; nodes visited often are "close" to u even beyond two hops. Twitter's WTF computed each user's circle of trust this way, using Monte Carlo walks whose memory cost is only the visit counters, then ran SALSA (a random walk alternating between a user's circle and the accounts they follow) to rank whom to follow. Walks bound the work per user by the number of steps, regardless of hubs, at the cost of sampling noise.

Beyond the graph. New users have almost no graph; and many real-world acquaintances share no mutual connection on the platform. Affiliations (same school and year, same employer and team, same group) catch them, bounded by taking members with the strongest overlap. Contact uploads, only with consent, match phone numbers and emails the user chose to share. Embeddings from a two-tower model (rec4) trained on accepted connections, with user features and graph features as inputs, find similar-network people via nearest-neighbour search. The sources' candidates are merged; their source becomes a feature for the ranker.

6 · Deep dive: features and two-sided ranking

Features. Graph: mutual friends, Adamic-Adar, Jaccard, number of mutual friends who connected recently, whether the candidate is a friend of a strong tie, random-walk visit counts. Affiliation: shared school, employer, group, overlap in time. Behaviour: profile views either way, prior impressions of this candidate and the user's responses (fatigue), how the candidate responds to requests generally (accept rate), how active each user is. Context: surface, time since joining. Trust: account age, verification, spam score. Degrees of both. What is deliberately absent: sensitive attributes (ethnicity, religion, health), precise location, and contact-upload details beyond a match flag.

The objective. The value of a suggestion is an accepted connection that leads to real interaction, and its cost includes bothering the receiver. A multi-task model (hd11) predicts p(send | shown), p(accept | sent), p(ignore or report | sent), and optionally the expected interaction after connecting. The ranking score is p(send) × p(accept) × value − λ × p(send) × p(negative). Work an example: candidate A has p(send) 0.10 and p(accept) 0.80, so 0.08 expected accepted connections; candidate B, a stranger with a large network and many mutual friends from a hub, has p(send) 0.20 but p(accept) 0.15, so 0.03, and p(negative) 0.5. A send-only ranker puts B first; the two-sided ranker puts A first by a wide margin. This is also the main defence against spam: accounts whose requests are ignored get low p(accept) and fall out of rankings.

Re-ranking. Diversity (not ten suggestions from the same company; rec12), exposure caps (no person suggested to more than a set number of users a day, so popular people are not flooded and requests stay manageable), reserved slots for newer users with small networks, and freshness (a suggestion shown and ignored five times is retired).

7 · Deep dive: privacy, safety, spam and fairness

What a suggestion reveals. Every suggestion is an implicit statement: "the system thinks you know this person". The reason makes it explicit. Rules: reasons show only signals visible to the viewer (mutual friends whose friendships the viewer can see; affiliations the candidate made visible); suggestions derived from someone else's contact upload carry no reason and require a second signal before being shown, so a stranger who has your number does not get you suggested on that basis alone; precise location co-presence is never a signal, because it can reveal visits (clinics, shelters, places of worship); and opt-outs from being suggested are honoured globally.

Safety. Blocks are symmetric hard filters, checked at serving time against live state. Minors are not shown adult strangers, and adults are not shown minors outside existing real-world ties the platform can verify (shared school with age-appropriate rules, mutual family connections). Accounts under investigation are excluded.

Spam and fake accounts. Spammers want to be suggested. They create clusters of fake accounts that connect to each other and to real users, manufacturing mutual friends. Defences: account-trust features and filters; the two-sided objective; per-account limits on how often they are suggested; detection of anomalous clusters (dense groups of new accounts with many outgoing requests and low acceptance); and rate limits on requests from new or low-acceptance accounts.

Fairness and feedback loops. PYMK changes the graph it learns from. Popular users are suggested more, gain more connections and become more popular. New users with few connections have few friends-of-friends and get few suggestions: a cold-start trap at exactly the moment retention is decided. Homophily (people connect with similar people) can make suggestions reinforce existing divisions. Measures: the concentration of exposure (share of all suggestion impressions going to the top 1% of users), accept rates and suggestion quality by network size and by region, and the time a new user takes to reach ten connections. Interventions: exposure caps, reserved exposure for newcomers, and diversity of affiliation in re-ranking.

8 · Deep dive: graph storage and the two-hop query

The graph lives in two forms. The system of record is a sharded, replicated store of edges (in2), optimised for writes (new connections) and per-user reads. The graph serving tier holds adjacency lists in memory for fast traversal: sharded by user ID, each adjacency list stored as a sorted array of IDs (so intersecting two lists to count mutual friends is a merge), with a compact encoding (delta-encoded sorted IDs compress well, but cost decode time). A two-hop query for u reads u's list from its shard, groups the friends by shard, sends one batched request per shard returning each friend's capped neighbour list, and merges counts in the caller. With 200 friends spread over 40 shards, that is one round trip of 40 parallel requests, perhaps 10 to 20 ms. That is fine for incremental updates and for real-time candidates after a new connection, but not something to run on every page view, which is why candidates are precomputed.

The WTF decision is worth discussing in an interview. In 2010 Twitter's team calculated that, at about eight bytes per edge naively and about five in practice, a server with 64 GB for data could hold roughly eight billion edges, and that memory growth would keep the graph fitting for 24 to 36 months. Holding the whole graph on each server made replication the scaling and fault-tolerance strategy, avoided graph partitioning entirely, and let them launch in a few months. The costs, which they described, were the scaling ceiling and little room for edge and vertex metadata. The lesson is not "use one machine" but "do the arithmetic before choosing the architecture".

9 · Evaluation plan

Offline. Link prediction on snapshots: take the graph at time T, generate and rank candidates, and check recall and precision at k against edges formed in (T, T + 30 days]. Report per user segment (new, small network, large network) and per candidate source. Correct for the feedback loop: edges formed because the old system suggested them favour models that imitate it, so weight positives by the inverse probability of having been shown (rec10), report edges formed outside PYMK as a separate slice, and use a small exploration share in production to collect less biased labels. Ranking models are also evaluated on logged impressions (send and accept prediction quality, calibration).

Online. The primary metric is accepted connections per user that lead to interaction within 30 days (WTF's equivalent concern led them beyond follow-through rate to an "engagement per impression" metric measured after acceptance). Guardrails: ignore-and-report rate per request received, requests received per user, opt-out rate, privacy complaints, and new-user time to ten connections. Network interference is the trap: a treated user sends more requests, many to control users, whose metrics then change. Cluster-randomised experiments (Ugander et al.) assign whole graph communities to arms so most edges stay within an arm; two-sided metrics attribute each request's outcome to the arm of the sender. Without this, user-level tests overstate or understate the effect.

10 · Failure modes and trade-offs

FailureSymptomDefence
Hub blow-upFoF job runs for hours; skewed shardsPer-friend caps, hub skipping, random walks
Revealing suggestionComplaints: "how does it know?"Signal and reason rules, two-signal requirement
Spam amplificationNew accounts suggested widely; low accept rateTrust features, accept-weighted objective, caps
Stale filtersBlocked person suggestedServing-time checks against live state
Cold-start trapNew users churn with few connectionsContacts, affiliations, reserved exposure
Biased evaluationOffline gains vanish onlinePropensity weighting, exploration, cluster tests

The trade-offs to name: recall of candidates against fan-out cost; send rate against receiver burden; personalisation from rich signals against privacy; growth of connections against network health (spam, popularity concentration); and precomputation freshness against cost.

11 · What changes at 10× scale

At 5 billion users and 500 billion edges the graph serving tier becomes thousands of machines, and cross-shard two-hop queries become expensive enough that graph-aware partitioning (placing densely connected communities on the same shard) pays for its complexity. Candidate generation shifts further toward embeddings and random walks with bounded work, with friends-of-friends computed incrementally only. Regional and legal differences multiply: data residency for the graph, different rules on contact uploads and minors. And experiments need cluster randomisation by default, because at that density almost every request crosses arms.
deep:
Directed graphs change the question

In a follow network, edges are one-way and the asymmetry matters: following a celebrity says you are interested, not that you know them. WTF's authors noted that Twitter's graph is closer to an interest graph than a social graph, and separated two problems: "interested in" (accounts you would like to read) and "similar to" (users with similar follows). SALSA fits this well: its walk alternates between a user's circle of trust (hubs) and the accounts they follow (authorities), ranking authorities by how much trusted hubs follow them. Mutual-friend measures still work for the social part, but interest suggestions behave more like content recommendation, and the two-sided accept term disappears because following needs no acceptance.

Ensembles of candidate generators

WTF reported that the production algorithm blended results from about 20 different algorithms. That is typical: no single generator covers everyone (new users need contacts and affiliations; heavy users need deep graph walks; dormant users returning need recency). The ranking model sees each candidate's sources as features and learns how much to trust each per segment, and the candidate quotas per source are tuned so cheap generators do not crowd out rare but valuable ones.

Incremental computation and the "just connected" moment

The most valuable time for suggestions is right after a new connection: the user is engaged and the new friend's network is fresh territory. Precomputed lists are a day old at that moment. A streaming job reading new-edge events computes the new friend's capped neighbourhood, scores it with a light model, and pushes it into the user's candidate list within seconds, while the batch job remains the source of truth. This is also where WTF's design had to compensate: its in-memory graphs were refreshed from daily snapshots, so it built a separate real-time path for new users.

Graph-aware sharding

Hashing users to shards spreads load evenly but puts most friends of a user on other shards, so every two-hop query fans out widely. Partitioning by communities (people in the same city, school or company placed together) keeps more edges local and cuts fan-out, at the cost of hot shards for large communities and rebalancing as the graph changes. WTF's authors called partitioning large, changing, power-law graphs a very difficult problem, which is one reason they avoided it. Most systems start with hashing plus replication of hub adjacency lists and adopt community-aware placement only when cross-shard traffic dominates.

Explainability is a product feature and a risk

Reasons ("12 mutual friends") raise acceptance, because they make the suggestion credible. But each reason type must be checked for what it discloses, to whom, and in combination: "you both went to X" plus "3 mutual friends" plus the suggestion's position may reveal more than any one signal. A review process for every new reason type, and a rule that reasons are computed only from data visible to the viewer, keeps explainability from becoming a leak.

What the graph does to the metrics

Because PYMK grows the graph, its effects compound: more connections mean more friends-of-friends, more candidates, more connections. Short experiments understate long-term effects, and long-term holdouts (a small group with a frozen older algorithm for months) are the only way to measure them. The same compounding makes harms grow too: a ranker that slightly over-suggests popular users concentrates the graph over months, which a two-week test will not show.

Tie strength makes the graph weighted

Not all friendships are equal: a colleague you message daily and a classmate you have not spoken to in ten years are both one edge. Weighting edges by tie strength (recent interactions, messages, profile views, shared photos) improves almost every part of the system: per-friend fan-out caps sample strong ties first, mutual friends who are strong ties of both users count more, and random walks follow strong ties more often. The cost is that the graph is no longer just IDs: each adjacency entry carries a weight that must be updated as interactions happen, which is the edge-metadata problem WTF's authors identified as a limit of their compact in-memory design (an 8-bit weight added 12.5% to their memory per edge). A practical compromise keeps weights quantised to a few bits and refreshes them daily.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The celebrity that broke the batch job. A public figure's account, configured as a mutual-connection profile, reached two million connections. The friends-of-friends job's shard holding that adjacency list ran for hours, and every connection of that account became a "friend of a friend" of two million people with one mutual friend each. Hubs above a degree threshold are now excluded from two-hop enumeration and handled as an interest signal instead.

The suggestion that revealed a contact upload. A user was suggested to a stranger with the reason "you may know each other", because the stranger had uploaded the user's phone number. The user inferred that the stranger had their number. The rule since: candidates whose only signal is someone else's contact upload are shown without a reason and only if a second independent signal exists.

The spam ring. A cluster of a few thousand new accounts connected to each other and then sent requests to real users at a steady rate, each request showing dozens of mutual friends (all fake). Acceptance from real users was low, which the two-sided model eventually picked up, but only after a week. Cluster detection on dense new-account subgraphs with low external acceptance now removes such candidates within hours.

The experiment that lied. A new ranker showed +6% accepted connections in a user-level A/B test, mostly because treated users sent many more requests to control users, who accepted them; control's own suggestions were crowded out. A cluster-randomised rerun measured +2%. The team now runs graph-cluster randomisation for every PYMK experiment.

What to monitor

Per surface and segment: impressions, send rate, accept rate, ignore and report rate, requests received per user, new users' time to ten connections, candidate-source mix, exposure concentration, opt-out rate, privacy complaints, offline job duration and the largest shard's time, candidate staleness, serving latency.

Knobs people tune

Per-friend fan-out cap; hub threshold; candidate quotas per source; λ for negative outcomes; exposure caps per person; reserved slots for new users; diversity strength; impression fatigue rules; refresh cadence per activity tier.

The real case: Twitter's WTF

"WTF: The Who to Follow Service at Twitter" (Gupta, Goel, Lin, Sharma, Wang and Zadeh, WWW 2013) describes a service that launched in summer 2010 after a few months of work by a small team. The design decision its authors highlight is holding the entire Twitter graph in memory on a single server: in August 2012 the graph had over 20 billion edges among active users, with power-law degrees (over 1,000 users with more than a million followers), and the team calculated about five bytes per edge in practice, using servers that grew from 72 GB to 144 GB of RAM. Their in-memory engine, Cassovary (open-sourced in 2012), stored adjacency lists as shared arrays of 32-bit integers; fault tolerance and scale came from replicas each holding the full graph, loaded from daily snapshots. Each server generated about 100 recommendations for a user in under 500 ms per thread. The algorithms started from a user's "circle of trust", computed with Monte Carlo random walks similar to personalised PageRank, then applied SALSA with about 500 top circle-of-trust accounts as hubs; in their reported experiment, SALSA had the highest follow-through rate, well above personalised PageRank and closure-based suggestions, while the production system blended about 20 algorithms. They also described the design's limits (memory ceiling, little room for features) and a move toward Hadoop and machine-learned models. It is a rare first-party account of the trade-offs this lesson is about.
myths: Rank by number of mutual friends and you are done.

Mutual-friend count is the strongest single signal, but a mutual friend who has 5,000 friends says little, while one with 40 says a lot; Adamic-Adar weighting by 1 / log(degree) fixes much of that. And the objective is not "likely to know" but "likely to send a request that is accepted and leads to interaction", which needs a model over many features, two-sided.
Friends-of-friends is cheap because people have a few hundred friends.

Friends of friends multiply: a user with 200 friends whose friends average 600 friends (the friendship paradox makes friends' degrees higher than average) reaches 120,000 two-hop paths. Across the graph, the work is the sum of each node's degree squared, which a single hub with a million connections dominates on its own. Fan-out caps, hub down-weighting and incremental computation are required.
Optimise the number of connection requests sent.

Requests are cheap for the sender and a cost for the receiver. A ranker that maximises sends learns to suggest people who will not accept, annoying receivers and helping spammers. The objective is accepted connections, ideally weighted by later interaction, with ignored and reported requests as negative outcomes.
If the data is in our systems, using it to suggest people is fine.

A suggestion can reveal information: that someone uploaded your phone number, that you visited the same clinic, that a private connection exists. Suggestions must be built only from signals the user would expect, must not show reasons that disclose another person's private data, and must respect blocks, opt-outs and protections for minors.
Offline link-prediction accuracy predicts online success.

Offline evaluation predicts which edges will form after a snapshot, but many of those edges formed because the old recommender suggested them, so a new model is graded on how well it imitates the old one. Online tests are also hard: treated users send requests to control users, so the groups are not independent. Use offline metrics for screening and cluster-randomised or two-sided online tests for decisions.
The graph must be distributed from day one.

Twitter's Who to Follow service launched in 2010 holding the entire follow graph in memory on a single server, a choice its authors defended as the fastest way to ship, with a later move to a distributed architecture. Whether the graph fits on one machine is an arithmetic question about edges and bytes per edge, worth doing before choosing an architecture.
lab:
Goal: build a heavy-tailed random graph, measure friends-of-friends fan-out and the friendship paradox, see what a hub does to the sum of squared degrees, and compare common neighbours, Jaccard and Adamic-Adar for predicting held-out edges. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as pymk_lab.py and run python pymk_lab.py (it takes under a minute).
  2. Read the degree statistics: mean degree, mean degree of a friend (larger: the friendship paradox), and the ratio E[d²]/E[d].
  3. Read the fan-out lines: the sum of degree squared across the graph, the share contributed by the top 1% of nodes, and the average two-hop paths per user with and without a per-friend cap of 20.
  4. Read recall at 10 for the three scores on held-out edges. Adamic-Adar usually edges out common neighbours; Jaccard often does worse on graphs like this.
  5. Change M (edges added per new node) or add a single hub connected to 2,000 random nodes and re-run the fan-out lines.
"""Friends-of-friends fan-out and link prediction on a preferential-attachment graph. Python 3.12."""
import math, random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

rng = random.Random(5)
N, M = 20_000, 5
adj = defaultdict(set); targets = []                 # preferential attachment (Barabasi-Albert style)
for v in range(N):
    picks = set()
    while len(picks) < min(M, v):
        picks.add(rng.choice(targets) if targets else rng.randrange(v))
    for u in picks:
        adj[v].add(u); adj[u].add(v); targets += [u, v]
deg = {v: len(adj[v]) for v in range(N)}
d = list(deg.values()); mean = sum(d) / N; mean_sq = sum(x * x for x in d) / N
friend_mean = sum(deg[u] for v in range(N) for u in adj[v]) / sum(d)
print(f"mean degree {mean:.1f}  mean friend degree {friend_mean:.1f}  E[d^2]/E[d] {mean_sq / mean:.1f}")

sq = sorted((x * x for x in d), reverse=True)
print(f"sum of deg^2 = {sum(sq):,}  top 1% of nodes contribute {sum(sq[:N // 100]) / sum(sq):.0%}")
sample = rng.sample(range(N), 1_000)
paths = sum(sum(deg[w] for w in adj[u]) for u in sample) / len(sample)
capped = sum(sum(min(deg[w], 20) for w in adj[u]) for u in sample) / len(sample)
print(f"avg two-hop paths per user {paths:,.0f}; with cap 20 per friend {capped:,.0f}")

# hold out 2,000 edges, score candidates for their endpoints
edges = [(u, v) for u in range(N) for v in adj[u] if u < v]
held = rng.sample(edges, 2_000)
for u, v in held: adj[u].discard(v); adj[v].discard(u)
deg = {v: len(adj[v]) for v in range(N)}
def scores(u):
    cn, aa = Counter(), Counter()
    for w in adj[u]:
        for c in adj[w]:
            if c != u and c not in adj[u]:
                cn[c] += 1; aa[c] += 1 / math.log(max(deg[w], 2))
    jac = {c: cn[c] / len(adj[u] | adj[c]) for c in cn}
    return cn, aa, jac
hits = {"common": 0, "adamic-adar": 0, "jaccard": 0}
for u, v in held[:500]:
    cn, aa, jac = scores(u)
    for name, s in (("common", cn), ("adamic-adar", aa), ("jaccard", jac)):
        top = sorted(s, key=s.get, reverse=True)[:10]
        hits[name] += v in top
for name, h in hits.items(): print(f"recall@10 {name:12} {h / 500:.3f}")

What to look for: a mean friend degree several times the mean degree; the top 1% of nodes contributing a large share of the sum of squared degrees, which is the hub problem; a cap of 20 per friend cutting two-hop paths sharply; and recall at 10 low in absolute terms (a random graph has little real structure, unlike human networks full of triangles) but with Adamic-Adar at or above common neighbours. The absolute numbers are not meaningful; the comparisons are.
recap: People You May Know suggests connections by generating candidates from the social graph and other signals, ranking them on the probability of an accepted, valuable connection, and filtering for privacy, safety and diversity.
With 500 million users and an average of 200 friends, the graph has 50 billion undirected edges, 100 billion adjacency entries, about 800 GB at 8 bytes each, so it is sharded by user across machines.

Friends-of-friends fan-out for a typical user is about 200 × 600 = 120,000 two-hop paths because friends have more friends than average (the friendship paradox), and the total work across the graph is the sum of degree squared, dominated by hubs.
Counting mutual friends is counting the triangles a new edge would close; Adamic-Adar weights each mutual friend by 1 / log(degree) so popular hubs count less.
Fan-out is controlled by capping or sampling each friend's neighbours, down-weighting hubs, precomputing for active users, and triggering incremental updates when a user makes a new connection.
Other candidate sources cover what the graph misses: shared affiliations, consented contact uploads, and embedding similarity from a model trained on accepted connections.

The ranker is two-sided: it predicts the probability the viewer sends a request and the probability the candidate accepts, minus a penalty for ignores and reports, so spam and one-sided suggestions are pushed down.
Privacy rules decide what a suggestion may be based on and what reason it may show; blocks, opt-outs and protections for minors are hard filters.
Offline evaluation predicts edges formed after a snapshot and is biased by the old recommender; online tests must handle network interference with cluster randomisation and two-sided metrics.

Twitter's WTF held a graph of over 20 billion edges in memory on single servers using about five bytes per edge, generated about 100 recommendations per user in under 500 ms per thread, and found its SALSA-based algorithm had the highest follow-through rate.
glossary: A link-prediction score summing 1 / log(degree) over mutual friends, so mutual friends with few connections count more.
For each user, the list of users they are connected to; the standard way to store a sparse graph.
The number of mutual friends two users have; the simplest link-prediction score.
The number of connections a user has.
A user, their friends, and the connections among those friends.
The number of nodes or paths a query must touch, such as all friends of all friends.
In Twitter's WTF paper, the number of follows generated divided by the number of recommendation impressions.
On average, a person's friends have more friends than the person does, because well-connected people appear in many friend lists.
The tendency of people to connect with others similar to themselves.
A node with a very large degree, such as a celebrity or a large organisation's account.
Mutual friends divided by the size of the union of two users' friend lists.
Predicting which pairs of nodes in a graph will become connected.
In an experiment, treated users affecting control users through the graph, which breaks the independence an A/B test assumes.
A random walk from a user that keeps restarting at that user; nodes visited often are close to the user in the graph.
People You May Know: the common name for connection-suggestion features in social and professional networks.
A random-walk algorithm on a bipartite graph that alternates forward and backward steps; Twitter used it to rank whom to follow from a user's circle of trust.
Three users who are all connected to each other; adding a suggested edge between two users who share a friend closes a triangle.
Ranking that accounts for both parties: the viewer's probability of sending a request and the candidate's probability of accepting.
drill:
Work it out

Your network has 300 million users with an average of 150 connections; the average degree of a friend is 450. (a) How many adjacency entries and how much memory at 8 bytes each? (b) What is the total two-hop work, Σ deg²? (c) With a per-friend cap of 50 and hubs over 5,000 skipped, what is the worst-case daily work for 120 million active users? (d) How long would that take at 5 × 10⁸ path visits a second per 100-machine cluster?

Answer

(a) Edges: 300 million × 150 / 2 = 22.5 billion; adjacency entries 45 billion; × 8 bytes = 360 GB raw, before metadata and replication.

(b) E[d²] = mean friend degree × mean degree = 450 × 150 = 67,500. Σ deg² = 300 million × 67,500 ≈ 2 × 10¹³.

(c) Each active user's work is at most deg(u) × 50; on average 150 × 50 = 7,500 (hubs skipped only reduce it). 120 million × 7,500 = 9 × 10¹¹ path visits.

(d) 9 × 10¹¹ / 5 × 10⁸ = 1,800 seconds, about 30 minutes, against about 11 hours for the uncapped total at the same rate. Comfortable daily; incremental updates handle the rest of the day.

Diagnose it

After a ranking change, accepted connections per user rose 4% in the A/B test, but two weeks after launch, complaints about "requests from strangers" doubled and the accept rate per request received fell from 38% to 31%. What happened, and how should it have been caught?

Answer

The change probably increased sends more than accepts: more suggestions of weakly connected people, each with some chance of acceptance, so accepted connections per sender rose while receivers got many more unwanted requests. A user-level test credits the sender's arm with the accepts and does not charge it for the burden on receivers, many of whom were in control; network interference made the gain look larger. Check requests received per user, ignore and report rates per request received, and accept rate by mutual-friend bucket, before and after. It should have been caught by two-sided guardrails (receiver burden and negative outcomes per request received) and by cluster-randomised testing. Fix: raise λ on negative outcomes, require a minimum p(accept), add exposure caps per receiver, and re-test with cluster randomisation.
qa: E
What candidate sources would you use for People You May Know?

Friends of friends ranked by mutual-friend measures; shared affiliations such as school, employer and groups; contacts the user chose to upload, matched to accounts with consent; embedding nearest neighbours from a model trained on accepted connections; and fresh triggers, such as the friends of someone the user just connected with. Each source covers cases the others miss, so their candidates are merged and de-duplicated before ranking.
E
Why is Adamic-Adar better than raw mutual-friend count?

A mutual friend with thousands of connections is weak evidence that two people know each other, because that hub connects many people who never met; a mutual friend with 30 connections is strong evidence. Adamic-Adar sums 1 / log(degree of each mutual friend), so small, tight-knit mutual friends dominate the score.
E
What hard filters run before ranking?

Already connected, pending requests either way, previously dismissed suggestions, users who blocked or were blocked by the viewer, users who opted out of being suggested, deactivated and suspicious accounts, and safety rules such as not suggesting unknown adults to minors. Filters are applied after candidate generation and again at serving time, because blocks and connections change in real time.
M
Estimate the friends-of-friends fan-out for a typical user and for the whole graph.

A user with 200 friends whose friends have on average about 600 friends (higher than the 200 average because of the friendship paradox) has about 120,000 two-hop paths and perhaps half as many distinct candidates. Across the graph the work is the sum of degree squared: 500 million users × E[d²] of about 120,000 is 6 × 10¹³ pairs, and one hub with a million connections contributes 10¹² by itself. Full recomputation daily is not feasible; caps, sampling and incremental updates are.
Follow-up: Where does E[d²] = 120,000 come from? — From the friendship paradox: the average friend's degree is E[d²] / E[d], so if friends average 600 and users average 200, E[d²] = 600 × 200.
M
How do you keep friends-of-friends computation tractable?

Cap or sample each friend's neighbours (for example the 100 strongest ties), skip or heavily down-weight hubs above a degree threshold, compute only for users active recently, precompute a candidate list per user daily or weekly, and update incrementally when an edge is added: when u connects with v, v's friends become u's candidates immediately at the cost of reading one adjacency list.
M
What does the ranking model predict, and why two-sided?

It predicts the probability the viewer sends a request to the candidate, the probability the candidate accepts if they do, and the probability of a negative outcome (ignore, report, block). The score is roughly p(send) × p(accept) minus a weighted negative term, optionally times expected later interaction. Ranking on sends alone would favour people unlikely to accept and reward spammers; the accept term protects receivers.
M
How would you store the graph and serve two-hop queries?

Adjacency lists sharded by user ID across in-memory graph servers with replicas: 100 billion entries at 8 bytes is about 800 GB, so tens of machines including replication and overhead. A two-hop query reads the user's list from one shard, then batches one request per shard for the friends' lists, merges and counts in the caller. Precomputed candidate lists for active users live in a key-value store so serving does not run the two-hop query on every page view.
M
What privacy problems can People You May Know create?

Suggestions can disclose things: that someone uploaded your phone number, that two people share a sensitive affiliation, or that a private connection exists via a displayed mutual friend. Mitigations: use only signals users would expect, never show reasons derived from someone else's private data (such as their contact upload), show mutual friends only when those friendships are visible to the viewer, honour opt-outs from being suggested, and exclude sensitive signals such as precise location co-presence.
H
Why is offline evaluation of PYMK biased, and what do you do about it?

Offline link prediction takes a graph snapshot and checks whether the model ranks highly the edges formed in the following weeks, but many of those edges formed because the current system suggested them, so the metric rewards imitating the current system and penalises suggestions it never showed. Mitigations: weight positives by inverse propensity of having been shown, include edges formed outside PYMK (from invitations or messages) as a separate slice, and keep a small exploration share of suggestions to gather less biased labels. Final decisions come from online tests.
Follow-up: How much exploration? — A few per cent of slots, with candidates sampled from lower-ranked but plausible ones, enough to estimate their accept rates without a visible quality drop.
H
Design the online experiment for a new PYMK ranker.

User-level A/B tests are contaminated: treated users send requests to control users, whose accept behaviour and connection counts change. Randomise by graph clusters (communities found by a partitioning algorithm) so most edges stay within a treatment arm, or measure two-sided outcomes per request. Primary metric: accepted connections per user that lead to interaction within 30 days; guardrails: ignored and reported requests per request received, requests received per user (receiver burden), and privacy complaints. Run long enough to see past novelty.
H
How do you stop PYMK amplifying spam and fake accounts?

Feed an account-trust score into ranking and filters so new or suspicious accounts are rarely suggested; include the accept and report probabilities so accounts whose requests are ignored lose exposure quickly; rate-limit requests from new accounts and from accounts with low acceptance; watch for accounts that appear in many users' candidate lists through manufactured mutual friends (fake clusters connecting to each other and to real users); and treat a burst of acceptances from one cluster as a signal, not a success.
H
Is there a fairness problem in People You May Know?

Yes, several. Popular users get suggested more and gain connections faster, so the rich get richer; new users with small networks get few suggestions and few connections, which hurts retention; and homophily can narrow networks along demographic lines. Measure exposure distribution (how concentrated suggestions are) and accept rates across user groups and network sizes, reserve exposure for new users, cap how often one person is suggested per day, and re-rank for diversity of affiliation, while avoiding sensitive attributes as ranking features.

t: Design notification ranking and send-time optimisation
sum: Deciding what to send, to whom, when and on which channel for 300 million users and 6 billion candidate notifications a day: uplift instead of response models, the value of a push channel you can lose, fatigue and volume caps solved with a shadow price, send-time prediction and digests, holdouts for long-term effects, and LinkedIn's measured trade-off between email volume, activity and complaints.

why:
A social app sends notifications. At first there are three kinds: someone messaged you, someone commented on your post, someone you know joined. They work: users come back. So every team adds their own. The video team sends "videos you might like". The events team sends "an event near you". Growth sends "you have 3 new friend suggestions". Marketing sends "you haven't posted in a while". Each team runs an A/B test, each test shows more visits, and each notification ships.

A year later the average user receives fourteen notifications a day. Push opt-in among new users has fallen. The share of users who have disabled notifications entirely has doubled. Notification click-through rate is down by half, and each team's response is to send more, because their own A/B tests still show gains. A senior engineer looks at the numbers and asks the questions nobody asked: how many of those visits would have happened anyway? What is a user who disabled push worth compared with one who did not? And who decides, for one user on one evening, whether the eighth notification of the day should be sent at all?

The senior design question is to build that decision system: what to send, to whom, when and on which channel. It must rank candidate notifications across all teams by their incremental effect rather than their click probability, account for the long-term cost of fatigue and lost channels, enforce volume limits in a principled way, choose send times and aggregate into digests, keep urgent messages instant, and be evaluated on site-wide, long-term outcomes with holdouts. Delivery itself (provider APIs, retries, idempotency) is the notification service of in4; this case is the brain in front of it.

The lesson follows the interview: requirements and targets; estimates for candidates, scoring, delivery and the value of a channel; the API and data; the architecture; deep dives on uplift versus response models, fatigue and volume with a worked value curve and a shadow price, and send-time optimisation with aggregation; the evaluation plan with holdouts; failure modes; and ten times the scale. The real case is LinkedIn's published work on email volume, which measured exactly the trade-off between volume, engagement and complaints and changed its objective as a result.
primer:
What the system decides

Events happen all day: a friend posts, someone replies to you, a price drops, a live stream starts. Each event can become a candidate notification for some users. The ranking system decides, per user and candidate: send or not; on which channel (push to the phone, email, SMS, or only a badge and an entry in the in-app inbox); when (now, later today at a better time, or folded into tomorrow's digest); and in what form (alone, or aggregated with similar ones). It decides under limits: each user's tolerance for interruptions, quiet hours at night, legal rules for marketing messages, and the costs of channels such as SMS.

The mental model: a personal assistant who guards your attention

Imagine a good executive assistant. Calls from your family and your boss go straight through. Everything else waits: they tell you about the five minor things in one summary after lunch, not in five interruptions. They do not bother you with news you would see anyway when you check your inbox. They know when you like to be reached and when you do not. They notice when you start ignoring their messages and send fewer. And they understand that if they annoy you enough, you will tell them to stop calling altogether, and then even the important calls will not get through.

That assistant is the design. Urgent and personal messages bypass ranking. Everything else is ranked by whether telling you now makes a difference (uplift), not by whether you would react (response). Minor items are batched (aggregation) and timed (send-time optimisation). Volume adapts to your responses (fatigue). And the cost of annoying you includes losing the channel for good (channel value). The analogy breaks in one place: an assistant serves one person, while this system arbitrates between many teams who each want your attention, so it needs a common currency for deciding whose notification goes out.

The currency: incremental value per send

To let notifications from different teams compete fairly, everything is converted into one number: the net incremental value of sending this notification, to this user, on this channel, now. It has two parts. The gain is the extra probability of a visit (or another valued action) that the notification causes, times what such a visit is worth to the business. The cost is the probability the notification makes the user disable notifications, unsubscribe or uninstall, times what that channel is worth over the future, plus any money the channel costs (an SMS). A comment notification and a video recommendation are then comparable, and the user's daily limit is spent on the candidates with the highest net value. Every deep dive in this lesson is about estimating one of these quantities honestly.

A reader who stops here has the shape: candidates from every team, filtered by eligibility, scored by incremental value minus the risk of losing the channel, admitted under a per-user threshold, timed and aggregated, delivered, and measured on site-wide engagement with holdouts.

1 · Requirements

Functional. Accept candidate notifications from any team through one API with a type, recipients, urgency class and payload; filter by user preferences, quiet hours, opt-outs and legal rules (marketing consent); de-duplicate and aggregate; decide send or not, channel and time; hand accepted notifications to the delivery service (in4); track delivery, opens, visits, dismissals, disables and unsubscribes; and expose per-type metrics to owning teams. Out of scope, said aloud: delivery mechanics, the content of each notification, and in-app feed ranking.

Quality targets. Increase site-wide weekly active users and sessions from all sources, not notification clicks; keep push-disable, unsubscribe and spam-report rates below set ceilings; never delay or drop transactional and security notifications.

Latency targets. Urgent notifications delivered within 2 seconds at p99 from the event; ranked notifications decided within a minute of the event; scheduled sends within 5 minutes of their chosen time.

Volume and cost targets. Per-user limits by channel (for example at most a set number of ranked pushes a day and emails a week), quiet hours by local time, SMS only for critical types because each costs money.

Clarifying questions. "Which notification types exist, and which are transactional?" "What is the business objective: daily actives, sessions, revenue?" "Do we have any randomised data today?" "How valuable is a user with push enabled versus disabled?" "Which regions and marketing laws apply?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Candidates. 300 million monthly users, 100 million daily. Each user is a candidate recipient for about 20 notifications a day (friends' posts, comments, recommendations, reminders): 6 billion candidates a day, about 70,000 a second on average and 200,000 at the evening peak. Scoring each with a gradient-boosted model or small neural network at tens of microseconds, plus feature lookups, is a few hundred CPU cores: substantial but ordinary. Feature fetches (user's recent activity, recent notifications, per-type history) dominate cost, so features are batched per user: score all of a user's pending candidates together.

Sends. If the system sends about 10% of candidates: 600 million a day, mostly push and in-app, some email. Evening peaks reach about 50,000 pushes a second to the platform push services (Apple's and Google's). Email at an assumed $0.0001 per message is $10,000 a day at 100 million emails; SMS at an assumed $0.0075 is reserved for critical messages.

Scheduler. If half of sends are delayed for timing or aggregation by an average of 4 hours, about 300 million a day pass through the delay queue, and at any moment about 50 million are waiting (Little's law: 300 million / 24 hours × 4 hours). The scheduler (in5) holds them in time-bucketed partitions and re-checks each before sending.

Logs. 6 billion candidate decisions a day at about 200 bytes each (features hashed, scores, decision, policy version) is 1.2 TB a day, kept long enough to train and audit; outcomes join them over the following days.

The value of a channel. Suppose users with push enabled generate, on average, 2 more active days a month than comparable users with push disabled, and an active day is worth $0.20 to the business (from advertising or subscriptions). Push is then worth about $0.40 a month per user; over the expected remaining lifetime of the channel, discounted, call it $4. If each push carries a 0.05% chance that the user disables push, each push costs 0.0005 × $4 = $0.002 in expected channel loss. That number turns "annoyance" into something the ranker can subtract.

The insight to say out loud. The computation is cheap; the decisions are expensive, because a wrong send costs a sliver of a channel worth dollars and a right send earns a sliver of a visit worth cents. The system lives in the difference between small probabilities, which is why calibration, randomised data and long-term measurement dominate the design.

3 · API and data

POST /v1/candidates
{ "type": "comment_on_post", "urgency": "ranked",       # transactional | urgent | ranked | digest_only
  "event_id": "ev_8c1...", "recipients": ["u_1", "u_2"],
  "payload_ref": "comment/c_771", "expires_at": "2026-10-09T18:00Z",
  "aggregation_key": "post/p_55:comments" }
-> 202 { "accepted": 2 }

GET /v1/types/{type}/metrics   # sends, opens, incremental visits, disables, by segment
PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences  { "push": {"comment_on_post": true, "recommendations": false},
                                  "quiet_hours": {"start": "22:00", "end": "08:00"} }

Data. Candidates and decisions: user, type, event, scores (uplift, p(disable), value), λ at decision time, decision (send, drop, delay, aggregate), channel, scheduled time, policy version, and whether the candidate was in the random holdback. Outcomes: delivered, opened, visit within a window from any source, dismissed, disabled, unsubscribed, reported. User state: preferences, time zone, channel status, notifications received in the last day and week, recent activity pattern by hour. Type registry: owner, urgency class, default channel, aggregation rules, legal category.

4 · High-level design

Teams publish candidates to a Kafka topic. Candidate expansion resolves recipients (followers of a poster, members of a group) with fan-out limits. Transactional and urgent types skip ranking and go straight to delivery, after preference and channel checks. Everything else passes eligibility (preferences, quiet hours, opt-outs, marketing consent, de-duplication against what the user has already seen in the app), then aggregation (attach to a pending digest with the same key if one exists), then scoring: per candidate and channel, predicted uplift on visits, p(disable or unsubscribe), and the resulting net value. The volume optimiser compares net value with the user's threshold λ, adjusted for what they have already received today. Accepted candidates go to the send-time scheduler, which places them in the delay queue at their chosen time; at that time they are re-checked (still relevant? user already visited? digest grown?) and sent to delivery. A small random share of eligible candidates (say 3%) is held back regardless of score and logged as such: the control data for uplift.

Walk one candidate. At 19:12 Ana comments on Ben's post. Candidate: notify Ben, type comment_on_post, ranked, aggregation key "post/p_55:comments". Ben has push on, it is 19:12 in his time zone (no quiet hours), he has had two pushes today. No pending digest for that post. Scores: uplift on a visit in the next 24 hours 0.06 (Ben is a weekly user who opens about every third day), p(disable) 0.0004, value per incremental visit $0.20, channel value $4: net value = 0.06 × 0.20 − 0.0004 × 4 = 0.012 − 0.0016 = $0.0104. Ben's λ after two pushes today is $0.006, so the push is accepted. Send-time model: Ben usually opens the app around 21:00, and the uplift at 21:00 is predicted slightly higher; urgency allows delay, so it is scheduled for 20:55 with the aggregation window open. At 20:30 two more comments arrive and join the digest. At 20:55 the system re-checks (Ben has not opened the app since) and sends one push: "Ana and 2 others commented on your post".

5 · Deep dive: uplift, not response

Four kinds of user. For any notification, users fall into four groups: persuadables visit only if notified; sure things visit anyway; lost causes do not visit either way; and sleeping dogs are made worse by the notification (they disable push or churn). Only persuadables justify a send. A response model, p(visit | sent), cannot tell persuadables from sure things: both have high response. An uplift model estimates p(visit | sent) − p(visit | not sent) for this user and this notification.

A worked comparison. Two users, one "new posts from people you follow" notification each, budget for one send:

Userp(visit | sent)p(visit | not sent)UpliftResponse model picksUplift model picks
Daily user0.920.900.02✓
Lapsing user0.150.050.10✓

The response model sends to the daily user and gains 0.02 expected visits; the uplift model sends to the lapsing user and gains 0.10, five times more. LinkedIn's published segment numbers show this effect in a real system: when they changed their email objective from email-attributed sessions to site-wide weekly active users, the share of generated emails actually sent to daily-active members fell from 0.76 to 0.22, while for dormant members it rose from 0.32 to 0.40. Daily-active members were active anyway; the emails had been taking credit.

Getting the data. You never observe the same user both notified and not notified for the same event, so uplift cannot be learned from ordinary logs, where sends were chosen by the previous policy. The system therefore withholds a small random share of eligible candidates (3% here) and logs them as controls. Models are trained on this randomised data: the two-model approach fits p(visit | sent) and p(visit | not sent) separately and subtracts; the single-model approach includes "was sent" as a feature and evaluates both settings; other methods transform the outcome so one model learns the difference directly (Gutierrez and Gérardy review them). With 6 billion candidates a day, 3% is 180 million randomised controls a day, plenty for training per notification type and segment.

Evaluating uplift models. Accuracy on observed outcomes is meaningless because the quantity of interest is never observed for one person. Instead, on held-out randomised data, sort users by predicted uplift and plot the Qini curve: as you target the top 10%, 20%, … the cumulative difference between treated and control outcomes, compared with the straight line of random targeting. A good model's curve rises steeply at first (it finds the persuadables) and may bend down at the end (the sleeping dogs).

6 · Deep dive: fatigue, channel value and volume

Diminishing returns. The first push of the day to a user is the most valuable; each additional one adds less (the user is already engaged, or starts to tune notifications out) and costs more (the chance they disable notifications rises with daily volume). Model this with features for notifications received in the last 24 hours and 7 days, and opens among them, in both the uplift and the disable models.

A worked value curve. For a typical weekly user, suppose the k-th ranked push of the day has these predicted effects, with $0.20 per incremental visit and $4 of push channel value:

k-th push todayUplift (visits)Visit valuep(disable)Channel costNetClicks
10.100$0.0200.05%$0.002+$0.0180.12
20.060$0.0120.10%$0.004+$0.0080.10
30.035$0.0070.15%$0.006+$0.0010.09
40.020$0.0040.20%$0.008−$0.0040.08
50.012$0.00240.25%$0.010−$0.00760.07

The optimum is three pushes a day for this user: the fourth earns less in visits than it costs in expected channel loss. Notice the last column: clicks keep coming at 7 to 12% per push, so a team measuring notification clicks sees every additional push as a win. This is the core argument for the site-wide objective and the channel-value term.

Volume as a constraint with a shadow price. Across all users and candidates, the optimisation is: maximise total net value subject to each user's expected volume not exceeding a limit (and global constraints such as complaint rate). Turning each constraint into a price, the Lagrangian, gives a simple per-candidate rule: send if net value exceeds the user's threshold λ. λ is found so that expected sends meet the constraint, and it is personalised: high for a user who already receives many valuable candidates, low for a user with few. LinkedIn's email volume optimisation used this structure, with dual multipliers personalised per member so each member's "diet" contained the emails they valued most. A hard cap per user and channel stays as a backstop against model errors, and a minimum spacing between pushes (for example 30 minutes) prevents bursts.

Across teams. All notification types compete in one ranking under one λ. A team cannot buy volume by sending more candidates; it gets volume by producing candidates with higher incremental value. Transactional types are outside the budget. This is the organisational purpose of the system as much as the technical one.

7 · Deep dive: send time, channels and aggregation

Urgency classes. Transactional (password reset, payment, security alert) and urgent (a direct message from a close contact) are sent immediately. Ranked notifications may be delayed within their expiry. Digest-only items (weekly summaries, low-value recommendations) are never sent alone.

Timing. For a delayable candidate, the system predicts the uplift of sending at each hour in the next 24, using the user's activity pattern by hour and day, past responses by hour, and time since their last visit, then picks the best hour that is outside quiet hours and before expiry. The trap is the naive version, sending at the user's most active hour: a notification at 21:00 to someone who opens the app at 21:00 every night has little uplift, because they would have seen it anyway. Better hours are often just before the user's usual visit (to pull it forward) or at times when they are reachable but not habitually present. Time zones and travel matter: quiet hours use the device's current time zone.

Aggregation. Delaying creates the opportunity to combine. Candidates with the same aggregation key (comments on one post, likes on one photo) wait in a pending digest; when the scheduled time arrives, one notification summarises them. A busy creator who would get forty like-notifications an evening gets two. Aggregation also lowers volume against λ, letting more distinct valuable notifications through.

Channel choice. The same candidate has different value per channel: push interrupts and has high uplift and high disable risk; email has lower uplift, lower interruption, and unsubscribe risk per email type; in-app only (a badge and an inbox entry) costs nothing in channel risk but has uplift only when the user opens the app. The system scores each candidate per channel and picks the best net value, so some notifications become in-app only for users near their push limit.

8 · Evaluation plan

Offline. On the randomised holdback data: Qini curves and their area for uplift models per type and segment, calibration of uplift in bins, calibration of p(disable), and a policy simulation estimating net value and volume under a proposed λ (with inverse propensity weighting where the logging policy was not random).

Online. A/B tests with the user as the unit and site-wide primary metrics: weekly active users and sessions from all sources. Guardrails: push-disable rate, email unsubscribes and spam reports, app uninstalls, notification volume per user, and latency of urgent notifications. Results are reported by user segment (new, daily, weekly, dormant), because policies that help dormant users can annoy daily ones.

Holdouts. A long-term holdout (about 1% of users kept on the previous policy for six months) measures slow effects: channel attrition, habituation, retention. Per-type holdouts (a small share of users who never receive a given type) measure each type's total incremental value, which is how a team learns whether its notification is worth its share of attention. LinkedIn's random-drop bucket, which received about half of generated emails, is an example: it measured the true cost of volume reduction (2.6% fewer page views) against the benefit (send-all had 45% more negative responses).

9 · Policy, consent and the legal layer

Marketing messages are regulated in many jurisdictions: email marketing usually requires consent or an existing relationship plus a working unsubscribe link, and SMS marketing typically requires explicit opt-in. The system therefore tags every notification type with a legal category (transactional, service, marketing) and checks per-user consent records for the category and channel before ranking, as a hard filter rather than a model input. Unsubscribe links are per type, and an unsubscribe propagates within minutes, including to items already waiting in the delay queue, which is why the scheduler re-checks eligibility at send time. Quiet hours also have legal force in some places for marketing calls and messages. Treating these as configuration owned by a policy team, versioned and audited, keeps them out of model experiments where a ranking change could accidentally relax them.
