Delayed urgent messageUsers miss messagesUrgency classes bypass ranking; latency alert
Stale notification"New comment" on a post already readRe-check relevance at send time
Quiet-hours breachNight-time pushes, complaintsDevice time zone, hard filter at delivery

The trade-offs to name: short-term visits against long-term channel health; immediacy against aggregation; central control against team autonomy; exploration (random holdback, which withholds some valuable notifications) against immediate value; and personalisation of timing against predictability users may prefer.

11 · What changes at 10× scale

At 3 billion users and 60 billion candidates a day, scoring becomes a large streaming system partitioned by user, and feature fetches dominate cost, so per-user batching and caching of user state matter. The delay queue holds hundreds of millions of items, so time-bucketed storage with efficient re-check is critical. Push providers' rate limits and regional delivery capacity become planning inputs. And the optimisation moves toward sequential decision-making: treating the user's notification history as a state and each decision as an action with long-term reward, as in LinkedIn's work framing notifications as a Markov decision process trained with offline reinforcement learning.
deep:
Why sequential decisions beat one-shot scoring

The one-shot model scores each notification as if it were independent, but today's send changes tomorrow's response: a user who was notified three times today is less responsive tomorrow, and a user re-engaged today generates organic visits next week. Framing notifications as a Markov decision process (state: the user's recent notifications and activity; action: send or not; reward: visits minus penalties, over time) lets a policy optimise long-run value. Learning such a policy from logs is offline reinforcement learning, which must guard against overestimating actions the logging policy rarely took; Prabhakar et al. used conservative Q-learning for this in a notification system. In an interview, the point is the reason: notifications have delayed effects one-shot models cannot see.

Estimating channel value honestly

The $4 channel value in this lesson is the most important and least certain number in the system. Comparing users with push enabled and disabled is biased (people who disable are different), so better estimates come from natural experiments, such as users whose operating system changed default permissions, or from the long-term holdout's effect of volume on later activity. Because the value drives how aggressive the system is, teams often use a conservative estimate and revisit it yearly, and they segment it: a channel matters more for an occasional user than for one who opens the app daily anyway.

Permission is the first and largest decision

On iOS an app must ask permission before sending push notifications, and a user who declines is hard to win back, since the setting then lives in system settings. The system therefore treats the permission prompt as a decision too: ask after the user has seen a reason (a message they want to know about), not at first launch, and measure opt-in rate as a top-level metric. Every policy that burns trust shows up eventually in new users' opt-in rates, which is a leading indicator for channel value.

Negative-uplift detection

Some notifications hurt: a "you haven't posted in a while" reminder can make a lapsing user feel nagged and uninstall. Uplift models that include negative outcomes (disables, uninstalls, long-term activity) can predict negative uplift for some segments, and the policy must be able to withhold a notification type from them entirely. These users are where the response model fails worst, since they still click sometimes.

Interaction with in-app surfaces

A notification about a new comment is less valuable if the user will see it in the app's activity tab in an hour, and the in-app badge count itself is a notification. The ranking system should know what the user will see in the app (pending activity items, feed content) so it does not send what the app would show anyway, and badge counts should reflect ranked, de-duplicated items rather than every event, or the badge becomes noise users learn to ignore.

Fairness between notification types and creators

Central ranking can starve some types (an events team whose notifications have modest uplift for most users) and some creators (small accounts whose followers get their posts' notifications less often than large accounts'). Both may matter for the product's long-term health: creators who get no engagement leave. Minimum exposure rules for new creators, per-type exploration, and measuring the creator-side effect of notifications in holdouts keep the optimiser from narrowing the product to what is easiest to measure.

Exploration costs real value, so spend it carefully

The random holdback that makes uplift estimation possible withholds notifications the system believes are valuable. At 3% of 6 billion candidates, that is 180 million withheld a day; if the average withheld candidate had a net value of $0.005, the holdback costs about $900 a day, around $330,000 a year. That is a reasonable price for unbiased training data, but it argues for targeting exploration where it is most informative: per type and segment, hold back more where the uplift estimate is uncertain or the policy is about to change, and less where estimates are stable. The holdback must still be random within each stratum, and every withheld candidate must be logged with its stratum's holdback probability, so estimates can be reweighted correctly.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The quarter of rising CTR and falling users. A team switched to a response model and sent to users with the highest predicted click probability. Notification CTR rose 30%; weekly active users did not move; push disables among daily users rose. The model had moved notifications from lapsing users (low response, high uplift) to daily users (high response, no uplift). The fix was the random holdback and an uplift model, with site-wide actives as the decision metric.

The digest that never closed. An aggregation bug kept extending a digest's send time whenever a new like arrived, so popular creators received their "likes" notification only after activity died down, hours late. Digests now have a maximum delay from the first item, after which they send regardless.

The time-zone storm. Quiet hours were computed from the account's registered time zone. A user travelling across eight time zones received pushes at 3 a.m.; at scale, travel season produced a wave of complaints. Quiet hours now use the device's current time zone, reported with each session.

LinkedIn's email volume, measured. LinkedIn's engineering team published how it approached email volume in 2016. Their random-drop experiment sent about half of generated emails to one bucket and all of them to another: compared with sending everything, the half-volume bucket had 2.6% fewer total page views (with drops of 1.4% on the homepage to 4.5% on profiles and People You May Know), while the send-all bucket produced 45% more negative responses, meaning unsubscribes and spam reports, the latter capable of getting all of a sender's mail filtered by email providers. They first formulated volume optimisation as minimising emails subject to keeping email-driven sessions above a target and complaints below a tolerance, with a send rule comparing expected positive and weighted negative outcomes. Then they changed the objective to site-wide weekly active users, because their data showed many daily-active members were active regardless of email, and solved it with per-member dual multipliers. The send ratio for daily-active members fell from 0.76 to 0.22, weekly-active from 0.75 to 0.61, monthly-active stayed about the same (0.67 to 0.66), and dormant members rose from 0.32 to 0.40: the uplift logic of this lesson, visible in a production system. Pinterest published a similar budgeting approach for notifications (Zhao et al., KDD 2018), predicting a user's utility and allocating a weekly volume budget per user.

What to monitor

Monitoring must show both sides of every decision, the visits a notification earned and the channels it cost, per type and segment, so no team reads only its own clicks. Per type and segment: candidates, sends, send ratio, opens, incremental visits from holdback comparisons, disables, unsubscribes, spam reports, uninstalls; per user distribution of daily volume; λ distribution; urgent-notification latency; delay-queue depth and lateness; quiet-hour violations (should be zero); opt-in rate for new users; site-wide actives in the long-term holdout versus the rest.

Knobs people tune

Holdback share; channel value per segment; volume limits and caps per channel; minimum spacing; λ targets; aggregation windows and maximum delays; quiet hours defaults; urgency classification of types; exploration per type.
myths: Send to the users most likely to click.

The users most likely to click are often the ones who would have opened the app anyway. A response model ranks them first and claims credit for visits that would have happened regardless. An uplift model ranks by the difference a notification makes: probability of a visit if sent minus probability if not sent. LinkedIn moved from an email-attributed metric to site-wide activity for this reason, and its send ratio for daily-active members fell from 0.76 to 0.22 while sends to dormant members rose.
Notification click-through rate (CTR) is the success metric.

CTR rises when you send fewer, better notifications and falls when you send more, and it ignores what happens to everything else. The metrics that matter are site-wide: active users and sessions from all sources, against guardrails for disabled push, unsubscribes, spam reports and uninstalls. A team optimising its own notification's CTR can steal attention from other teams' notifications without the product gaining anything.
More notifications always mean more engagement, at least short-term.

Usually true in the short term: LinkedIn found that cutting email volume roughly in half at random reduced total page views by 2.6%. But sending everything produced 45% more negative responses (unsubscribes and spam reports), and a disabled push channel or an unsubscribed email type is lost for all future sends. Short-term gains are paid for with a channel's future value.
Volume caps are a crude safety net.

A fixed cap per user is crude. The principled version is a constraint solved with a shadow price: each send must earn more than a per-user threshold λ, which rises for users already receiving many notifications. Caps are then a backstop on top of an optimiser that already stops when the next notification's value is below its cost.
Send-time optimisation means sending at the user's most active hour.

Sending when the user is most active can mean notifying someone who was about to open the app anyway. Timing should maximise the notification's incremental effect while respecting urgency (messages now), quiet hours, time zones, and aggregation, since delaying a like notification a few hours lets it be combined with four others into one digest.
A/B tests of notification changes measure their long-term effect.

Two-week tests capture the immediate visit boost but not the slow accumulation of disabled channels, habituation (users learning to ignore notifications), or the long-run value of a habit formed. Long-term holdouts, where a small share of users keep the old policy or receive no notifications of a type for months, are how teams measure those effects.
lab:
Goal: see why uplift targeting beats response targeting at the same volume, and find the optimal daily push count from a value curve. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as notify_lab.py and run python notify_lab.py.
  2. Block 1 simulates 100,000 users in three segments (daily, weekly, lapsing) with different visit probabilities with and without a notification. Read incremental visits for random, response-model and uplift-model targeting at the same budget of 20,000 sends.
  3. Note the response-model targeting's high click rate and low incremental visits.
  4. Block 2 computes the net value of the k-th push of the day and prints the optimum k. Change CHANNEL_VALUE to $1 and $10 and watch the optimum move.
  5. Block 3 runs a randomised holdback of 3% and estimates the uplift per segment from it, to show the estimates are noisy but unbiased.
"""Uplift vs response targeting, the value curve, and a random holdback. Python 3.12, stdlib only."""
import random

rng = random.Random(11)
SEGMENTS = {  # share, p(visit | not sent), p(visit | sent)
    "daily":   (0.30, 0.90, 0.92),
    "weekly":  (0.45, 0.30, 0.38),
    "lapsing": (0.25, 0.05, 0.15)}
users = []
for _ in range(100_000):
    r, acc = rng.random(), 0.0
    for seg, (share, p0, p1) in SEGMENTS.items():
        acc += share
        if r < acc:
            jitter = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2)
            users.append((seg, min(1, p0 * jitter), min(1, p1 * jitter))); break

BUDGET = 20_000
def evaluate(order):
    chosen = set(order[:BUDGET])
    visits_sent = sum(p1 for i, (_, p0, p1) in enumerate(users) if i in chosen)
    visits_base = sum(p0 for i, (_, p0, p1) in enumerate(users) if i in chosen)
    return visits_sent - visits_base, visits_sent / BUDGET
idx = list(range(len(users)))
for name, key in [("random", lambda i: rng.random()),
                  ("response", lambda i: -users[i][2]),           # p(visit | sent)
                  ("uplift", lambda i: -(users[i][2] - users[i][1]))]:
    inc, resp = evaluate(sorted(idx, key=key))
    print(f"{name:9} incremental visits {inc:7.0f}   'response rate' {resp:.2f}")

VISIT_VALUE, CHANNEL_VALUE = 0.20, 4.0
uplift_k = [0.100, 0.060, 0.035, 0.020, 0.012, 0.007]
best, total = 0, 0.0
print("\nk  uplift  p_disable  net")
for k, u in enumerate(uplift_k, start=1):
    p_dis = 0.0005 * k
    net = u * VISIT_VALUE - p_dis * CHANNEL_VALUE
    print(f"{k}  {u:.3f}   {p_dis:.4f}   {net:+.4f}")
    if net > 0: best, total = k, total + net
print(f"optimal pushes/day: {best}, net value/user/day ${total:.4f}")

print("\nuplift estimated from a 3% random holdback:")
for seg in SEGMENTS:
    sent = ctrl = vs = vc = 0
    for s, p0, p1 in users:
        if s != seg: continue
        if rng.random() < 0.03: ctrl += 1; vc += rng.random() < p0
        else: sent += 1; vs += rng.random() < p1
    print(f"  {seg:8} estimated {vs / sent - vc / ctrl:+.3f}  (controls: {ctrl})")

What to look for: the response model with the highest "response rate" (it picks daily users) and the lowest incremental visits; the uplift model picking lapsing and weekly users with far more incremental visits than either; an optimum of three pushes a day at a $4 channel value, more at $1 and fewer at $10; and holdback estimates near the true segment uplifts (2, 8 and 10 points) but with visible noise in the smaller segments, which is why holdbacks run continuously and aggregate over days.
recap: A notification system decides for each candidate event whether to send it, to whom, on which channel and when, under per-user volume limits, with the goal of long-term engagement rather than notification clicks.
At 300 million users and about 20 candidates per user a day, 6 billion candidates are scored daily, about 70,000 a second on average, and roughly 600 million are sent.
A response model estimates p(visit | sent); an uplift model estimates p(visit | sent) − p(visit | not sent), the incremental effect, which is what deserves credit.

In the worked example, a daily-active user with 92% versus 90% visit probability has an uplift of 2 points, while a lapsing user with 15% versus 5% has 10 points; a response model sends to the first, an uplift model to the second.
Uplift models need randomised data, so a small share of candidate notifications is withheld at random to provide a control group, and models are evaluated with uplift (Qini) curves on that data.
Each send also risks losing the channel: if p(disable) is 0.05% per send and an enabled push channel is worth $4 of future value, every push costs about $0.002 in expected channel loss.

Volume is set where the next notification's incremental value no longer exceeds its cost; with the lesson's numbers that is about three pushes a day for a typical user, while clicks keep rising with volume.
Per-user volume constraints are solved with a shadow price λ: send only items whose net value exceeds λ, with λ personalised, as LinkedIn's email volume optimisation did with per-member multipliers.
Send-time optimisation predicts when a notification will have the most incremental effect, respects urgency, quiet hours and time zones, and aggregates delayable notifications into digests.

LinkedIn's random-drop experiment found halving email cost 2.6% of page views while sending everything caused 45% more complaints; moving to a site-wide active-users objective cut sends to daily-active members sharply and raised them for dormant ones.
glossary: Combining several related notifications into one, such as "5 people liked your photo", usually by delaying the first ones briefly.
A way to reach a user: push notification, email, SMS, in-app badge or inbox.
The expected future value of being able to reach a user on a channel; lost when they disable push or unsubscribe.
Declining response and rising annoyance as a user receives more notifications.
A group of users deliberately kept from a treatment (a notification type, or a new policy) to measure its effect, often for months.
A way to solve an optimisation with a constraint by turning the constraint into a price: here, the minimum net value a notification must have to be sent.
A user who will act only if notified; the group uplift modelling tries to find.
An evaluation curve for uplift models: cumulative incremental outcomes as you target more users in model order, compared with random targeting.
Times (often night in the user's time zone) when non-urgent notifications are not delivered.
A model of the probability that a user acts after receiving a notification, without asking whether they would have acted anyway.
A user for whom a notification makes things worse, for example prompting them to disable notifications or churn.
Short message service: text messages to a phone number; costly per message and tightly regulated for marketing.
A user who will act whether notified or not; notifying them adds nothing.
The difference a treatment makes: probability of the outcome if treated minus probability if not treated, for the same user.
drill:
Work it out

A notification type is sent to 50 million users a week. Its A/B test showed +1.2% notification-attributed sessions. The randomised holdback shows visit probability within 24 hours of 0.41 when sent and 0.395 when held back. Push-disable probability per send is 0.03%, push channel value $4, and an incremental visit is worth $0.20. (a) What is the incremental value per send? (b) The expected channel cost per send? (c) Should it keep its share of the budget?

Answer

(a) Uplift = 0.41 − 0.395 = 0.015 visits per send × $0.20 = $0.003.

(b) 0.0003 × $4 = $0.0012.

(c) Net $0.0018 per send, positive but small: about $90,000 a week across 50 million sends. Whether it keeps its budget depends on λ: if other types' marginal candidates earn more than $0.0018 net, this type should yield to them for users near their limits. The attributed-sessions result is irrelevant: most of those sessions would have happened (39.5% visit anyway). Recommend making it digest-only or in-app-only for users already near their push limit, and checking per segment, since its uplift is probably concentrated in less active users.

Diagnose it

Two months after launching send-time optimisation, weekly actives in the treatment group are flat, notification opens are up 15%, and the share of pushes sent between 20:00 and 22:00 has risen from 25% to 60%. What went wrong?

Answer

The send-time model is probably optimising opens (a response measure) and has learned to send when users are already in the app or about to open it, the evening peak. Opens rise because users were going to look anyway; incremental visits do not. Concentrating pushes in two hours also competes with the user's own habit and with other notifications. Check uplift by send hour on holdback data: compare visit rates of held-back candidates whose chosen hour was 21:00 with sent ones. Fix: train the timing model on uplift by hour from randomised timing (randomly assign a share of delayable candidates to hours), cap the share of a user's notifications in any one hour, and evaluate on site-wide actives, not opens.
qa: E
What decisions does a notification ranking system make?

For each candidate event (a message, a like, a recommendation, a reminder), whether to send it at all, on which channel (push, email, in-app only), at what time, possibly combined with others into a digest, subject to user preferences, quiet hours, legal rules and volume limits. Each decision is made per user, because the same notification can help one user and annoy another.
E
Why is notification CTR a bad primary metric?

Because it can rise while the product gets worse: sending fewer notifications to only the keenest users raises CTR, and sending many raises clicks while lowering CTR and burning channels. It also only counts clicks on the notification, not whether the user would have come anyway or what happened to other surfaces. Site-wide active users or sessions with guardrails on disables and unsubscribes measure what matters.
E
Which notifications should bypass ranking?

Transactional and safety-critical ones the user expects immediately and would be harmed by missing: direct messages they opted into, security alerts, password resets, order and payment confirmations, and legally required notices. These go through delivery directly, still respecting channel preferences, and do not count against the ranked budget, or count separately.
M
Explain uplift versus response modelling with an example.

A response model ranks by p(visit | sent). A daily-active user might have 0.92 with a notification and 0.90 without; a lapsing user 0.15 and 0.05. The response model prefers the daily user (0.92 > 0.15), but the notification adds only 2 points of visit probability there and 10 points for the lapsing user. An uplift model estimates the difference and sends to the lapsing user. With a limited budget, ranking by uplift produces more incremental visits.

Follow-up: How do you train an uplift model? — On randomised data where some eligible notifications were withheld at random, either with two models (sent and not sent) whose predictions are subtracted, or one model with the treatment as a feature, evaluated with Qini or uplift curves on held-out randomised data.
M
How do you account for users disabling notifications?

Predict p(disable or unsubscribe | send) per notification from features such as recent volume, past dismissals and notification type, and multiply by the channel's value, the expected future value of being able to reach this user, estimated from what enabled users generate over the coming months. Subtract that expected loss from the send's value. With p(disable) 0.05% and channel value $4, each push costs $0.002, comparable to the value of a low-uplift notification.
M
How would you implement per-user volume limits?

As an optimisation: maximise total net value subject to each user's expected daily or weekly volume limit. The Lagrangian form gives each user a threshold λ: send a candidate only if its net value exceeds λ. λ is found per user (or per segment) so that the expected volume meets the limit, and it rises as a user's day fills up. Hard caps per channel remain as a backstop for model errors.
M
Design send-time optimisation.

Classify each candidate's urgency: immediate (messages, security), same-day, or flexible. For non-immediate ones, predict for each hour in the next day the incremental effect of a notification at that hour from the user's activity pattern and past responses, excluding quiet hours in their time zone, and schedule the send in a delay queue at the best hour. Before sending, re-check that the event is still relevant (the user may have already seen it in the app) and merge it with similar pending items into a digest.
M
Estimate the scoring and delivery load.

300 million users with about 20 candidates each a day is 6 billion candidates, about 70,000 scorings a second on average and perhaps 200,000 at peak; with a gradient-boosted or small neural model at tens of microseconds each, a few hundred CPU cores. About 600 million sends a day, with evening peaks around 50,000 pushes a second, go through the delivery service to push providers and email; the scheduler holds a few hundred million delayed items at any time.
H
Why do you need holdouts, and how would you design them?

Notification effects accumulate over months: habit formation, habituation, disabled channels, and the long-run value of re-engaged users. Short A/B tests see the immediate visit boost and miss those. Keep a long-term holdout (for example 1% of users on the previous policy for six months, and a small no-notification holdout per notification type) and compare active days, retention and channel status. Holdouts are costly because those users get a worse or different product, so they are small and rotated.
H
Two teams each own a notification type and each shows a positive A/B test. Together they hurt engagement. Why?

Each test measured its own notification's effect with everything else fixed, but the notifications compete for the same user attention and the same volume budget. Adding team A's notifications causes users to ignore or disable notifications in general, which hurts team B's too, and some of A's credited visits would have come from B's notifications. The fix is a central ranking and budget across types, a shared site-wide objective, and experiments measured on site-wide metrics with all notification types in place.

Follow-up: How do you allocate the budget between types? — By value: all candidates compete on net incremental value per send under one per-user threshold, so the budget goes where it does most good, with minimum guarantees only for transactional types.
H
How do you evaluate an uplift model offline?

Only on randomised data, because otherwise you never observe what would have happened without the notification. Score users in the randomised set, sort by predicted uplift, and plot the Qini curve: cumulative difference between treated and control outcomes as you target more users in model order, against the diagonal for random targeting. The area between them (AUUC or Qini coefficient) compares models. Check calibration of the uplift in bins, since the send rule subtracts costs from it.
H
What did LinkedIn learn about email volume?

In a random-drop experiment sending about half of generated emails, total page views fell 2.6% compared with sending all, while the send-all group had 45% more negative responses (unsubscribes and spam reports). Optimising first for email-attributed sessions under a complaint constraint, they then switched to site-wide weekly active users as the objective, because many daily-active members are active without email. The new policy sent to daily-active members far less (send ratio 0.76 to 0.22) and to dormant members more (0.32 to 0.40).

t: Design ETA prediction for a delivery and ride-hailing marketplace

prereq: cd5
A ride-hailing service keeps a live index of moving drivers, matches riders to nearby drivers by ETA, and prices trips; all of it consumes ETAs.
cd11
Maps routing runs shortest-path searches over a road graph of segments with travel-time weights, sped up by preprocessing such as contraction hierarchies, with traffic-aware weights.
ml5
Loss functions decide what a model predicts: squared error gives the mean, absolute error the median, pinball loss a chosen quantile.
hd8
A feature store serves the same feature definitions offline for training and online at low latency, with point-in-time correctness.
in9
Real-time aggregation counts and averages events in streaming windows and serves the results with low latency.

why:
A customer opens a food-delivery app at 19:05 and sees "arrives 19:35–19:45". A rider requests a car and sees "driver arriving in 4 minutes". Behind those two numbers, the marketplace has made dozens of decisions that all depended on predicted travel times: which of twenty nearby drivers to send, whether to batch two orders on one courier, what price to quote for the trip, when to tell the restaurant to start cooking. The ETA, estimated time of arrival, is the quiet number underneath the whole business.

When it is wrong, the damage spreads. If pickup ETAs are optimistic, riders wait longer than promised and cancel. If delivery promises are set at the average time, a large share of orders arrive late, because trips that go wrong go very wrong, and late food generates refunds and lost customers. If the ETA used for pricing is biased in one city at Friday rush hour, fares are wrong there all evening. If dispatch compares drivers with noisy ETAs, it sends the wrong driver often enough to waste thousands of driver-hours a week. And the predictions are needed fast and often: every app refresh, every candidate driver in every matching round, every price quote. At a large company this is one of the highest-volume models in production; Uber has described its ETA model as its highest-QPS model.

The senior design question is to build the ETA system: combine a routing engine's physics-like estimate with a machine-learned correction, feed it real-time traffic, decide what to predict for each use (mean, median or a quantile), serve it at hundreds of thousands of predictions a second within a few milliseconds, evaluate it where decisions are made (by city, hour and trip type), and understand how the predictions feed back into dispatch, pricing and the data itself. Routing and the ride-hailing marketplace are covered in cd11 and cd5; this case is the prediction system that sits between them.

The lesson follows the interview: requirements and targets; estimates for prediction volume, GPS traffic, labels and the latency budget; the API and data; the architecture; deep dives on the routing-plus-residual design and real-time traffic, segment versus trip models, the choice of loss and target with MAE and quantile loss worked by hand, and fast serving; the evaluation plan by city and time with switchback tests; feedback effects including the winner's curse; failure modes; and ten times the scale. The real case is Uber's DeepETA, described in an engineering post and a paper.
primer:
What an ETA is made of

A trip's duration is the sum of several legs, each predicted separately: the driver's or courier's travel to the pickup point, the wait at pickup (finding the rider, a restaurant preparing food), the travel from pickup to drop-off, and the last stretch on foot (parking, finding the building, the lift). The travel legs are where maps help: a routing engine represents roads as a graph of road segments (stretches between intersections), each with a traversal time from current or typical speeds, finds the best path and adds up the times (cd11). The other legs, and the routing engine's systematic errors, are where machine learning helps.

The mental model: an experienced dispatcher correcting the map

Picture an old taxi dispatcher with a map and a radio. The map says the airport is 25 minutes away. The dispatcher knows better: at 17:30 on a Friday the bridge backs up, pickups at the terminal take an extra five minutes to find the passenger, and drivers coming from the north always take the ring road, which the map does not prefer. The dispatcher starts from the map's number and corrects it from experience. When a customer asks "when will it get here?", the dispatcher gives a time they are fairly sure about, not the average, because a broken promise is worse than a cautious one.

That is the design: the routing engine is the map, with live traffic painted on it; the residual model is the dispatcher's experience, learned from millions of completed trips; the choice of quantile is the dispatcher's caution, set differently for different listeners. The analogy breaks on speed and scale. The dispatcher answers a few calls an hour; the system answers hundreds of thousands of questions a second, most of them asked by other software (dispatch comparing drivers, pricing quoting fares), within a few milliseconds each.

One service, several answers

Different consumers need different numbers from the same prediction, which is the most important idea to bring into the interview early. Dispatch needs an unbiased expected pickup time to compare drivers; pricing needs a mean trip time robust to rare disasters; a customer promise needs a time that will be met nine times out of ten. So the ETA service returns a small distribution (for example the mean and the 50th and 90th percentiles) and each consumer uses the one that matches its costs.

A reader who stops here has the shape: live traffic from GPS into a routing engine; a residual model that corrects the engine's ETA with learned experience; several targets for several consumers; and a feedback loop from decisions to data that the evaluation must respect.

1 · Requirements

Functional. Predict durations for each leg type (driver to pickup, pickup wait, pickup to drop-off, courier to restaurant, restaurant to door) for rides and deliveries in every city served; accept single requests and many-to-many batches (all candidate drivers to one rider); return the mean and selected quantiles, plus the route used; support a fallback answer if the model is unavailable. Out of scope, said aloud: the routing engine's internals (cd11), the dispatch optimiser (cd5) and restaurant preparation-time prediction, which is a separate model this service consumes.

Accuracy targets. MAE improvement over the engine-only ETA in every city with enough trips, with no city, hour-of-week band or trip type getting worse; absolute bias below 30 seconds per city and hour band; P90 coverage between 88% and 92% per city and trip type.

Latency and throughput. ETA service p99 under 50 ms including the routing query; model inference p99 under 5 ms; 300,000 predictions a second at peak, with linear horizontal scaling.

Availability. 99.99%: dispatch stops without ETAs. If the model fails, the service returns the engine ETA with a historical correction table, flagged as degraded.

Freshness. Live traffic reflected in routes within 2 minutes of a slowdown; models retrained at least weekly and validated per city before deployment.

Clarifying questions. "Which consumers, and what does each lose from early versus late errors?" "Rides, deliveries or both, in how many cities?" "Do we own the routing engine?" "What latency does dispatch need for a batch of 50 candidates?" "Which signals exist: GPS frequency, restaurant prep times, building data?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Trips and labels. 20 million trips a day across rides and deliveries. Each produces two or three legs with observed durations: about 50 million labels a day. Eight weeks of training data is about 2.8 billion rows; a feature row of a few hundred bytes makes that roughly 1 TB, ordinary for a distributed training job.

Prediction volume. Dispatch dominates. Each ride request considers about 20 candidate drivers over about 3 matching rounds (re-dispatch when a driver declines): 60 pickup ETAs per trip, 1.2 billion a day. Add trip ETAs for price quotes (many quotes do not convert), app refreshes of pickup and arrival times, and delivery planning: roughly 2 billion predictions a day, about 23,000 a second on average. Demand peaks around meals and commutes, and batched matching computes many-to-many matrices in bursts, so plan for about 300,000 a second at peak.

Model compute. If one prediction costs about 50 microseconds of CPU (mostly embedding lookups and a shallow network, batched), 300,000 a second is 15 CPU-seconds per second: about 15 cores of pure inference, perhaps 100 with feature assembly, serialisation and headroom. Cheap. The constraint is latency, not cost: the model must answer inside the dispatch request's budget without a GPU round trip.

Traffic stream. With 1 million drivers and couriers online at peak sending a GPS point every 4 seconds, about 250,000 pings a second flow into map matching. A road graph of about 100 million segments worldwide has live observations on a few million at any moment; speeds are averaged per segment in 1 to 5-minute windows and written to the traffic store, roughly a few million updates a minute.

The latency budget. Shown below: the routing query is the largest piece; the model gets a small, fixed slice.

The insight to say out loud. ETA prediction is cheap per call and called constantly; the engineering is in the latency budget and in serving many targets from one model, and the science is in choosing the right target for each consumer and evaluating where decisions are made.

3 · API and data

POST /v1/eta/batch
{ "leg": "driver_to_pickup", "line_of_business": "rides",
  "destination": {"lat": 40.7411, "lng": -73.9897},
  "origins": [{"id": "drv_1", "lat": ..., "lng": ...}, ... 20 more],
  "request_time": "2026-10-08T17:42:10Z",
  "targets": ["mean", "p50", "p90"] }
-> { "results": [{ "id": "drv_1", "engine_eta_s": 312, "mean_s": 348,
                    "p50_s": 335, "p90_s": 430, "route_id": "r_..." }, ...],
     "model": "deepeta@2026-10-06", "degraded": false }

Data. Road graph with segments, geometry, turn restrictions and historical speed profiles per segment by 15-minute slot of the week. Live traffic store: per segment, current speed, observation count, window end time. Trip logs: request time, origin, destination, leg type, route taken (map-matched), engine ETA and model predictions served at request time, the decision taken (which driver), and actual leg durations. Feature store (hd8): precomputed aggregates by geo cell and time slot (recent residual averages, pickup-wait statistics by location type), served online and reproduced point-in-time for training.

4 · High-level design

GPS pings stream through map matching into the traffic store. The routing engine answers path queries using live speeds where fresh and historical profiles elsewhere, producing a route and an engine ETA. The ETA service receives a request, issues the routing query (one-to-many for dispatch batches) and, in parallel, fetches features; it assembles one feature vector per origin, runs the residual model in-process for the batch, adds the predicted residuals to the engine ETAs, derives the requested targets, applies sanity bounds (no negative or absurd values; clamping) and returns. A fallback path returns engine ETA plus a correction from a table of average residuals by city, hour and leg type if the model or feature fetch times out. Offline, completed trips become labelled rows joined point-in-time with the features and the engine ETA served at request time; a training pipeline retrains on a rolling window, validates per city, hour band and leg type against the current model, and deploys through a canary.

Walk one request. A rider at 17:42 on a Thursday in a dense city requests a car. Dispatch sends one batch: 20 candidate drivers to the rider's location. The routing engine computes 20 routes in about 20 ms; for driver 7 the engine ETA is 312 seconds. Features for driver 7: origin and destination grid cells at three resolutions, hour and day, engine ETA and route distance, share of the route with live traffic data (85%) and the live-to-historical speed ratio (0.8, slower than usual), pickup location type (a large office building, known for slow pickups), leg type. The model predicts a residual of +36 seconds for the mean and quantile offsets, so mean 348, P50 335, P90 430 seconds. Dispatch ranks drivers by the mean (with the winner's-curse correction discussed later), picks driver 7, and the app shows the rider "6 min", rounding a value between P50 and the mean upward, since being early is fine and being late is not.

5 · Deep dive: routing engine plus residual, and real-time traffic

Why a residual. The routing engine is a physical model: roads, distances, speeds, turn costs. It is excellent at what it models and blind to what it does not: time spent finding the rider at a busy entrance, the slow last 200 metres through a car park, local drivers' preferred routes that differ from the engine's best path, systematic speed biases on particular roads. Predicting the residual, actual duration minus engine ETA, focuses the model on exactly those gaps. Uber calls this ETA post-processing and notes a practical advantage: new data sources and business needs are easier to absorb in the post-processing model than by refactoring the routing engine. It also gives a safe fallback, since the engine's ETA alone is a reasonable answer.

Live traffic. GPS points are noisy (tens of metres in cities, worse between tall buildings), so map matching finds the most likely sequence of road segments a vehicle drove, typically with a hidden Markov model over candidate segments near each point. From matched traversals, the stream computes each segment's travel time and aggregates it per window. Freshness and coverage are the issues: a segment observed by 12 vehicles in the last 3 minutes has a reliable live speed; one observed once 20 minutes ago does not. The engine blends live speed and the historical profile for that time of week with weights from observation count and age. Features for the residual model summarise how much of the route relied on live data and how far live speeds deviate from history, so the model learns when to distrust the engine.

6 · Deep dive: segment-level versus trip-level models

A segment-level model predicts each segment's traversal time (from live speed, history, time, weather, events); the ETA is the sum along the route. Strengths: it generalises to any route, including ones never driven; it supports routing itself (the engine needs per-segment weights); and errors can be traced to roads. Weaknesses: per-segment errors accumulate over hundreds of segments (if they are correlated, as congestion is, they do not cancel); and it cannot see what happens between segments and at the ends: waiting at lights depends on the turn, pickups depend on the building, deliveries on parking. Google's work on ETAs in Google Maps sits in between, using a graph neural network over "supersegments" (sequences of adjacent segments) so the model sees neighbouring traffic, and reported reducing negative ETA outcomes by over 40% in Sydney.

A trip-level model predicts the whole leg's duration or residual from trip features: origin, destination, time, engine ETA, route summary, leg type. Strengths: one prediction per trip with no error accumulation; it captures end effects and systematic engine biases; and it can be trained to whatever target and loss a consumer needs. Weakness: it depends on the route the engine chose and on the trip being similar to training data. The production design is a hybrid: segment-level traffic inside the routing engine, trip-level residual on top. That split also fits the organisation: the maps team owns the engine and its speeds, the ETA team owns the residual model and its targets.

7 · Deep dive: choosing the target: MAE, MSE and quantile loss

The loss decides the number. Train a model with squared error (MSE) and it predicts the conditional mean; with absolute error (MAE) it predicts the median; with pinball loss at level τ it predicts the τ-quantile. Pinball loss charges τ for each minute of under-prediction and (1 − τ) for each minute of over-prediction; at τ = 0.9, being a minute too low costs nine times as much as being a minute too high, so the model shifts up until only about 10% of outcomes exceed its prediction.

A worked example. Ten deliveries between the same restaurant and neighbourhood at the same hour took 14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23, 26 and 36 minutes. The distribution is right-skewed, as trip times almost always are (there is a floor, the free-flow time, and no ceiling on things going wrong).

PredictionValueMinimisesLate if promisedMean absolute error
Mean21.0 minMSE3 of 10 (30%)4.4 min
Median19.5 minMAE5 of 10 (50%)4.2 min
P90 (pinball τ = 0.9)26 minpinball 0.91 of 10 (10%)7.0 min

Check the cells. The mean is 210 / 10 = 21 minutes; its absolute errors are 7, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 5 and 15, which sum to 44, so its MAE is 4.4 minutes. The median (any value between 19 and 20; take 19.5) has errors 5.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 3.5, 6.5 and 16.5, summing to 42, so MAE 4.2: the median wins on MAE, as theory says, and the mean wins on squared error. The P90 value, 26 minutes, has errors 12, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 3, 0 and 10, summing to 70, MAE 7.0: the worst on average, yet the only one of the three that keeps its promise nine times in ten.

Choosing the quantile for a promise. A higher promise is met more often but quoted times grow, and customers order less when told 45 minutes instead of 35. If each extra quoted minute loses, say, 1% of conversions, and a late order costs a refund or goodwill credit plus some churn, the best quantile minimises expected cost per order; it is usually somewhere between P80 and P95, set per market and order type. Showing a range ("19:35–19:45", for example P50 to P90) communicates uncertainty and lets the promise sit at the upper end without looking slow.

Serving several targets from one model. One network with several output heads (mean, P50, P90) trained jointly, or a mean head plus quantile offsets, shares the expensive representation and costs little extra latency. Quantile heads trained separately can cross (a P90 below the P50 for some inputs), so outputs are post-processed to be monotone, or the model predicts non-negative gaps between successive quantiles. DeepETA took a related route: a single parameterised asymmetric Huber loss whose two parameters control robustness to outliers and the relative cost of under- versus over-prediction, so the same architecture can produce a robust mean for fares or a late-averse estimate elsewhere.

8 · Deep dive: p99 latency at 300,000 predictions a second

Mostly lookups. The fastest model is one that looks things up instead of computing them. Discretise every input: continuous features into quantile buckets (DeepETA found quantile buckets beat equal-width ones), categorical features directly, and locations into grid cells at several resolutions. Map each to an embedding row. With feature hashing, many grid cells share a fixed number of rows; DeepETA hashed each cell with several independent hash functions so collisions in one table are undone by the others. A prediction is then a few dozen O(1) lookups plus a shallow network: DeepETA reports hundreds of millions of parameters with only about 0.25% touched per prediction.

Cheap interactions. Features interact (rush hour matters downtown, not in suburbs). Self-attention over feature embeddings captures pairwise interactions but costs O(K²·d) for K features of dimension d; linear attention costs O(K·d²). With K = 40 and d = 8: 12,800 versus 2,560 operations, which is why DeepETA used a linear transformer.

Serving mechanics. Run inference in-process in the ETA service (or a sidecar) on CPUs to avoid network hops; batch all candidates of a dispatch request in one call; keep embedding tables in memory (a few GB) on every instance; precompute features that do not depend on the request; set a hard timeout with the fallback table; and load-test at peak with realistic batch sizes, since p99 under load, not average latency on a quiet machine, is the requirement.

9 · Evaluation plan

Offline. On recent held-out trips (the most recent week, never shuffled in time), report per city, hour-of-week band, leg type and distance band: MAE, mean signed error (bias), and for quantile heads coverage (share of actuals at or below the P90) and interval width. A new model must beat the current one in aggregate with a paired comparison on the same trips and must not degrade any cell with enough data beyond a tolerance; the worst cells are reviewed by hand. Special-day slices (holidays, storms, big events) are tracked separately.

Online. ETAs drive dispatch and pricing for everyone in a city, so user-level A/B tests leak: the treatment's dispatch choices change which drivers are available to control riders. Marketplaces use switchback experiments: each city alternates between treatment and control in randomised time slices (say 30 to 60 minutes), and analysis accounts for carry-over between adjacent slices. Metrics: accuracy on completed trips; rider conversion after seeing the ETA; cancellations; actual pickup wait; on-time delivery rate against the promise; driver utilisation. Guardrails: latency, fallback rate, and fare accuracy.

10 · Feedback loops and the winner's curse

The winner's curse. Dispatch picks the driver with the lowest predicted pickup ETA among, say, 20. If each prediction has independent noise with a standard deviation of a minute, the smallest of 20 noisy predictions is typically the one whose noise was most negative: the expected minimum of 20 standard normal draws is about −1.87. So the chosen driver's predicted ETA is optimistic by almost two minutes on average, even if the model is unbiased over all drivers. Riders see "3 min" and wait five. Defences: evaluate and calibrate on chosen assignments (the ETA shown to the rider comes from a model or correction trained on them), add features describing the selection (number of candidates, gap to the runner-up), and use prediction uncertainty in dispatch so a confident 4-minute estimate can beat a noisy 3.5-minute one.

Decisions shape data. Trips only happen when dispatch, pricing and the customer say yes. Areas and times where ETAs are long see fewer trips (customers decline), so the data under-represents the hard cases. Couriers may drive differently against a displayed promise. Logging the served predictions and decisions with every label, exploring a little in dispatch where it is cheap, weighting training data for selection, and monitoring bias in sparse cells keep the loop from drifting.

The trade-offs to name: accuracy against latency; one global model against per-region models; promise conservatism against conversion; fresh live traffic against noisy sparse data; and model complexity against debuggability, since an ETA error must be explainable to an operations team within minutes.

12 · What changes at 10× scale

At ten times the cities and trips, a single global model with location embeddings and segment bias layers (as DeepETA adopted) scales better than thousands of per-city models, but evaluation and gating per city become a large automated system in themselves. The traffic pipeline grows to millions of pings a second and becomes regionally partitioned. Dispatch moves toward batched, many-to-many matching over larger windows, increasing peak ETA volume further and making batch inference efficiency the main cost lever. And new products (multi-stop deliveries, scheduled rides) need distributions over longer horizons, pushing the service toward predicting full duration distributions rather than a few points.
deep:
Labels are defined by the consumer

"Actual duration" is less obvious than it looks. Driver-to-pickup ends when the driver arrives or when the rider gets in? Delivery ends when the courier arrives at the building or at the door? A courier who waits at the restaurant because the food is not ready inflates "courier to restaurant" with preparation time. Each leg needs a precise, instrumented start and end event, and contaminated labels (a driver who stopped for fuel, a trip cancelled mid-way) need filters, or the model learns to predict noise. Label definitions are versioned with the model, because changing them changes what MAE means.

Calibrating quantiles per cell

A P90 head can be well calibrated globally and wrong locally: 95% coverage in one suburb, 80% in a downtown core at rush hour. Since promises are made per cell, coverage is monitored per city, hour band and order type, and a lightweight post-hoc correction (shifting the quantile per cell from recent coverage, conformal-style) fixes residual miscalibration between retrains. This is the same idea as recalibrating a classifier's probabilities, applied to a time.

Uncertainty is a feature for dispatch

A point ETA hides how sure the model is. Two drivers both predicted at 4 minutes are not equal if one is on a highway with steady traffic and the other must cross a congested bridge. Exposing a spread (P90 − P50) lets dispatch prefer reliable assignments when the rider has been waiting, and lets delivery batching avoid pairing an order with an uncertain leg. It also helps with the winner's curse: penalising uncertainty when choosing the minimum reduces how often noise wins.

Bias adjustment by segment

Different trip types have different error distributions: deliveries versus rides, pickups versus drop-offs, short versus long trips, and different regions. DeepETA added a segment bias adjustment layer in its decoder, which adjusts the raw prediction per segment of the data, and reported it worked better than simply adding segment features; they chose it over a full multi-task decoder for latency reasons. The general lesson is that cheap per-segment output corrections can capture systematic differences without growing the model.

Route choice is part of the error

The engine's ETA assumes the driver takes the engine's route; many do not. Experienced drivers avoid a junction the engine likes, or follow a different navigation app. A residual model learns the average effect but not per driver. Predicting the route actually taken (or the probability of alternatives) and feeding that into the ETA is a further step, valuable mainly where alternatives differ greatly in time, such as river crossings.

When the world changes overnight

A bridge closes for months, a city changes its speed limits, a stadium opens. Historical profiles and learned embeddings now describe a world that no longer exists for those segments and cells. The routing engine absorbs map changes quickly; the residual model may keep correcting for an old pattern. Monitoring bias per cell catches it, and the remedies are faster retraining with recent data weighted more heavily, and manual overrides for known events. Robust systems treat "the map changed here" as an input event that triggers re-evaluation.

One global model or many local ones

Per-city models are easy to reason about and can be tuned locally, but thousands of them multiply training, validation and deployment work, and small cities have too little data for a good model. A single global model shares what is common (rush-hour effects, pickup behaviour at airports) and lets small cities borrow strength from large ones, with location embeddings and per-segment bias layers capturing local differences. Its risk is coupling: a change that helps the largest markets, which dominate the loss, can hurt small ones. The usual answer is a global model with a per-city evaluation gate, loss weighting so small cities are not drowned out, and the ability to pin a city to the previous version while a regression is investigated. DeepETA's stated goal of one model for every line of business worldwide is this choice, made explicitly.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The optimistic pickup. After a dispatch change increased candidates per request from 10 to 30, riders' complaints about late pickups rose although model MAE on all predictions was unchanged. With more candidates, the winner's curse grew: the minimum of 30 noisy estimates is more optimistic than the minimum of 10. Calibrating the rider-facing ETA on chosen assignments, with the candidate count as a feature, removed most of the gap.

The concert night. On a stadium event night, pickups near the venue took 12 minutes longer than predicted for two hours; the global dashboard barely moved. Per-cell bias alerts now page operations when a cell's recent residual mean departs from prediction by more than a threshold, and event calendars feed features and temporary corrections.

The silent traffic outage. A map-matching job fell behind during a deployment; the traffic store served speeds 25 minutes old during evening rush. ETAs were short across a city; on-time delivery fell. The routing engine now treats live speeds older than a threshold as missing (falling back to history), and ingestion lag is an alert with a dashboard next to ETA bias.

The mean in the promise. A delivery team displayed the mean prediction as the promised time to make quotes look fast; late orders rose to about a third. Switching the promise to a calibrated P85 with a range lowered conversion slightly and refunds substantially, a net gain worked out with exactly the expected-cost reasoning in section 7.

What to monitor

Per city, hour band and leg type: MAE, bias, P90 coverage, interval width, share of predictions in fallback; dispatch-chosen bias versus all-candidate bias; traffic freshness and coverage; model latency percentiles under load; on-time rate against promises; rider and customer complaints about timing.

Knobs people tune

Quantile used for each promise type; promise rounding; live-versus-historical blending weights and freshness thresholds; per-cell bias corrections; retraining window and recency weighting; timeout and fallback thresholds; batch sizes; uncertainty penalty in dispatch.

The real case: Uber's DeepETA

Uber described DeepETA in an engineering post (February 2022) and a paper. Its routing engine computes ETAs as sums of segment traversal times along the best path using map data and real-time traffic; DeepETA predicts the residual between that ETA and observed outcomes, an approach Uber calls ETA post-processing, using spatial and temporal features, real-time traffic information and the type of request. Uber had used very large gradient-boosted tree ensembles for this and moved to deep learning to keep scaling, with three requirements: a few milliseconds of latency, significantly better MAE than the tree model, and one model for all lines of business worldwide. After testing seven architectures, they chose an encoder with self-attention over feature embeddings, made fast with a linear transformer; all inputs are discretised and embedded (continuous features in quantile buckets), locations are encoded at multiple grid resolutions with multiple feature hashing, and only about 0.25% of the model's hundreds of millions of parameters are touched per prediction. A decoder with segment bias adjustment handles differences between deliveries and rides, pickups and drop-offs, short and long trips and regions; an asymmetric Huber loss with parameters for outlier robustness and asymmetry lets the same model serve different point estimates, such as a mean for fares or a late-averse estimate elsewhere. Uber described it as its highest-QPS model, served through its Michelangelo platform behind the routing front end, with automatic retraining and validation. The design maps onto every section of this lesson, which is why it is the reference answer to "how would you build ETAs?".
myths: The best ETA is the most accurate average.

It depends on who uses it. Dispatch wants an unbiased estimate to compare drivers; pricing wants the mean with outliers controlled; a customer promise ("arrives by 7:40") wants a high quantile, because being late costs far more than being early. Trip times are right-skewed, so promising the mean makes a large share of orders late. One ETA service should serve several targets.
Machine learning replaces the routing engine.

The routing engine already knows the road network, turn restrictions and current traffic speeds; throwing that away makes the model relearn geography. The practical design keeps the engine's ETA as the strongest feature and trains a model to predict the residual, the gap between the engine's ETA and what actually happened, as Uber does with DeepETA.
Lower MAE overall means a better model.

A global MAE improvement can hide a city or hour that got worse, and a model can lower MAE while becoming biased in one direction for one trip type. ETAs are evaluated by city, hour of week and trip type, for bias as well as error, and quantile predictions for coverage, because marketplace decisions are made locally.
Real-time traffic makes historical patterns unnecessary.

Live speeds exist only where vehicles are driving now; at 4 a.m. or on minor roads they are sparse or stale. The system blends live segment speeds with historical speed profiles by time of week, weighted by how fresh and how many observations each live estimate has.
The label is just the actual trip time.

The actual time depends on the route the driver chose, waits at pickup, a restaurant's preparation time, and on which driver dispatch chose, which was itself chosen because its predicted ETA was lowest. Labels must be defined per use (driver-to-pickup, pickup-to-dropoff, order-to-door) and corrected for these effects, especially the optimistic bias of always picking the lowest prediction.
A model that big cannot run in a few milliseconds.

DeepETA has hundreds of millions of parameters but touches roughly 0.25% of them per prediction, because most parameters are in embedding tables looked up by hashed, discretised inputs, followed by a shallow network. Size and latency are separate questions when the model is mostly lookups.
lab:
Goal: see what MSE, MAE and pinball loss each predict on skewed trip times, measure how often each would break a promise, and see the winner's curse in dispatch. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as eta_lab.py and run python eta_lab.py.
  2. Block 1 uses the lesson's ten trips: it searches for the constant that minimises each loss and prints the late rate if that value were promised. Check mean 21, median 19.5 (any value between 19 and 20 minimises MAE), and a P90 between 26 and 36.
  3. Block 2 draws 200,000 skewed trip times (log-normal) and repeats with τ = 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.95, printing coverage: each quantile should be exceeded about (1 − τ) of the time.
  4. Block 3 simulates dispatch: 20 drivers whose true ETAs are similar, predictions with noise of 60 seconds, choose the minimum prediction, and compare the chosen driver's predicted and true ETA. Change N_CAND to 5 and 50.
"""MSE vs MAE vs pinball for ETAs, quantile coverage, and the winner's curse. Python 3.12."""
import random, statistics

trips = [14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23, 26, 36]
def mse(c, xs): return sum((x - c) ** 2 for x in xs) / len(xs)
def mae(c, xs): return sum(abs(x - c) for x in xs) / len(xs)
def pinball(c, xs, tau): return sum(tau * (x - c) if x >= c else (1 - tau) * (c - x) for x in xs) / len(xs)
grid = [g / 10 for g in range(100, 400)]
for name, f in [("MSE", lambda c: mse(c, trips)), ("MAE", lambda c: mae(c, trips)),
                ("pinball 0.9", lambda c: pinball(c, trips, 0.9))]:
    best = min(grid, key=f)
    late = sum(x > best for x in trips) / len(trips)
    print(f"{name:12} best constant {best:5.1f} min  late if promised {late:.0%}  MAE {mae(best, trips):.2f}")

rng = random.Random(4)
big = [12 + rng.lognormvariate(2.0, 0.5) for _ in range(200_000)]  # floor + skewed delay
big.sort()
print(f"\nmean {statistics.fmean(big):.1f}  median {big[len(big)//2]:.1f}")
for tau in (0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95):
    q = big[int(tau * len(big))]
    print(f"tau {tau:.2f}: quantile {q:5.1f} min, exceeded by {sum(x > q for x in big) / len(big):.1%}")
m = statistics.fmean(big)
print(f"promising the mean ({m:.1f}) is late {sum(x > m for x in big) / len(big):.0%} of the time")

N_CAND, NOISE, ROUNDS = 20, 60.0, 20_000
gaps = []
for _ in range(ROUNDS):
    true = [240 + rng.gauss(0, 30) for _ in range(N_CAND)]           # similar true pickup ETAs (s)
    pred = [t + rng.gauss(0, NOISE) for t in true]                   # unbiased but noisy
    i = min(range(N_CAND), key=pred.__getitem__)
    gaps.append(true[i] - pred[i])                                   # positive = optimistic
print(f"\nwinner's curse with {N_CAND} candidates: chosen driver arrives "
      f"{statistics.fmean(gaps):.0f} s later than predicted on average")

What to look for: each loss choosing a different constant from the same data, with the pinball-0.9 constant breaking the fewest promises and having the worst MAE; on the large sample, coverage close to 1 − τ for each quantile and promising the mean late roughly 40% of the time for this skew; and a winner's-curse gap of well over a minute with 20 candidates that grows with 50 and shrinks with 5, even though every individual prediction is unbiased.
recap: ETA prediction serves the whole marketplace: dispatch compares drivers by pickup ETA, pricing uses trip ETA for upfront fares, and the app shows customers arrival times and delivery promises.

The routing engine computes an ETA as the sum of segment traversal times along the best path using live and historical speeds; a machine-learned model predicts the residual between that ETA and the real outcome.

ETA is among the highest-volume predictions in the company: with dispatch evaluating many drivers per request and apps refreshing ETAs, this lesson's marketplace needs about 300,000 predictions a second at peak, with a model budget of about 5 ms at p99.
Real-time traffic comes from GPS pings map-matched to road segments and averaged in streaming windows, blended with historical time-of-week profiles where live data is thin.
Segment-level models generalise across routes but miss trip-level effects such as parking, pickup search and restaurant waits; trip-level residual models capture those, and the hybrid uses both.

Squared error gives the mean, absolute error the median and pinball loss a chosen quantile; trip times are right-skewed, so promising the mean makes many orders late, and promises use a high quantile such as P85 or P90.
In the lesson's ten-trip example the mean is 21 minutes, the median 19.5 and promising the mean is late 30% of the time, while promising 26 minutes is late 10% of the time.
Evaluation is by city, hour of week and trip type: MAE, bias, quantile coverage and interval width, with marketplace A/B tests run as switchbacks because ETAs change dispatch for everyone in a city.

Dispatch picks the driver with the lowest predicted ETA, so the chosen driver's prediction is biased low (the winner's curse); training on chosen assignments and correcting for selection keeps pickup ETAs honest.

Uber's DeepETA predicts the residual on top of its routing engine with a linear-attention encoder over discretised, embedded features, multi-resolution hashed location embeddings, segment bias adjustment and an asymmetric Huber loss, within a latency of a few milliseconds.
glossary: A loss that is squared near zero and linear far from it, with different weights for over- and under-prediction; DeepETA uses it to trade robustness against outliers and the cost of being late.
How often the actual value falls at or below a predicted quantile; a P90 prediction should cover about 90% of outcomes.
Estimated time of arrival: here, the predicted duration of a leg such as driver to pickup or pickup to drop-off.
Mapping a large set of categories (such as map grid cells) into a fixed number of embedding rows with a hash function; collisions share a row.
Mean absolute error: the average size of errors, ignoring sign; minimised by predicting the median.
Assigning noisy GPS points to the road segments a vehicle actually drove on.
Mean squared error: the average of squared errors; minimised by predicting the mean and sensitive to outliers.
The 50th and 90th percentiles of the predicted duration: half of trips should finish within the P50, nine in ten within the P90.
A loss that charges τ per unit of under-prediction and 1 − τ per unit of over-prediction, minimised by the τ-quantile.
A model that predicts the error of another estimate (here the routing engine's ETA) rather than the target itself.
A stretch of road between two intersections or shape points; the edge of the routing graph with a traversal time.
The service that finds the best path through the road graph and sums segment times into an ETA.
A marketplace experiment that alternates treatment and control over time slices within a city, so all users in a slice share one policy.
When choosing the option with the best estimate, that estimate is likely to be too optimistic, because noise helped it win.
drill:
Work it out

A delivery market promises at P80 today: 20% of orders are late. Each late order costs $3 in credits and churn. Moving to P90 would add 4 minutes to the average quoted time, and each quoted minute loses 0.8% of orders, each worth $2.50 in contribution. The market takes 100,000 orders a day at the current promise. (a) What does lateness cost today? (b) What would the change save in lateness and cost in conversions? (c) Should you switch?

Answer

(a) 20% × 100,000 × $3 = $60,000 a day.

(b) Conversions: 4 × 0.8% = 3.2% fewer orders, 3,200 × $2.50 = $8,000 a day lost. Remaining 96,800 orders at 10% late × $3 = $29,040, so lateness cost falls by about $31,000 a day.

(c) Net gain about $23,000 a day: switch, provided the P90 is calibrated per cell (otherwise the expected 10% may be 15% in some areas) and the conversion elasticity was measured for this market rather than assumed. Then check P85 and P95 the same way: the best quantile is where the marginal conversion loss equals the marginal lateness saving, and it varies by market.

Diagnose it

A new ETA model improves global MAE by 4% offline and in the switchback test. Two weeks after launch, on-time delivery is down 3 points in one large city during weekday dinner hours, and the city's operations team says promises there feel too tight. What do you check and change?

Answer

A global improvement can hide a local regression in bias or coverage. Check per-cell metrics for that city and hour band: bias (mean signed error) and P90 coverage for the new versus old model, by leg type. A likely finding is that the new model reduced MAE by moving predictions closer to the median, while its quantile head under-covers in that cell (for example 82% instead of 90%), perhaps because restaurant preparation-time features changed, a new traffic pattern emerged, or the city has fewer training rows relative to its complexity. Also check traffic freshness at those hours and any change in dispatch inputs. Change: add per-cell coverage to the launch gate (no cell may lose more than a set amount), apply a per-cell quantile correction from recent coverage immediately, and retrain with that city's recent data weighted more heavily.
qa: E
Who uses ETAs in a marketplace, and do they need the same number?

Dispatch uses driver-to-pickup ETAs to choose drivers and needs unbiased estimates for comparison; pricing uses trip ETAs for upfront fares and needs the mean with outliers controlled; the app shows riders pickup times and delivery customers a promise, which needs a high quantile because lateness is costly; operations use ETAs to plan batching and courier assignment. So the service returns several targets, not one.
E
Why predict a residual on top of the routing engine?

The routing engine already encodes the road network, turn costs, the chosen route and live speeds, so its ETA is the single strongest predictor. A model predicting only the gap between it and reality learns the systematic errors (pickup search, parking, intersections, local habits) without relearning geography, needs less data, and degrades gracefully: if the model fails, the engine's ETA is still usable.
E
What does each loss function make a model predict?

Mean squared error is minimised by the mean, mean absolute error by the median, and pinball loss with parameter τ by the τ-quantile. Huber loss behaves like squared error near zero and absolute error far away, so it estimates something between mean and median and resists outliers; making it asymmetric shifts it toward over- or under-prediction.
M
Why is the mean ETA the wrong target for a delivery promise?

Trip times are right-skewed: most trips cluster near the typical time and a few run much longer. The mean is pulled up by the tail but still sits below many outcomes, so promising it makes a large share of orders late, and lateness hurts customers far more than earliness. In the lesson's example, the mean of 21 minutes is beaten on 30% of trips; a promise at the P90 (about 26 minutes) is late about 10% of the time. The promise target is chosen from the cost of lateness versus the cost of a longer quoted time, which lowers conversion.

Follow-up: How would you choose the quantile? — Estimate the conversion loss per extra quoted minute and the cost of a late order (refunds, complaints, churn), then pick the quantile minimising expected cost, per market and order type.
M
Estimate prediction volume and latency.

With 20 million trips a day, each request evaluating about 20 candidate drivers over 3 matching rounds is 1.2 billion pickup ETAs a day, plus trip ETAs for pricing and app refreshes, roughly 2 billion a day: about 23,000 a second on average and, with peaks and batched matching, about 300,000 at peak. The model has about 5 ms at p99 inside an ETA service budget of about 50 ms that also includes the routing query; so it runs on CPU in-process or nearby, with features precomputed and inputs batched within a millisecond.
M
Compare segment-level and trip-level models.

A segment-level model predicts each road segment's traversal time from live and historical speeds, and the ETA is their sum: it generalises to any route and supports route choice, but errors accumulate and it cannot see trip-level effects such as finding the rider, parking, building entrances or restaurant waits. A trip-level model predicts the whole trip's duration or residual from origin, destination, time and the route summary: it captures those end effects and its errors do not compound, but it depends on the route chosen. Production systems combine them: a segment-level engine plus a trip-level residual.
M
How do you build real-time traffic features?

Drivers' apps send GPS pings every few seconds; a streaming job map-matches them to road segments, computes traversal speeds, and averages them per segment in windows of one to five minutes with counts. The routing engine uses these live speeds where enough fresh observations exist and blends toward historical speed profiles by time of week where they do not. The residual model gets aggregates along the route, such as the share of the route with live data and the live-to-historical speed ratio.
M
How would you evaluate a new ETA model offline?

On held-out recent trips, by city, hour of week, trip type (pickup, drop-off, delivery) and distance band: MAE, mean signed error (bias), and for quantile outputs coverage (share of actuals below the P90) and interval width. Compare with the current model on the same trips with paired statistics, and look at the worst cells, not just the global average, because marketplace decisions are local. Also check behaviour on unusual days (holidays, storms) kept as a separate slice.
H
What is the winner's curse in dispatch and how do you handle it?

Dispatch picks the driver with the lowest predicted pickup ETA among, say, 20 candidates. Each prediction has noise, so the minimum is more likely to be one whose noise was negative: the chosen driver's prediction is systematically too low, and observed pickup times run late against the predictions shown. The training data also contain only chosen drivers. Mitigations: evaluate and calibrate on chosen assignments specifically, add a correction that depends on the number of candidates and the prediction uncertainty, include features of the selection context, and show riders a pickup ETA from a model trained on chosen assignments rather than the raw score used for ranking.

Follow-up: How big can it be? — With 20 candidates and prediction noise of about a minute, the expected minimum of the noise alone is around 1.9 standard deviations below zero, so roughly two minutes of optimism unless corrected.
H
How do you A/B test a new ETA model in a marketplace?

User-level randomisation fails because ETAs drive dispatch: the treatment model's choices change which drivers are free for control riders. Use switchback experiments, alternating treatment and control in time slices (for example 30 to 60 minutes) per city, with slices randomised and analysed with methods that account for carry-over between slices. Primary metrics: ETA accuracy on completed trips and marketplace outcomes such as rider conversion, cancellations, pickup wait, on-time delivery rate and driver utilisation; guardrails: latency and fallback rate.
H
How does DeepETA stay within a few milliseconds with hundreds of millions of parameters?

Most parameters sit in embedding tables, and every input is discretised (continuous features into quantile buckets, locations into multi-resolution grid cells mapped with several hash functions), so a prediction is mostly O(1) table lookups touching about 0.25% of parameters. The network on top is shallow, and its attention over about 40 feature embeddings uses a linear transformer, which costs O(K·d²) instead of O(K²·d): with K = 40 features of dimension 8, 2,560 operations instead of 12,800.
H
How do ETA predictions feed back into the data they are trained on?

Dispatch and pricing act on ETAs: areas predicted slow get fewer dispatches or higher prices, so fewer trips (and labels) come from there, and the remaining ones are a selected sample. Promises change customer behaviour (a long quoted time loses orders, so long trips are under-represented). Drivers may also behave differently against a displayed ETA. Defences: log the predictions and decisions with each label, use exploration in dispatch where cheap, weight training data for selection where possible, and monitor bias in under-sampled areas and times.

t: Design a fine-tuning and training platform for many teams
sum: A shared platform running 40 teams' training and fine-tuning jobs on 2,048 GPUs: job submission, gang scheduling and why partial allocation deadlocks, quotas with borrowing and preemption, utilisation maths and backfill, checkpoint size and the optimal checkpoint interval worked by hand, data and checkpoint storage, experiment tracking, evaluation gates and a model registry, automatic failure recovery, cost attribution, and what Llama 3's 54 days of interruptions teach.
