(Per-step times are assumptions for illustration: 40 ms per image per guided step at batch 4, 20 ms per unguided distilled step, 0.1 s decoding. Benchmark your own pipeline at production settings, including encoders, decoder and safety models.)

7 · Deep dive: fleet sizing and queueing

Offered load. Little's law gives the average number of GPUs busy: arrival rate × GPU-seconds per job. At peak, 116 quality requests a second × 5.2 s = 603 GPUs of offered load. With exactly 603 GPUs, the queue grows without limit, because any random burst can never be worked off. The question is how many more are needed to keep waits short.

Erlang C. For random (Poisson) arrivals and c identical servers, the Erlang C formula gives the probability that an arriving job finds all servers busy and must wait, P(wait). Given that it waits, the wait is roughly exponential with rate (c − a) / S, where a is the offered load and S the service time, so the probability of waiting longer than t is P(wait) × e−(c − a)t/S. Working the numbers for the quality tier at peak:

GPUs (c)UtilisationP(wait)Mean waitp95 waitp99 wait
61098.9%70%534 ms2.0 s3.2 s
62097.3%39%119 ms632 ms1.1 s
64094.3%9%13 ms82 ms310 ms
66091.4%1.3%1 ms027 ms

The striking thing is how hot a large pool can run: at 91% utilisation, only 1.3% of jobs wait at all. This is the economy of scale of pooling: with hundreds of servers, the chance that all of them are busy at once is small even when each is busy most of the time.

Fragmentation costs real GPUs. Split the same 660 GPUs into six regional pools of 110, each carrying a sixth of the traffic, and the p99 wait rises from 27 ms to about 1.8 s; to bring the split fleet under the 1 s target needs roughly 690 GPUs. Every split (by region, model version, tenant, resolution) has this cost, so the design keeps one pool per model per region, routes jobs across availability zones, and lets the quality tier borrow idle fast-tier GPUs that have both models loaded.

Where the model lies. Erlang C assumes random arrivals and memoryless service times. Real traffic is burstier: a viral prompt can triple arrivals within minutes, and Monday mornings ramp faster than autoscaling. Service times have tails (large resolutions, upscales). Batching windows and model loading add delay that the formula ignores. So the formula sets the order of magnitude, and a discrete-event simulation driven by real arrival traces sets the final number. In practice teams provision about 10–20% above the Erlang answer for the forecast peak, keep warm spare capacity, and protect latency with admission control.

Admission control and graceful degradation. When the predicted wait for a new job exceeds the tier's limit, accepting it only makes every job late. The scheduler instead degrades in a fixed order: free-tier requests drop to two images, then move to the fast model, then receive a "busy, try again in a minute" response with a retry time; paid quality jobs are protected longest. This keeps the fleet out of the regime where waits grow without bound.

Scaling up quickly. A new GPU worker is useless until its model is loaded: several gigabytes of weights. Keeping weights on local disks of standby nodes, using pre-built container images with the model baked in, and keeping a warm pool of idle-but-loaded workers (paid for, as insurance) bring scale-up from many minutes to tens of seconds.

8 · Deep dive: prompt and output safety

Before the GPU: prompt checks. A rule layer blocks prompts with terms that are never acceptable and normalises tricks (misspellings, spacing, homoglyphs, translations). A text classifier scores categories: sexual content, sexual content involving minors, violence and gore, hate, self-harm, real-person likeness in sexual or defamatory contexts, and brand or copyrighted-character misuse if policy restricts it. Thresholds per category are chosen from precision and recall on labelled prompt sets, with the asymmetry of hd6: for the most severe categories, recall comes first and some over-blocking is accepted. If the rewriter is used, its output is checked too.

After the GPU: output checks. Every generated image is classified for nudity, sexual content, violence, apparent minors and the likeness of known public figures. The combination matters: nudity plus an apparent minor is the highest severity and is blocked and escalated regardless of any score elsewhere. For services that accept uploaded images (image-to-image, inpainting), inputs are hash-matched against databases of known child sexual abuse material and other known abusive images before processing, and outputs are hash-matched too; in the United States, providers who become aware of apparent child sexual abuse material are legally required to report it to NCMEC. Blocked outputs are not delivered; the user sees a policy message; the job, prompt, scores and images are retained in a restricted store for review and legal obligations.

Account-level signals. Determined abusers probe: they try dozens of variants until one passes. Each block adds to a per-account risk score; above a threshold, the account gets slower limits, stricter thresholds, mandatory human review of outputs, or suspension. Velocity on a named real person (many generations of one celebrity's name with suggestive terms) triggers review even if each image passed.

Human review and appeals. A small team reviews samples of blocked and passed items (to measure precision and recall), high-severity escalations and user appeals. Reviewer exposure to disturbing content is limited by policy, with blurring by default and wellbeing support.

9 · Deep dive: provenance with C2PA and watermarks

The manifest. C2PA, the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity's specification (version 2.3 is current at the time of writing; the concepts here are stable across 2.x), defines a manifest: a set of assertions (statements about the asset), wrapped in a claim that is digitally signed by the claim generator, here the image service, using an X.509 certificate. For a generated image, the key assertion is c2pa.actions starting with a c2pa.created action whose digitalSourceType is the IPTC value http://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia, which declares that the media was created by a trained generative model. The manifest is tied to the file by a hard binding, a cryptographic hash of the asset's bytes, so any change to the file invalidates the signature check. Manifests are embedded in the file (in JPEG, in a container format called JUMBF) and can also be stored externally.

Why metadata is not enough. Many platforms strip metadata on upload, and a screenshot creates a new file with none. The specification addresses this with soft bindings: content identifiers that survive some changes, either an invisible watermark embedded in the pixels or a fingerprint computed from the content. The specification's actions include c2pa.watermarked.bound for a watermark inserted to create a soft binding, and it calls a manifest that can be rediscovered through a soft binding in a manifest repository a durable Content Credential. So the service embeds a watermark carrying an identifier, records that identifier in the manifest, and stores the manifest in a repository; a verifier holding a stripped copy detects the watermark and looks the manifest up.

The order of operations. Watermark first, then sign: the hard binding hashes the final bytes, so embedding a watermark after signing would break the binding. Safety before both, so blocked images are never stamped or stored for delivery. Signing keys live in a hardware security module; the signing service is on the critical path, so it is replicated and its latency (a few milliseconds) budgeted.

Limits to state honestly. Invisible watermarks can be weakened by heavy cropping, resizing, re-encoding, rotation and deliberate removal attacks; detection is probabilistic and has false positives. A missing manifest or watermark proves nothing, because other generators may add neither. Provenance therefore supports, rather than replaces, detection classifiers and policy, and the service publishes a detection endpoint for trust-and-safety partners, with documented error rates.

10 · Caching and variations

Exact caching stores results keyed by everything that determines the output: model version, scheduler, steps, guidance scale, resolution, normalised prompt (after rewriting), seed and batch configuration. It helps in specific cases: featured or template prompts shown on a landing page, re-downloads, and identical requests from many users during a viral trend (where serving the cached set, or a cached set with fresh seeds generated in the background, protects the fleet). It does not help in general, because most prompts are unique and users expect fresh images. Note the determinism caveat: different GPU types and batch compositions can change outputs slightly even with the same seed, so a cache hit is "the images this configuration produced", not a mathematical guarantee.

Cheaper intermediate products. Text-encoder outputs for a prompt can be cached and reused for variations, upscales and retries, saving a few tens of milliseconds per job. More valuable is the structure of variations. A new-seed variation reuses the prompt encoding and costs a full generation otherwise. A subtle variation uses image-to-image: noise the chosen image to strength 0.3 and denoise from there, running only about 30% of the steps (9 of 30), about a third of the cost of a fresh generation, with results that keep the composition. Upscaling uses a dedicated model that is much cheaper per output pixel than generating at the higher resolution. Product design that steers users toward variations and upscales of a chosen image, rather than repeated fresh generations, lowers GPU-seconds per satisfied user.

11 · Abuse and rate limits

Limits are enforced at admission, with a shared counter store (cd12). Concurrency: one or two jobs in flight per user, which stops a script from filling the queue. Credits: a daily allowance per tier, consumed per image weighted by GPU-seconds (a quality image costs more credits than a fast one). Risk-based throttling: new accounts, accounts with recent blocks and traffic from suspicious networks get lower limits and stricter thresholds. Free tier on the cheap model, which also limits the damage of mass-created accounts. Velocity detection on prompt hashes and named targets catches coordinated campaigns. Every limit returns a clear error with a retry time, so honest clients behave well and the system can tell retries from attacks.

12 · Evaluation plan

Offline quality. A fixed, versioned prompt set (a few thousand prompts) by category: people, animals, text in images, counting, spatial relations, styles, edge cases. For each model: prompt adherence with automated checks in the style of GenEval, which uses object detectors to verify object presence, co-occurrence, counts, colours and positions; alignment scores such as CLIPScore, used with care because they reward keyword matching and miss counts and relations; human side-by-side preference on a sample, randomised left and right, judged on adherence and overall quality; and FID only as a coarse distribution check, since it does not measure prompt following.

Offline safety. A red-team prompt set per category, refreshed with real attack patterns from blocked logs, measuring block recall at prompt and output stages; a benign set (including medical, artistic nudity and historical violence where policy allows) measuring over-blocking; output-classifier precision and recall on a labelled image set, especially for apparent minors.

Cost and latency gates. GPU-seconds per image and p95 latency on the production pipeline at production batch sizes. A model that is 3% preferred but 40% more expensive is a business decision, not an automatic win.

Online. A/B tests by user with the share of requests where at least one image is saved, downloaded or used in a design as the primary metric; regenerate rate (a sign of dissatisfaction), time to images, abandonment while waiting, report rate and appeal overturn rate as guardrails.

13 · Failure modes and trade-offs

FailureSymptomDefence
Traffic spikeWaits grow without boundAdmission control, tier degradation, warm spare GPUs, viral-prompt cache
Fragmented poolsHigh waits at moderate utilisationOne pool per model per region, spill-over
Slow scale-upNew GPUs idle for minutesWeights on local disk, baked images, warm pool
Disguised harmful promptBad output deliveredOutput classifier, account risk scores, red-team refresh
Over-blockingBenign requests refusedBenign test set, per-category thresholds, appeals
Signing service downNo images delivered, or unsigned onesReplicated signer; fail closed (queue delivery), never deliver unsigned
Model update regressesLower save rateOffline gates, staged rollout, quick rollback by version

The trade-offs to name: steps and guidance against cost; distilled speed against diversity and control; utilisation against latency, with pooling changing the curve; safety recall against over-blocking; provenance robustness against image quality (stronger watermarks are more visible); caching against freshness and variety.

14 · What changes at 10× scale

At 200 million images a day, the fleet is several thousand GPUs and the economics change. Model efficiency becomes the main project: distillation of the quality model to fewer steps, quantisation, step caching and custom kernels each save hundreds of GPUs. Capacity strategy: reserved capacity covers the daily base; peaks run on burst capacity in several regions, and global routing sends free-tier work to whichever region has spare GPUs, since a few hundred milliseconds of extra network time is invisible next to generation time. Safety at scale: classifiers run on dedicated pools, human review is sampled statistically rather than exhaustive, and abuse detection becomes a graph problem across accounts, payment methods and devices. Provenance volume (200 million signatures a day) requires a horizontally scaled signing service, which is cheap but must never be the reason images are delivered unsigned.
deep:
Why large pools can run hot

The intuition that servers must stay at 60–70% utilisation comes from small systems. Waiting happens when all servers are busy at once, and with many servers the number busy fluctuates around the mean by roughly the square root of the mean. A pool with an offered load of 600 GPUs fluctuates by about ±25, so 660 GPUs (two to three standard deviations of headroom) is rarely saturated; a pool with a load of 100 fluctuates by about ±10, so it needs proportionally more headroom. This "square-root staffing" rule, borrowed from call centres, says spare capacity should grow with the square root of the load, not proportionally, which is exactly why consolidation saves so many GPUs and fragmentation wastes them.

Distillation moves cost from inference to training, and changes the product

A few-step student is expensive to train once and cheap forever after, which pays off quickly at millions of images a day. But distillation changes behaviour: adversarial objectives sharpen images and can reduce diversity across seeds, and dropping guidance removes a knob some users rely on (strong prompt adherence at high guidance scales). Products therefore expose tiers rather than silently swapping models, and evaluate diversity explicitly (how different are four images from one prompt?) along with preference.

Decoder and safety costs matter once denoising is cheap

With 30 guided steps, the VAE decoder and safety classifiers are a few per cent of the cost and nobody looks at them. With a four-step student, the decoder can be half of the GPU time per image, and the safety classifier a noticeable share. Optimising them (a lighter decoder, decoding at a lower resolution for previews, batching classifiers across jobs) becomes worthwhile. This is a general pattern: when one stage is optimised by an order of magnitude, the next stage becomes the bottleneck, and profiling has to be repeated.

Safety thresholds interact with tiers and with each other

A prompt classifier tuned for high recall blocks some benign prompts; an output classifier after it sees only what passed, so its measured precision and recall depend on the prompt threshold. Changing one threshold changes the other's operating point, and evaluating each in isolation misleads. The right evaluation runs the full chain on labelled prompt sets and measures end-to-end delivered-harm rate and end-to-end over-blocking, then tunes thresholds jointly. Tiers complicate it further: a paid professional tier may allow artistic nudity that the free tier blocks, so thresholds are per policy profile, and the profile is part of the job record.

Provenance is a trust system, not a feature flag

A C2PA signature is only as meaningful as the trust placed in the signer's certificate and in what the signer claims. A service that signs "created by a trained model" for every image is making an honest claim; one that signs edited real photographs as unedited would be misusing the system. Verifiers check the certificate chain against trust lists, the hard binding against the file and the assertions for consistency. For the service, this means key management (keys in hardware modules, rotation, revocation plans), careful claims (record the model and the operation, not more), and a public explanation of what its credentials mean.

Prompt rewriting is both a quality lever and a risk

Short prompts produce generic images; a language model that expands them into detailed descriptions usually produces images users prefer, and it is a natural place to apply style presets and policy (for example, never adding real names). But the rewriter can introduce content the user did not ask for, bias the output (adding demographic details), or be manipulated into producing disallowed descriptions. So its output passes the same prompt safety check, the user can see and edit the expanded prompt, and its effect is measured in A/B tests like any model change.

Cost per satisfied user, not cost per image

GPU-seconds per image is the engineering metric, but the business pays for outcomes: a user who finds an image they keep. A change that halves the cost per image but doubles the number of regenerations before a user is satisfied saves nothing. So the cost metric that guides product decisions is GPU-seconds per saved or used image, measured in A/B tests. It explains several design choices that look odd from the infrastructure side: offering four images at once (more chance one is right, fewer rounds), investing in prompt rewriting (better first attempts), and making subtle variations prominent (a cheap path from "almost" to "yes"). It also explains why a slightly more expensive model can lower total cost if users settle on its first batch more often.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The viral template. A creator shared a prompt template, and requests tripled within ten minutes. Admission control did not exist, so every request was accepted, queue waits climbed past a minute, users retried, and the retries made it worse. The fleet was saturated for an hour while autoscaling, which waited for new nodes to download model weights, added capacity slowly. Afterwards: admission control that degrades free requests first, weights baked into node images with a warm pool, and an automatic exact cache for any prompt template exceeding a request-rate threshold.

The misspelled celebrity. A prompt using a deliberately misspelled celebrity name plus suggestive terms passed the prompt classifier, and the output classifier at the time checked nudity but not real-person likeness, so sexualised images of a real person were delivered and circulated. The fixes: a likeness classifier on outputs combined with the nudity score, normalisation of misspellings in the prompt layer, velocity detection on named people, and the attack added to the red-team set.

The unsigned week. A deployment changed the order of post-processing so that images were resized for the CDN after signing. Every manifest's hard binding failed verification for a week before a partner reported it. Signing is now the last step, a verification check runs on a sample of delivered files continuously, and failures page the on-call engineer.

What to monitor

Per tier: queue depth, wait percentiles, GPU-seconds per job by stage, GPU utilisation, admission rejections and degradations. Fleet: warm spare capacity, scale-up time, worker failures, model versions in service. Safety: prompt and output block rates by category, account strikes, review backlog, appeal overturn rate. Provenance: signing latency and errors, sampled verification failures, watermark detection rate on sampled outputs after common transformations. Product: save and download rate, regenerate rate, time to images, abandonment.

Knobs people tune

Steps and guidance per tier; default resolution and images per request; batch size; fleet size and spare-capacity margin; admission thresholds and degradation order; safety thresholds per category and policy profile; watermark strength; credit weights per operation; cache triggers for viral templates.

The real cases: SDXL, ADD, Diffusers and C2PA

The SDXL report (Podell et al., 2023) describes the kind of model a quality tier serves: a UNet backbone about three times larger than earlier Stable Diffusion versions, 2.6 billion parameters, two text encoders, training around 1,024 × 1,024 pixels with multiple aspect ratios, and an optional refinement stage. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (Sauer et al., 2023), the method behind SDXL Turbo, shows the fast-tier alternative: 1–4 sampling steps, no classifier-free guidance at inference, outperforming earlier few-step methods in a single step and matching SDXL in four steps at 512 × 512 in the authors' evaluation. Hugging Face's Diffusers documentation on accelerating inference, checked on 10 October 2026, lists the serving levers every pipeline should start from: bfloat16 or float16 weights, scaled dot-product attention with its automatic choice of efficient kernels, and torch.compile, demonstrated on an SDXL pipeline. The C2PA specification (version 2.3 at the time of writing) defines the manifest, the c2pa.created action with digitalSourceType trainedAlgorithmicMedia for generated media, hard bindings by hash, soft bindings by watermark or fingerprint, the c2pa.watermarked.bound action, and the idea of a durable Content Credential that can be rediscovered through a soft binding. The GPU-seconds and fleet numbers in this lesson are worked from stated assumptions; the method (measure the pipeline, compute offered load, size with Erlang C, validate by simulation) is what transfers.
myths: Image generation cost is per request, like a text API call.

Cost is GPU-seconds, and GPU-seconds scale with denoising steps, resolution (roughly with the number of latent positions, and faster than linearly once attention dominates), guidance (classifier-free guidance doubles the model evaluations per step unless distilled away) and images per request. A four-image request at 1,024 × 1,024 with 30 guided steps can cost twenty to thirty times a one-image request on a four-step distilled model.
Run the GPUs at 70% utilisation to keep latency safe.

Queueing delay depends on pool size as well as utilisation. In the worked example, one pool of 660 GPUs at 91% busy has a 99th-percentile wait of about 27 ms, while the same 660 split into six regional pools of 110 has a 99th-percentile wait of about 1.8 seconds. Large pooled fleets can run hot; small or fragmented ones cannot.
A watermark proves an image is AI-generated.

An invisible watermark is evidence when it is detected, but its absence proves nothing: it can be weakened by cropping, resizing, screenshots or deliberate attack, and other generators may not add one. C2PA provenance adds signed metadata about how an image was made, but platforms often strip metadata. Provenance is layered: signed manifest, watermark as a soft binding to find the manifest again, and detection classifiers, each with known gaps.
Checking the prompt is enough to keep outputs safe.

Benign-looking prompts can produce policy-violating images, and harmful requests are disguised with misspellings, other languages and indirect descriptions. Safety needs both a prompt check (cheap, before spending GPU time) and an output image check (catches what the prompt check missed), plus account-level signals for users who probe repeatedly.
Same prompt plus same seed always gives the same image, so caching is easy.

Only with the same model version, scheduler, resolution, guidance scale, step count and often the same GPU type and batch composition; floating-point differences across hardware and batch sizes can change outputs. Exact caching works for repeated identical requests on pinned configurations (featured prompts, re-downloads), not as a general deduplication of similar prompts.
FID tells you which model users will prefer.

FID compares feature statistics of generated and real image sets; it says little about whether an image follows a specific prompt, gets counts and positions right, or looks good to people. Production evaluation combines prompt-adherence checks (object, count, colour, position), CLIP-based alignment scores with care, and human side-by-side preference on a fixed prompt set.
lab:
Goal: build a discrete-event GPU queue simulator, check it against the Erlang C numbers in section 7, see how much worse split pools and traffic bursts are, and find the fleet size that meets a 1-second p99 wait. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as gpu_queue.py and run python gpu_queue.py.
  2. Read the first table: one pool, Poisson arrivals at 116 requests a second, 5.2 GPU-seconds each, for several fleet sizes. The p99 waits should be close to the Erlang C table (the service times here vary a little, so not identical).
  3. Read the second table: the same total GPUs as six independent pools. Waits are far longer at the same utilisation.
  4. Read the third table: one pool with a burst (arrivals tripled for 60 seconds). Find how many GPUs keep p99 under 1 s, and compare with how many you would rather protect with admission control.
  5. Change SERVICE_S to 0.8 (the fast tier) and rerun.
"""GPU queue simulator: FCFS, c identical GPUs. Python 3.12, stdlib only."""
import heapq, math, random
RATE, SERVICE_S, SIM_S = 116.0, 5.2, 900          # requests/s, GPU-s per request, seconds
def arrivals(rate, seconds, rng, burst=None):
    t, out = 0.0, []
    while t < seconds:
        r = rate * (3 if burst and burst[0] <= t < burst[1] else 1)
        t += rng.expovariate(r); out.append(t)
    return out
def run(times, c, rng):
    free = [0.0] * c; heapq.heapify(free); waits = []; busy = 0.0
    for t in times:                                 # FCFS: earliest-free GPU takes the job
        f = heapq.heappop(free); start = max(t, f)
        s = SERVICE_S * math.exp(rng.gauss(0, 0.15) - 0.15**2 / 2)
        waits.append(start - t); busy += s; heapq.heappush(free, start + s)
    waits.sort(); n = len(waits)
    q = lambda p: waits[min(n - 1, int(p * n))]
    return q(0.5), q(0.95), q(0.99), busy / (c * times[-1])
def table(title, c_list, pools=1, burst=None):
    print(f"\n{title}\n  GPUs   util    p50     p95     p99   (seconds of wait)")
    for c in c_list:
        rng = random.Random(1); res = []
        for _ in range(pools):                     # each pool gets 1/pools of the traffic
            res.append(run(arrivals(RATE / pools, SIM_S, rng, burst), c // pools, rng))
        p50, p95, p99 = (max(r[i] for r in res) for i in range(3))
        util = sum(r[3] for r in res) / pools
        print(f"  {c:5} {util:5.1%} {p50:7.2f} {p95:7.2f} {p99:7.2f}")
table("One pool, Poisson", [610, 620, 640, 660, 700])
table("Six pools, same total (worst pool shown)", [612, 630, 642, 660, 690], pools=6)
table("One pool, 3x burst for 60 s", [660, 800, 1000, 1400], burst=(300, 360))
print(f"\nOffered load = {RATE * SERVICE_S:.0f} GPUs")

What to look for: waits near zero at 660 GPUs in one pool but seconds of p99 wait at the same total split six ways; and in the burst table, that riding out a tripling with capacity alone needs far more GPUs than the steady state, which is why admission control and degradation are cheaper than buying for the spike.
recap: A text-to-image service accepts a prompt, checks it, optionally rewrites it, queues the job by tier, runs text encoding, many denoising steps and decoding on a GPU, checks the output image, adds provenance and returns stored images.

Cost is GPU-seconds: steps × time per step, doubled by classifier-free guidance unless distilled, growing with resolution, plus text encoding and decoding; in the worked example a quality image costs about 1.3 GPU-seconds and a four-step distilled image about 0.2.
At 20 million images a day, an all-quality fleet needs about 7,200 GPU-hours a day (about $18,000 at $2.50 an hour); serving 70% on the fast tier cuts that to about 2,900 GPU-hours.

Queue sizing uses arrival rate × service time to get offered load in GPUs, then Erlang C for the waiting probability: 116 four-image requests a second at 5.2 GPU-seconds each is 603 GPUs of load, and 660 pooled GPUs keep the 99th-percentile wait near 27 ms.

Pooling matters as much as utilisation: the same 660 GPUs split into six pools give a 99th-percentile wait of about 1.8 seconds, and real traffic is burstier than the Poisson model, so keep headroom and admission control.

Safety runs before and after generation: a prompt classifier and rules before spending GPU time, an output image classifier and known-abuse hash matching after, with account-level strikes and rate limits for repeated probing.

Provenance uses a C2PA manifest signed by the service, with a c2pa.created action whose digitalSourceType is trainedAlgorithmicMedia, bound to the file by a hash, plus an invisible watermark as a soft binding that survives metadata stripping better than metadata does.
Variations are cheaper than fresh generations: new seeds reuse the text encoding, and image-to-image at strength 0.3 runs only about 30% of the denoising steps.
Abuse control combines per-user concurrency limits, credits per day, risk-scored throttling, free tiers restricted to the cheap model, and velocity detection on prompts and targets.

Quality is evaluated with prompt-adherence benchmarks such as GenEval, alignment scores, human side-by-side preference, safety recall on red-team prompts and over-blocking on benign prompts, and online save, download and regenerate rates.

drill:
Estimate it

Your product moves from four images per request to two by default, and from 30 to 20 guided steps on the quality tier, keeping 5 million requests a day, a peak of twice the average, 40 ms per guided step per image and 0.1 s decoding per image. (a) GPU-seconds per request and offered load at peak? (b) Daily GPU-hours and cost at $2.50 an hour, all quality? (c) Roughly how many GPUs at peak for a sub-second p99 wait in one pool?

Answer

(a) Per image: 20 × 0.04 + 0.1 = 0.9 GPU-seconds; per two-image request 1.8 GPU-seconds. Peak arrivals: 5,000,000 / 86,400 × 2 ≈ 116 requests a second, so offered load = 116 × 1.8 ≈ 209 GPUs.

(b) 10 million images × 0.9 = 9 million GPU-seconds = 2,500 GPU-hours a day, about $6,250 a day, a third of the original $18,000 (half from fewer images, the rest from fewer steps).

(c) With an offered load near 209, square-root staffing suggests headroom of a few times √209 ≈ 14, so about 230–240 GPUs keeps waits short in one pool (Erlang C or the lab's simulator gives the exact figure), plus 10–20% for burstiness. Check that the product change does not raise regenerations: if users now generate twice as often to see four options, the saving disappears, which is why such changes are A/B tested on cost per satisfied user, not cost per request.

Diagnose it

After a model update, output-level blocks for "sexual content" fall from 0.8% to 0.3% of images, prompt-level blocks are unchanged, and user reports of explicit images rise threefold. What happened, and what do you check?

Answer

Fewer blocks plus more reports means the output classifier is missing more, not that the model is safer. Likely causes: the new model's images differ in style or distribution from what the output classifier was trained on (a classic distribution shift), so its scores dropped below threshold for images people still find explicit; or the post-processing order changed and the classifier now sees a downscaled preview. Check: run the labelled image set and a sample of reported images through the classifier and compare score distributions between old and new model outputs; confirm which image the classifier receives; review a stratified sample of passed images by hand. Fixes: recalibrate or retrain the classifier on the new model's outputs before full rollout, temporarily lower the threshold, and add "output-classifier recall on the new model's images" to the model release gate so a model update cannot ship without its safety classifier being re-validated.
qa: E
What drives the cost of generating one image?

GPU time, which is the number of denoising steps times the time per step, plus text encoding and decoding. Time per step grows with resolution because there are more latent positions to process, and classifier-free guidance doubles the evaluations per step. Images per request multiply everything. Distilled few-step models cut steps from about 30 to 1–4 and often drop guidance, which is why fast tiers are many times cheaper.
E
Why check both the prompt and the output image?

The prompt check is cheap and stops obviously disallowed requests before spending GPU time. But harmful outputs come from innocent-looking or disguised prompts, and models sometimes produce unexpected content, so the generated image is also classified before anyone sees it. Each check covers the other's blind spots, and account-level signals catch users who probe both.
E
What is a C2PA manifest and what does it prove?

A signed record attached to a file describing how it was made: here a creation action declaring the image came from a trained generative model, signed with the service's certificate and bound to the exact bytes by a hash. It proves that the signer made that claim about this exact file. It does not survive metadata stripping on its own, and its absence proves nothing, which is why it is paired with a watermark that can lead back to the manifest.
M
Estimate the GPU fleet for 5 million four-image requests a day.

20 million images. At 1.3 GPU-seconds per quality image, that is 26 million GPU-seconds, about 7,200 GPU-hours a day or 300 GPUs busy on average; at a peak twice the average, about 600 GPUs of load, so roughly 650–700 GPUs with headroom. At $2.50 an hour that is about $18,000 a day. If 70% of images use a four-step distilled model at 0.2 GPU-seconds, the average drops to 0.53 GPU-seconds per image and the bill to about $7,400 a day.

Follow-up: Where would you check your per-image number? — Benchmark the actual pipeline at the production resolution, batch size and precision, including text encoders, decoder and safety models, on the target GPU; vendor or paper numbers rarely include the whole pipeline.
M
How do you size the queue so that waits stay short?

Compute offered load: arrival rate times GPU-seconds per job; 116 requests a second at 5.2 seconds is 603 GPUs of work. Then use Erlang C (or a simulation) for the probability of waiting and the wait distribution at each fleet size: 620 GPUs gives a 99th-percentile wait around 1.1 s, 660 around 27 ms. Add margin for burstiness and model-loading time, and keep a single shared pool per region rather than many small ones.
M
Design the tiers: fast and quality.

Fast: a few-step distilled model, smaller default resolution, one or four images, a latency target around 2 seconds, used for free users and drafts. Quality: the full model with 25–30 guided steps at higher resolution, target under 8–10 seconds, for paid users and final renders. Separate queues so a quality backlog cannot slow fast jobs; quality jobs can borrow idle fast capacity but not the reverse at peak. Show progress (a preview from an early step) on the quality tier.
M
How do variations and caching reduce cost?

Variations reuse the text encoding and change only the seed; subtle variations use image-to-image from the chosen image at low strength, which runs only that fraction of the steps (30% at strength 0.3). Exact caching serves repeated identical requests on pinned configurations, such as featured prompts and re-downloads. Similar but different prompts are not cached, because a different prompt is a different request and the user expects a new image.

Follow-up: Why not cache by prompt embedding similarity? — Users asking for a red car and a blue car want different images; a semantic cache would return wrong results and remove the variety that is the product.
M
What rate limits and abuse controls do you put in?

Per-user concurrency (one or two jobs in flight), per-minute and per-day credits, a free tier limited to the cheap model, stricter limits for new or risky accounts, cooldowns and strikes after repeated blocked prompts, and velocity detection on prompt hashes and named targets (many generations of one real person). Limits are enforced at admission before queueing, with clear errors and retry times.
H
Why does pooling GPUs matter so much for latency?

Because waiting depends on how often all servers are busy at once, and with many servers random fluctuations average out. At 91% utilisation, one pool of 660 GPUs rarely has all of them busy (1.3% of arrivals wait, p99 wait about 27 ms), while six pools of 110 each, at the same utilisation, have every server busy far more often (p99 about 1.8 s). So prefer large shared pools per region, route across zones, avoid per-tenant or per-model fragmentation, and when you must split (several models), let spare capacity spill over.

Follow-up: What breaks the Erlang model? — Bursty arrivals (a viral prompt), heavy-tailed service times (large resolutions), batching windows and cold model loads. Validate with a simulation driven by real arrival traces.
H
Design the provenance and watermarking path.

After the output passes safety, embed an invisible watermark in the pixels, then create a C2PA manifest: a c2pa.created action with digitalSourceType trainedAlgorithmicMedia, the model and service as the software agent, a hard binding hash of the final file, and an action recording the watermark as a soft binding. Sign with the service's certificate and embed the manifest in the file, and store a copy in a manifest repository keyed by the watermark. A verifier who receives a stripped copy can detect the watermark and look up the manifest. Provide a detection service for trust-and-safety partners, and document the limits: watermarks weaken under heavy edits and attack.
Follow-up: Why sign after the watermark? — The hard binding hash covers the final bytes; any change after signing, including adding the watermark, would invalidate the manifest.
H
A viral prompt triples traffic in ten minutes. What happens and what did you design in advance?

Offered load jumps from about 600 to 1,800 GPUs of work; a fleet of 700 saturates, queues grow without bound and every user waits. In advance: admission control that rejects or defers new work when queue wait exceeds a limit, priority for paid tiers, automatic downgrade of free requests to the fast model and fewer images, warm spare capacity and fast scale-up (preloaded model images, weights on local disk), and an exact cache for the viral prompt template. The worst outcome is accepting everything and timing out everyone.
H
How do you evaluate a new model before replacing the old one?

Offline: a fixed prompt set by category, run through both models; automated prompt-adherence checks (object presence, counts, colours, positions, as in GenEval), alignment scores, and human side-by-side preference with randomised order; safety recall on red-team prompts and over-blocking on benign prompts; and cost per image and latency on the production pipeline. Online: an A/B test with save, download and share rates as primary metrics, regenerate rate and report rate as guardrails, and time to image.

lm10
Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (IVF, HNSW, product quantisation) trade recall for speed and memory; recall@k is measured against exact search.
rec4
Two-tower retrieval embeds queries and items separately, trains with in-batch and hard negatives, and serves items from an ANN index that must be kept fresh.
rec1
Search stacks have stages: cheap retrieval of thousands of candidates, then ranking of hundreds with richer features, then business rules and diversity.
hd9
A search ranking system learns to order candidates from click and purchase logs with learning-to-rank, evaluated offline by NDCG and online by A/B tests.
why:
A shopper sees a jacket on someone in a café and wants one like it. Typing a description fails: "green jacket with big pockets and a hood" returns ten thousand jackets, none quite right. A marketplace with a billion product images could find it from a photo, if it had visual search. A second shopper photographs their living room and wants the lamp in the corner, the rug and the side table, each one matched to products for sale: "shop the look".

A first attempt is simple: take a pretrained image model, compute a feature vector for every catalogue image, and return the nearest vectors to the query photo's vector. In testing with catalogue photos as queries it looks magical. With real photos it falls apart. The photo of the café jacket returns pictures of cafés, because the model encodes the whole scene. A phone photo in dim light of a white sneaker returns grey sneakers on white backgrounds, because the catalogue's studio lighting dominates. Nearest-neighbour search over a billion vectors of 2,048 floats needs 8 TB of memory and takes seconds per query. Items that sold an hour ago keep appearing, because the index is rebuilt weekly. And when the team upgrades the image model, results become random, because the new query vectors are compared with old catalogue vectors.

The senior design question is to build visual search properly: detection and cropping so queries are about objects, not scenes; embedding models trained for the gap between street photos and catalogue shots; queries that mix image and text ("this, but in red"); an index that fits a billion vectors in memory with product quantisation, worked out by hand; freshness for a catalogue that changes by millions of listings a day; re-ranking with business signals so the first result is something you can actually buy; a latency budget of a few hundred milliseconds; and metrics that separate "the index works" from "the results are right" from "people buy things".

The lesson follows the interview: requirements; estimates for traffic, compute and especially index memory; the API; the high-level design; deep dives on detection and embeddings, product quantisation and index sizing, multimodal queries, freshness and model upgrades, and re-ranking; the latency budget; evaluation; failure modes; and what changes at ten times the scale. The real cases are eBay's and Pinterest's published visual search systems, and the Faiss library's documentation for index choices.
primer:
What the system does

Visual search takes an image as the query and returns catalogue items that look like what is in it. The core trick, used by every system of this kind, is an embedding: a model turns each image (or each object cut out of an image) into a vector of a few hundred numbers, trained so that pictures of the same or similar products land close together. Searching then becomes finding the nearest vectors among a billion, which an approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index does in milliseconds by examining only a tiny fraction of them. Around that core sit a detector that finds objects in the query, a ranking stage that brings in price, stock and quality, and pipelines that keep a fast-changing catalogue searchable.

The mental model: a librarian who remembers faces

Imagine a vast warehouse of products and a librarian who, instead of reading labels, has memorised a compact "face" for every item: a short description in their own private code that captures shape, colour, pattern and style. When you hand them a photo, they first look at what you are pointing at (not the café behind it), form the same kind of compact face for it, and walk straight to the aisle where similar faces are stored, comparing only the items there. Then, from the twenty closest, they pick out the ones actually in stock, at sensible prices, from reliable sellers.

The detector is looking at what you are pointing at. The embedding is the compact face. The IVF index is the aisles: vectors are grouped into clusters and only the nearest clusters are searched. Product quantisation is the librarian's shorthand, which lets a billion faces fit in memory at the cost of some precision. Refinement is taking a closer look at the top few with the full picture. Re-ranking is preferring what you can actually buy. The analogy breaks in one useful place: the librarian's code is learned from data, and if it was learned mostly from studio photos it will describe your dim phone photo badly, no matter how good the aisle system is. Index quality and embedding quality are separate problems.

Three facts that shape the design

First, the query and the catalogue look different: phone photos of objects in the world against studio images on white, so the embedding must be trained for that gap and the detector must isolate objects. Second, memory decides the index: a billion vectors is the scale where uncompressed storage costs terabytes of RAM, so compression and its accuracy loss are the central trade-off. Third, the catalogue never stops changing: on a marketplace, listings appear and sell every minute (eBay's paper calls this volatile inventory), so the index must absorb changes without full rebuilds. A reader who stops here has the shape: detect, embed, search a compressed sharded index with a fresh delta and tombstones, refine, re-rank with business signals, and evaluate the index, the embedding and the business outcome separately.

1 · Requirements

Functional. Search by photo (camera or upload) across a catalogue of 300 million active listings with about 1 billion images; detect multiple objects in a photo and let the user choose one or browse all ("shop the look"); refine with text ("in red", "under $50") and filters (category, price, size, location); "more like this" from any listing image; results show available listings only. Out of scope, said aloud: visual search inside video, and duplicate-listing detection for trust and safety (related, but a separate pipeline).

Latency targets. Server-side p50 under 150 ms and p95 under 300 ms from image received to results returned; the client resizes the photo to about 512 pixels on the long side before upload so upload time stays small.

Freshness targets. New listings searchable within 5 minutes; sold or removed listings gone from results within 1 minute.

Quality targets. On labelled street-to-shop pairs, exact-product recall@10 (the right product among the top ten) at least 60% in fashion and home; on labelled similarity judgements, precision@10 at least 80%; online, a measurable lift in purchases per search over text search for visual categories.

Cost targets. Index serving in RAM affordable per replica (well under a terabyte); re-embedding the full catalogue achievable within a day.

Clarifying questions. "How many images and how fast does the catalogue change?" "Which categories matter most?" "Is there a text search we can blend with?" "Do sellers upload studio photos or phone photos?" "What does success mean: clicks, purchases, or fewer failed text searches?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Traffic. 20 million visual searches a day is about 230 a second on average; with an evening peak about three times the average, 700 queries a second. Each query may yield several crops, but the user usually searches one; assume 1.3 embeddings and index searches per query on average.

Query compute. Detection at about 25 ms and embedding at about 10 ms per crop on a GPU (batched across concurrent queries) is roughly 40 ms of GPU time per query, so 700 × 0.04 ≈ 28 GPUs busy at peak, about 40 with headroom. Small next to the index serving, but enough to need batching and autoscaling.

Index memory, the estimate that shapes the design. One billion vectors at 256 dimensions:

RepresentationBytes per vectorTotal for 1B
float32256 × 4 = 1,0241.02 TB
float16512512 GB
HNSW over float32, M = 321,024 + 32 × 2 × 4 = 1,2801.28 TB
Binary 4,096-bit codes (eBay's choice)512512 GB
IVF-PQ, 32-byte codes + 8-byte ID4040 GB
IVF-PQ, 64-byte codes + 8-byte ID7272 GB

The HNSW figure uses the Faiss wiki's formula, (d × 4 + M × 2 × 4) bytes per vector. The choice is IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes: 72 GB plus about 1 GB of IVF centroids (a million lists × 256 dimensions × 4 bytes) fits comfortably in one large server's memory per replica, where HNSW at 1.28 TB would need a dozen. The cost of compression is accuracy, recovered by refining the top candidates with float16 vectors: 512 GB in total, kept on local NVMe SSDs across the shards.

Ingestion. 10 million new or changed listing images a day is about 116 a second; detection plus embedding at about 35 ms of GPU each is about 4 GPUs. A full re-embed when the model changes is the big one: 1 billion images × about 3 ms each (embedding only, crops cached) = 3 million GPU-seconds, about 830 GPU-hours, a day on 35 GPUs. That number decides how often you can afford to change models.

The insight to say out loud. Compute is modest; memory and freshness are the hard constraints, and embedding quality decides whether any of it is useful. Product quantisation makes a billion vectors fit; the delta index and tombstones make it fresh; the training data makes it right.

3 · API

POST /v1/visual-search
Content-Type: multipart/form-data
  image: (JPEG, long side ≤ 512 px)
  text: "in red"                       # optional modifier
  filters: {"category": null, "price_max": 50, "ship_to": "GB"}
-> { "objects": [ { "box": [x0,y0,x1,y1], "label": "jacket", "score": 0.94,
                    "selected": true },
                  { "box": [...], "label": "boots", "score": 0.88 } ],
     "results": [ { "listing_id": "L83...", "image_id": "...", "score": 0.82,
                    "price": 44.0, "in_stock": true }, ... ],
     "index_version": "emb-v7/ivfpq-2026-10-09", "request_id": "..." }

POST /v1/visual-search/object   { "request_id": "...", "object_index": 1 }  # pick another crop
GET  /v1/listings/{id}/similar                                               # more like this

Two choices matter. The response returns all detected objects with boxes, so the client can draw tappable dots and the user can switch objects without re-uploading (Pinterest's Flashlight showed clickable dots on detected objects). And it returns the index version, because query embeddings and catalogue embeddings must come from the same model; logging the version makes mismatches visible.

4 · Data model

Catalogue images: image ID, listing ID, URL, detected objects with boxes and labels, embedding per object for the current model version, perceptual hash for near-duplicate detection, predicted attributes (category, colour, pattern, material), timestamps. Listings (from the marketplace): status, price, seller, location, attributes the seller entered, engagement statistics. Index versions: model version, codebooks, list centroids, shard layout, build time, the set of image IDs included. Tombstones: image IDs removed since the last build, replicated to every shard. Query logs: query embedding (or a hash of it), crops, results shown, clicks and purchases, for training and evaluation, with retention limits because user photos are personal data.

5 · High-level design

The query path: an API layer receives the image and runs decode and resize; the detection service (GPU, batched) returns boxes; the selected crop goes to the embedding service (GPU, batched), which returns a normalised 256-dimensional vector; the search broker fans out to all index shards in parallel; each shard searches its main IVF-PQ index and its delta index, removes tombstoned and filtered-out items, refines its top candidates with float16 vectors from local SSD, and returns its best 200; the broker merges to the top 500; the re-ranker fetches business features from a feature store and scores the candidates with a learning-to-rank model; a diversity step removes near-duplicates; results return. The ingestion path listens to listing events, fetches images, runs the same detection and embedding models in batch, writes vectors to the shards' delta indexes and attributes to the feature store, and sends deletions to the tombstone set. A nightly index builder produces a new main index per shard, and a model lifecycle pipeline handles re-embedding when the embedding model changes.

6 · Deep dive: detection, cropping and embeddings

Detection first. A user's photo of an outfit contains several products and a lot of background. An object detector (mm10) returns a box, label and confidence for each product it finds. Pinterest's visual discovery paper describes the progression from whole-image features to detected objects, and the payoff: by indexing objects rather than whole images, Lens could find objects within images; their SSD-based detector ran at 290 × 290 pixels in 93 ms on an older AWS GPU (an NVIDIA GRID K520), which shows that detection fits an interactive budget even on modest hardware. Crops get a margin of about 10% so the embedding sees the object's edges, and very small or low-confidence detections are dropped.

Index objects, not just images. The same detector runs on catalogue images at ingestion, so a listing photo of a model wearing a jacket, jeans and boots yields three searchable objects, each mapped back to the listing (and flagged as primary or secondary, since the listing sells the jacket, not the boots). Query crops then match catalogue crops: like with like.

Embeddings that bridge the domain gap. A generic pretrained model encodes everything in a photo: lighting, background, camera angle. What matters is the product's identity and style. The embedding model is therefore fine-tuned with metric learning: training pairs of a user photo (or crop) and the matching catalogue image are pulled together, and other products pushed apart, with a contrastive loss of the kind CLIP and two-tower models use (mm2, rec4). Hard negatives (same category and colour, different product) teach the fine distinctions that decide exact-match search. Pairs come from several sources: user uploads followed by a purchase, sellers' multiple photos of one item, and augmentation that puts catalogue images on varied backgrounds with varied lighting. Category matters: the features that distinguish two sofas differ from those that distinguish two watches, so a shared backbone with category-specific heads, or category-specific models for the biggest categories, is common.

eBay's design as a contrast. eBay's 2017 system used one modified ResNet-50 with two output streams: one predicts the listing's category, the other produces a 4,096-bit binary hash (a sigmoid layer thresholded at 0.5), with both trained to predict category so the hash carries semantic information. Search was limited to the top predicted categories, then ranked by Hamming distance between binary hashes (the count of differing bits), then re-ranked by agreement between predicted aspects (colour, brand, style) and the listing's aspects. Each hash is 512 bytes, keeping storage under 100 GB for 200 million images. It shows the same three ideas this design uses (narrow the search, compress the vectors, re-rank with attributes) in a different form.

7 · Deep dive: product quantisation and index sizing for 1B vectors

Product quantisation, step by step. Take the 256-dimensional embedding and split it into m = 64 sub-vectors of 4 dimensions each. For each of the 64 sub-spaces, run k-means on a training sample to learn a codebook of 256 centroids. To encode a vector, replace each sub-vector with the index (0–255, one byte) of its nearest centroid: 64 bytes instead of 1,024. The codebooks themselves are tiny: 64 × 256 × 4 floats = 256 KB. To search, use asymmetric distance computation (ADC), introduced in Jégou, Douze and Schmid's 2011 paper: the query stays uncompressed; compute a table of distances from each query sub-vector to each of that sub-space's 256 centroids (16,384 numbers), and then the approximate distance to any database vector is the sum of 64 table lookups indexed by its codes. No database vector is ever decompressed.

IVF on top. Scanning a billion codes per query, even at 64 lookups each, is too slow. An inverted file (IVF) first clusters the vectors into lists with a coarse quantiser; each vector is stored in the list of its nearest centroid (in practice PQ encodes the residual, the vector minus its list centroid, which is more accurate). A query finds its nearest nprobe lists and scans only those. The Faiss wiki's guidance for 100 million to 1 billion vectors is IVF1048576_HNSW32: about a million lists (220), with the list centroids themselves searched by a small HNSW graph because a million centroids is too many to compare exhaustively. With a billion vectors in a million lists, each list holds about 1,000 vectors; probing 64 lists scans about 64,000 codes, roughly 4 MB of data and a couple of milliseconds of CPU in total, split across shards.

Refinement. PQ distances are approximate, so the true nearest neighbour may rank 30th. Each shard takes its top 1,000 by PQ distance and recomputes exact distances with float16 vectors (512 bytes each) read from local SSD: 1,000 random reads, issued in parallel, take a few milliseconds on NVMe. The Faiss paper calls this pattern refining with a second, more accurate index. It typically recovers most of the recall lost to compression.

Sharding and replication. The 72 GB index plus delta and tombstones is split into four shards by vector (each holds a quarter of the catalogue), about 19 GB each, so each shard scans a quarter of the probed codes and a failure affects a quarter of the catalogue rather than all of it. Every query fans out to all four shards; the broker waits for all, with a timeout after which it returns results from the shards that answered (a partial result is better than none). Each shard is replicated three times across availability zones. At 700 queries a second with 1.3 searches each, each shard handles about 900 searches a second, spread over three replicas: comfortable for a many-core server, leaving headroom for a zone loss.

Tuning the knobs. nprobe, the number of candidates refined and the PQ code size trade recall against latency and memory. They are tuned by measuring ANN recall@100 against exact search on a sample of real queries (exact search over a billion vectors is slow but fine offline on a sample), choosing the cheapest setting that keeps ANN recall above, say, 95%.

8 · Deep dive: multimodal queries

"This dress, but in red", "similar sofa under $500", "this lamp in brass": users want to modify a visual query with words. Three approaches, in order of effort.

Attribute filters from text. Parse the text for attributes the catalogue knows (colour, material, price, size) and apply them as filters on the visual search: search by the dress image within colour = red. Precise when the attribute is reliable (seller-entered or predicted with high confidence), useless for vague modifiers ("more casual"). Filters interact with ANN indexes: a selective filter can leave too few results among the probed lists, so the shard increases nprobe or falls back to scanning the filtered subset when it is small (the filtered-search problem in detail is in hd26).

Embedding arithmetic in a joint space. If the image embedding lives in a joint image-text space (a CLIP-style model, mm2), combine the normalised image vector with a weighted text vector for "red dress" and search with the sum. It needs no new model and handles vaguer modifiers, but it is approximate: the sum can drift toward "anything red". The weight is tuned on labelled examples.

Composed retrieval models. Train a model on triplets (reference image, modification text, target image) to produce one query vector from both inputs. It handles the modification properly but needs triplet data, which is scarce; marketplaces can mine it from sessions where a user searched with an image and then clicked a variant.

A practical design uses the attribute route for clear structured modifiers, embedding arithmetic for the rest, and measures both on a labelled set of modified queries.

9 · Deep dive: freshness and model upgrades

Additions. When a listing is created, the ingestion pipeline fetches its images, detects and embeds them in micro-batches (a few seconds of batching for GPU efficiency), and inserts the vectors into the owning shard's delta index: a small in-memory index (flat or HNSW, since it holds at most a day's additions, about 10 million vectors across shards, 2.5 million per shard) searched in parallel with the main index on every query. Its results merge with the main index's before refinement. New listings are searchable within minutes.

Deletions. Sold, ended or removed listings must disappear quickly, because showing sold items is the most visible freshness failure. IVF-PQ lists are packed arrays that are expensive to edit, so deletions go to a tombstone set (a hash set or bitmap of image IDs) replicated to every shard and checked when candidates are collected. A deletion takes effect within seconds. Items that change (new price, new photo) are a deletion plus an addition.

Rebuilds. Nightly, an index builder produces a new main index per shard from the full current catalogue: assign vectors to lists, encode with the current codebooks, write the files, and swap them in atomically on each replica, after which the delta and tombstones are reset. Codebooks and list centroids are retrained occasionally (monthly, or when monitoring shows the distribution has drifted, for example after a new category launch), since the Faiss paper notes that techniques fitted to the data distribution, including IVF and PQ, degrade when the distribution changes significantly.

Model upgrades. A new embedding model produces vectors in a new space; mixing them with the old index produces nonsense. The upgrade is a migration: re-embed the catalogue in batch (about 830 GPU-hours), train new codebooks, build a complete new index version alongside the old, dual-write new listings to both, evaluate offline, A/B test with query embedding and index switched together by version, then cut over and keep the old version briefly for rollback. Because this is expensive, teams batch model improvements into a few upgrades a year, or train new models to be backward compatible with old embeddings so they can be mixed during a gradual migration.

10 · Deep dive: re-ranking with business signals

Retrieval returns 500 candidates ordered by visual distance. Ranking decides what the user sees, and visual similarity is only one input. The re-ranker is a learning-to-rank model (hd9), often gradient-boosted trees for speed, trained on logged searches with clicks and purchases as labels, using features: visual similarity (after refinement), category agreement between the query's predicted category and the listing's, attribute agreement (predicted colour, pattern and brand against the listing's), price and price relative to the category median, in-stock status and quantity, seller rating and return rate, shipping location and estimated delivery time, listing freshness, and historical click-through and conversion for the listing. eBay's paper describes a hand-weighted version of attribute agreement: predicted aspects that match the listing's aspects earn reward points, with larger weights for size, brand and price. Learned ranking generalises that idea.

Diversity. Marketplaces have many near-identical listings (a seller lists the same item in ten sizes with the same photo; several sellers use the manufacturer's image). Without a diversity step, the top ten can be ten copies of one product. A perceptual hash groups near-duplicate images, and the ranker keeps the best listing from each group (or groups them in the interface).

Position bias and feedback loops. Training on clicks teaches the ranker what was shown, not what was best. Logged position features at training time (set to a constant at serving), occasional randomisation of lower positions and labelled evaluation sets counter the loop, as in hd9.

11 · The latency budget

Stagep50Notes
Decode and resize10 msclient already resized to 512 px
Detection25 msGPU, batched across concurrent queries
Embedding12 msGPU, batched
Shard fan-out: coarse search, PQ scan, delta, tombstones15 msparallel across four shards, slowest shard counts
Refinement (1,000 SSD reads per shard)8 msparallel I/O
Merge and feature fetch25 msfeature store batch read for 500 candidates
Re-rank and diversity20 mstrees on CPU

The fan-out makes the slowest shard set the latency, so tail control matters: a hedged request to another replica if a shard has not answered by its p95, and a hard timeout after which partial results are returned. The GPU stages batch requests for efficiency, which adds a few milliseconds of waiting at low load and saves many at high load.

12 · Evaluation plan

Three layers, measured separately. Index fidelity: ANN recall@100 of the production index against exact search with the same embedding, on a sample of real query embeddings; this catches index regressions (bad codebooks, wrong nprobe) independently of model quality. Relevance: on labelled sets, exact-product recall@10 for street-to-shop pairs (did the purchased product appear?), and similar-product precision@10 from human raters judging "would this satisfy the shopper?", by category, by query type (camera photo, screenshot, catalogue image) and by detected object size. Business impact: online A/B tests by user, with purchases or add-to-cart per visual search as the primary metric, and click-through, zero-click rate, follow-up text searches (a sign the visual search failed), latency and complaint rate as guardrails.

Report by category. Visual search helps some categories far more than others. Pinterest reported that adding visual features to Related Pins increased engagement by 3.2% across 5 million query Pins and 4.0% when expanded to 100 million, with the largest gains in visual categories (art 8.8%, tattoos 8.0%, illustrations 7.9%) and the smallest in text-driven ones (quotes 2.0%, fitness planning 0.2%). An average hides where the system works and where it does not.

Freshness metrics. Time from listing creation to searchable (p50, p99), share of results that are sold or removed at click time (should be near zero), delta index size before rebuild.

13 · Failure modes and trade-offs

FailureSymptomDefence

Wrong cropResults match the background objectShow detected objects; detector evaluation on user photos
