Near-duplicate floodTop ten are one productPerceptual-hash grouping, diversity rules

The trade-offs to name: compression against accuracy (PQ code size, refinement depth); nprobe against latency; freshness against rebuild cost; category routing against recall; generic embeddings (cheap, broad) against category-specific ones (accurate, more models to maintain); visual similarity against business value in ranking.

14 · What changes at 10× scale

At 10 billion images, IVF-PQ at 72 bytes per vector is 720 GB per replica, so the index spreads over many more shards, or moves to a disk-resident graph index such as DiskANN (hd26), which keeps compressed vectors in RAM and the graph and full vectors on SSD. Re-embedding becomes a week of hundreds of GPUs, so backward-compatible embedding training becomes essential and model upgrades rarer. Query traffic at 7,000 a second makes GPU batching for detection and embedding a serious fleet, and caching embeddings for repeated query images (screenshots of popular products are shared widely) pays off. And multimodal queries are likely to shift toward a single joint model for images and text, so text search and visual search can share one index and one ranker.
deep:
Why PQ works: dimensions are not equally informative, and codebooks adapt

Product quantisation assumes each sub-vector can be summarised by one of 256 representatives without losing much. That holds when the sub-spaces capture roughly independent, balanced parts of the variance. When variance is concentrated in a few dimensions, some codebooks waste their 256 slots on noise while others are starved. OPQ (optimised product quantisation) learns a rotation of the vector space before splitting it, spreading variance evenly across sub-spaces; the Faiss paper describes it as a preprocessing step that makes PQ more accurate when the data's variance sits in a few components. For embeddings from models trained with normalised outputs, the gain is often modest; for raw CNN features it can be large. It is cheap to try and should be measured on recall.

Residual encoding is why IVF-PQ beats PQ alone

Encoding a vector directly with PQ spends the codebooks on describing where the vector is in the whole space. In IVF-PQ, the coarse quantiser already says which of a million regions the vector is in, so PQ encodes only the residual, the small offset from the region's centroid. Residuals are smaller and more uniform than raw vectors, so the same 64 bytes describe them more accurately. This is also why more lists improve accuracy as well as speed, up to the point where the coarse search itself becomes the bottleneck, which is where the HNSW coarse quantiser comes in.

Detection quality silently caps search quality

If the detector misses the object the user cares about, or boxes it badly, the best embedding cannot help, and the failure looks like bad search rather than bad detection. Detection must therefore be evaluated on user photos specifically (not catalogue images, where objects are centred and isolated), with recall of the products users actually tapped, and the interface should let users adjust the crop. A useful diagnostic is to compare search success when users accept the automatic crop against when they adjust it: a large gap means the detector, not the embedding, is the bottleneck.

Binary codes versus PQ is a speed-accuracy-simplicity choice

eBay's 4,096-bit binary hashes compare with Hamming distance, which modern CPUs compute with a few instructions per 64 bits, and need no codebooks, so they are simple and very fast. But at 512 bytes per image they are eight times larger than 64-byte PQ codes, and binary codes generally preserve distances less finely for the same size. eBay compensated by searching only within the top predicted categories, which shrinks the scan dramatically. PQ with refinement gives better accuracy per byte; binary codes give simplicity and speed. Newer quantisers such as RaBitQ, documented in the Faiss wiki at about one bit per dimension plus a small overhead, revisit the binary idea with better accuracy.

Embedding versioning is a data-management problem

Every stored embedding is tied to a model version, and everything downstream (indexes, caches, deduplication, recommendation features built on the same embeddings) inherits that version. Teams that treat embeddings as plain columns discover during the first upgrade that a dozen systems quietly depend on the old space. The fix is organisational as much as technical: an embedding registry recording which systems consume which version, dual-writing during migrations, and deprecation dates. Backward-compatible training (adding a loss that keeps new embeddings comparable to old ones) trades a little accuracy for the ability to upgrade incrementally.

Visual search and text search should share a ranker

Users move between modes: photo, then text refinement, then filters. If visual search and text search have different rankers and different notions of relevance, results jump around confusingly. Sharing the ranking stage (the same learning-to-rank model with query-type features) and the same candidate features means business rules, diversity and personalisation behave consistently, and improvements to the ranker benefit both. Joint image-text embedding models make the convergence natural: a single index can serve image queries, text queries and combined ones.

Narrowing the search is a recall bet

Every shortcut that searches less (probing fewer IVF lists, searching only the top predicted categories as eBay did, filtering by attributes parsed from text) is a bet that the right answer lies inside the narrowed space. When the bet loses, the item is not ranked low; it is absent, and no ranker can recover it. The defence is to measure each narrowing step's own recall on labelled data (how often is the purchased product inside the top three predicted categories?) and to hedge: search the top few categories rather than one, raise nprobe for queries whose nearest lists are almost equally close, and fall back to a wider search when the narrowed one returns weak scores.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The half-migrated model. During an embedding-model upgrade, the query service was deployed with the new model a day before the index swap completed on one of four shards. Results from that shard were essentially random and, merged with the others, quietly degraded quality for 25% of candidates. No error fired. The fix: every shard reports its index version, the broker rejects shards whose version differs from the query embedding's, and dashboards show version per shard.

Sold-out first results. After a traffic peak, the tombstone replication stream lagged by twenty minutes, and the top results for popular products were listings that had sold out. Click-to-dead-listing rate jumped from 0.1% to 4%. Tombstone lag is now an alerting metric with a one-minute threshold, and the re-ranker also checks live availability from the listing service for the top twenty results.

The background bias. A new category (home décor) launched with an embedding fine-tuned mostly on fashion pairs. Searches for lamps returned lamps photographed in similar rooms rather than similar lamps. Offline ANN recall was excellent; relevance on a newly labelled décor set was poor. Fine-tuning with décor street-to-shop pairs and object-level crops fixed it, and category-level relevance became part of the release gate.

What to monitor

Query path: latency by stage and by shard, timeouts and partial results, GPU batch sizes and queueing, detection counts per image. Index: ANN recall on a fixed query sample after every rebuild, delta size, tombstone count and replication lag, memory per shard, version per shard. Quality: daily sampled relevance judgements by category, click-through, purchases per search, follow-up text searches, click-to-dead-listing rate. Ingestion: time to searchable, embedding failures, backlog.

Knobs people tune

nprobe and refinement depth per category; PQ code size; delta index size before forced rebuild; tombstone check strategy; detector confidence threshold and crop margin; weight of text in embedding arithmetic; re-ranker features and diversity thresholds; GPU batch window.

The real cases: eBay and Pinterest

eBay's "Visual Search at eBay" (Yang et al., KDD 2017) describes a system built for a marketplace whose inventory is volatile: items are listed and sold every minute. A single modified ResNet-50 predicts category and produces a 4,096-bit binary semantic hash in one forward pass; search is limited to the top predicted categories, ranked by Hamming distance and re-ranked by aspect agreement (with more weight on size, brand and price); each hash takes 512 bytes, keeping storage under 100 GB for 200 million images. It powered visual search in eBay ShopBot and Close5. Pinterest's "Visual Discovery at Pinterest" (Zhai et al., WWW 2017) traces Related Pins (2014), Similar Looks (2015), Flashlight (2016) and Lens (2017); applies object detection to billions of images so that objects rather than whole images are indexed; reports an SSD detector at 290 × 290 in 93 ms on an NVIDIA GRID K520; and measures engagement gains from visual features of 3.2% on 5 million query Pins and 4.0% on 100 million, strongest in visual categories. Both papers predate today's joint image-text models, but their architecture (detect, embed, compress, narrow, re-rank with attributes, measure engagement by category) is the template this design follows. The index arithmetic uses the Faiss wiki's published memory formula for HNSW, its PQ code sizes and its recommendation of an IVF with about a million lists for 100 million to 1 billion vectors.
myths: Visual search is nearest neighbours on a pretrained image model's features.

Generic features find images that look alike overall (same background, same lighting), not the same product. Customers photograph items on a street or a sofa; catalogues show them on white backgrounds. Production systems detect and crop the object first and train embeddings on pairs of user photos and product images so the same product lands close despite the gap.
A billion vectors need a cluster of huge machines.

At 256 dimensions, a billion float32 vectors take 1 TB, and HNSW adds links on top (about 1.28 TB at M = 32). Product quantisation to 64 bytes plus an 8-byte ID is 72 GB, which fits on one large server per replica; full-precision vectors for re-ranking the top candidates can sit on local SSD. Compression is what makes billion-scale search affordable.
Recall@k of the ANN index is the quality metric.

ANN recall only says how faithfully the index reproduces exact nearest neighbours of the embedding; if the embedding puts the wrong products close together, a perfect index returns them perfectly. Quality needs relevance labels (is this the same or a similar product?) and online purchase and click metrics, measured separately from index fidelity.
Upgrade the embedding model and the index just gets better.

Vectors from different models live in different spaces: a query embedded by the new model and compared with catalogue vectors from the old one returns nonsense. A model upgrade means re-embedding the whole catalogue (about 830 GPU-hours for a billion images at 3 ms each), building a new index version, and switching queries and index together.
Visual similarity is enough to rank results.

The most similar listing may be sold out, overpriced, from a poor seller or ten copies of the same photo from one shop. Retrieval finds candidates by appearance; ranking then mixes in availability, price, seller quality, predicted attributes and engagement history, and enforces diversity.
lab:
Goal: build the index memory calculator behind section 2: bytes per vector and total memory for flat, float16, HNSW, binary and IVF-PQ options; shard and replica counts for a given server size; and the GPU-hours of a full re-embed. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as pq_memory.py and run python pq_memory.py.
  2. Read the memory table for 1 billion 256-dimensional vectors and confirm the lesson's numbers: 1,024 GB float32, 1,280 GB HNSW at M = 32, and about 73 GB for PQ64 with IDs once the coarse centroids (about 1 GB) are added.
  3. Read the shard plan: how many 256 GB servers each option needs per replica, and in total with three replicas.
  4. Change D to 768 (a typical text-embedding size) and see HNSW grow to over 3 TB while PQ64 stays at 72 GB: PQ's size depends on the code length, not the dimension.
  5. Change N to 10 billion and read the re-embed estimate; then halve MS_PER_IMAGE to see why faster embedding models make upgrades practical.
"""Vector index memory, shard and re-embed calculator. Python 3.12, stdlib only."""
import math
N, D = 1_000_000_000, 256            # vectors, dimensions
ID_BYTES, RAM_GB, USABLE, REPLICAS = 8, 256, 0.7, 3
NLIST, MS_PER_IMAGE, GPUS = 1 << 20, 3.0, 35

def options(d):
    return {
        "float32 flat":       4 * d,
        "float16 flat":       2 * d,
        "SQ8 (1 byte/dim)":   d,
        "HNSW M=32 (fp32)":   4 * d + 32 * 2 * 4,      # Faiss wiki: d*4 + M*2*4
        "binary 4096-bit":    4096 // 8,
        "IVF-PQ32 + id":      32 + ID_BYTES,
        "IVF-PQ64 + id":      64 + ID_BYTES,
        "IVF-PQ64 + id + fp16 on SSD": 64 + ID_BYTES,    # RAM only; SSD listed below
    }
print(f"N = {N:,} vectors, d = {D}\n")
print(f"{'option':30} {'B/vec':>7} {'RAM GB':>9} {'servers/replica':>16} {'total':>6}")
for name, b in options(D).items():
    gb = N * b / 1e9
    if "IVF" in name: gb += NLIST * D * 4 / 1e9          # coarse centroids
    per = math.ceil(gb / (RAM_GB * USABLE))
    print(f"{name:30} {b:7} {gb:9,.0f} {per:16} {per * REPLICAS:6}")
print(f"\nfp16 vectors for refinement on SSD: {N * 2 * D / 1e9:,.0f} GB")
pq_m = 64; sub = D // pq_m
print(f"PQ{pq_m}: {pq_m} sub-vectors of {sub} dims, codebooks "
      f"{pq_m * 256 * sub * 4 / 1024:.0f} KB, lookup table {pq_m * 256:,} entries per query")
per_list = N / NLIST
for nprobe in (16, 64, 256):
    print(f"nprobe {nprobe:4}: scans ~{nprobe * per_list:,.0f} codes "
          f"(~{nprobe * per_list * pq_m / 1e6:.1f} MB) per query")
gpu_h = N * MS_PER_IMAGE / 1000 / 3600
print(f"\nFull re-embed: {gpu_h:,.0f} GPU-hours = {gpu_h / GPUS:.1f} h on {GPUS} GPUs")

What to look for: a sixteen-fold gap between float32 and PQ64 and nearly eighteen-fold against HNSW; PQ memory independent of dimension; the scan size growing linearly with nprobe (which is why recall and latency trade off); and a re-embed measured in hundreds of GPU-hours, the hidden cost of every embedding-model change.
recap: Visual search takes a photo, finds the objects in it, embeds each object, retrieves similar catalogue images from an approximate nearest-neighbour index, and ranks them with business signals.
Detection and cropping matter because users photograph scenes; indexing and querying objects rather than whole images is what made Pinterest's Lens and Flashlight work.
Embeddings must bridge the domain gap between user photos and catalogue shots, so they are trained with matched pairs and hard negatives, often per category.
Multimodal queries such as "this but in red" combine an image embedding with text, either through a joint image-text space, a composed-retrieval model or an attribute filter derived from the text.
For 1 billion 256-dimensional vectors, float32 is 1 TB, HNSW about 1.28 TB, and IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes plus 8-byte IDs about 72 GB; full vectors for re-ranking the top 1,000 sit on SSD.

Product quantisation splits each vector into 64 sub-vectors of 4 dimensions and replaces each with the index of one of 256 learned centroids, a 16-fold compression with distances computed from lookup tables.
FAISS's guidance for 100 million to 1 billion vectors is an IVF with about a million lists and an HNSW coarse quantiser; probing 64 lists scans about 64,000 codes per query.

Freshness comes from a small delta index for new listings and a tombstone filter for sold ones, merged into the main index by periodic rebuilds; a model upgrade requires a full re-embed and a versioned switch.
A server-side budget of about 130 ms at the median covers decoding, detection, embedding, sharded search, refinement, feature fetch and re-ranking.

Evaluation separates index fidelity (ANN recall against exact search), relevance (exact and similar product recall on labelled pairs) and business impact (clicks, add-to-cart and purchases per search).
glossary: Computing distances between an uncompressed query and compressed database vectors by precomputing a lookup table of query-to-centroid distances for each sub-vector.
Search that returns most of the true nearest vectors while examining only a small fraction of the collection.
The first-level clustering in an IVF index that assigns each vector to a list; at billion scale it is itself searched with a small HNSW index.
The set of centroids learned for one sub-space in product quantisation; 256 centroids lets each code fit in one byte.
Searching with an image plus a text modification ("same shape, in red"), using a model that combines the two into one query vector.
A small, frequently updated index holding recent additions, searched alongside the large main index until the next rebuild.
The difference in appearance between query images (phone photos in real scenes) and catalogue images (studio shots), which generic features handle poorly.
The number of bit positions in which two binary codes differ; eBay's visual search compared 4,096-bit codes this way.
A training example that looks similar to the query but is a different product, used to teach the model fine distinctions.
Hierarchical navigable small world: a layered graph index in which each vector links to near neighbours, searched greedily from coarse to fine layers.
An index that clusters vectors into lists and searches only the lists nearest the query.
The number of IVF lists searched per query; higher raises recall and cost.
Optimised product quantisation: a learned rotation applied before PQ so variance is spread evenly across sub-vectors, improving accuracy.
A short fingerprint of an image that stays the same under small changes, used to find near-duplicate images.
Compressing a vector by splitting it into sub-vectors and storing, for each, the index of its nearest centroid in a learned codebook.
Recomputing exact distances for the top candidates from an approximate search using full-precision vectors, to fix quantisation errors.
One partition of the index, holding a subset of the vectors; queries fan out to all shards and merge their results.
Solid-state storage attached over a fast bus, able to serve hundreds of thousands of small random reads per second.
Matching a photo taken in the real world to the same product's catalogue image.
A marker that an item has been deleted, checked at query time until the index is rebuilt without it.
drill:
Estimate it

A furniture marketplace has 200 million images, embeds them at 512 dimensions, and serves 300 visual queries a second at peak. (a) Memory for float32, HNSW at M = 16, and IVF-PQ with 32-byte codes plus 8-byte IDs? (b) Which would you choose for servers with 256 GB of RAM, and how would you shard and replicate? (c) How long would a re-embed take on 20 GPUs at 4 ms per image?

Answer

(a) float32: 512 × 4 = 2,048 bytes × 200 million = 410 GB. HNSW at M = 16: 2,048 + 16 × 2 × 4 = 2,176 bytes, 435 GB. IVF-PQ32 + ID: 40 bytes, 8 GB (plus centroids: with 262,144 lists, the Faiss suggestion for 10–100 million scaled up, about 0.5 GB).

(b) IVF-PQ fits on one server per replica with plenty of room; with 512 dimensions, 32-byte codes are aggressive compression (16 dimensions per byte-code), so use 64-byte codes (72 bytes with ID, about 14 GB) and refine the top 500–1,000 with float16 vectors (1,024 bytes each, 205 GB in total) on local SSD. Two shards for parallelism and fault isolation, three replicas each across zones; at 300 queries a second each shard replica handles about 100 searches a second, very light. HNSW in RAM (435 GB) would need at least two servers per replica just for memory and would only pay off if latency or recall targets demanded it.

(c) 200 million × 4 ms = 800,000 GPU-seconds ≈ 222 GPU-hours ÷ 20 GPUs ≈ 11 hours, an overnight job, so model upgrades are practical a few times a year with a versioned index switch.

Diagnose it

After a nightly rebuild, purchases per visual search drop 6% in all categories at once. Latency, detection counts and the embedding model version are unchanged. What do you check?

Answer

A drop everywhere that starts with a rebuild, with the embedding unchanged, points at the index rather than the model. Check ANN recall@100 against exact search on the fixed query sample for the new build versus the previous one: if it fell (say from 96% to 85%), the index is the cause. Then find why: codebooks or list centroids retrained on a bad sample (for example a sample dominated by one new category), a configuration change in nprobe or refinement depth, a shard built from a partial catalogue (check vector counts per shard against the catalogue), or residuals encoded against the wrong centroids after a mismatched training step. Roll back to the previous build (keep it for exactly this reason), fix the build, and add an automatic gate: a rebuild is not swapped in unless its recall on the fixed sample is within a point of the previous build and its vector counts match the catalogue.
qa: E
Walk through what happens when a user searches with a photo.

The image is resized and decoded; a detector finds the products in it (dress, bag, shoes) and the user picks one or the top one is used; the crop is embedded by an image model; the embedding is searched in a sharded approximate nearest-neighbour index for a few hundred candidates; full-precision vectors refine the order; a ranking model adds price, availability, seller quality and engagement; near-duplicates are removed; results return in a few hundred milliseconds.
E
Why detect and crop before embedding?

Because users photograph scenes, not products: a photo of an outfit contains a jacket, jeans, shoes, a street and a person. Embedding the whole image matches other street scenes. Cropping to the object matches the catalogue, which shows single products, and lets one photo produce several searches (shop the look). Pinterest found that indexing and querying detected objects rather than whole images improved engagement.
E
What is product quantisation in one minute?

Split a vector into, say, 64 pieces of 4 numbers. For each piece, learn 256 representative values (a codebook) with k-means. Store each piece as the one-byte index of its nearest representative: 64 bytes instead of 1,024 for float32 at 256 dimensions. To search, compute a table of distances from each query piece to the 256 representatives, then a database vector's distance is the sum of 64 table lookups.
M
Size the index for 1 billion images.

At 256 dimensions: float32 is 1,024 bytes a vector, 1 TB in total; float16 512 GB; HNSW with M = 32 adds 256 bytes of links, about 1.28 TB. IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes plus an 8-byte ID is 72 GB, plus about 1 GB of IVF centroids for a million lists. Split into four shards of about 19 GB for parallelism, replicate three times across zones, and keep float16 vectors for refinement on local SSD (about 128 GB per shard).

Follow-up: Why not keep float16 in RAM? — You can (512 GB across shards), and refinement gets faster; it is a cost decision. SSD reads of 1,000 vectors per query take a few milliseconds with parallel I/O, which fits the budget at a fraction of the memory cost.
M
How do you keep the index fresh when 10 million listings change a day?

New listings are embedded within a minute or two and inserted into a small in-memory delta index on each shard, searched alongside the main index. Sold or removed listings are added to a tombstone set checked at query time, which takes effect in seconds. The main IVF-PQ index is rebuilt periodically (daily) including the deltas and excluding tombstones, and its codebooks are retrained occasionally when the data distribution drifts.
M
How do you handle "this dress, but in red"?

Three options with different costs. A joint image-text space lets you combine the normalised image embedding with the text embedding of "red dress", which works roughly and needs no new model. A composed-retrieval model trained on triplets (image, modification text, target image) does it properly. An attribute route parses "red" into a colour filter and searches by image within that filter. Many systems use the attribute filter for clear attributes and the learned combination for vaguer ones, and evaluate each on labelled examples.
M
What signals does the re-ranker use, and why not rank by similarity alone?

Visual similarity, category agreement, predicted attributes matching the listing's attributes (colour, brand, size), price, availability, seller rating, shipping location, freshness and historical click and purchase rates. Similarity alone surfaces sold-out items, extreme prices and many copies of one seller's photo. eBay re-ranked visual matches by agreement between predicted aspects and the listing's aspects, weighting size, brand and price more.
M
How is the embedding model trained for street-to-shop?

On pairs of a user photo or crop and the matching catalogue image, with a contrastive or triplet loss so matching pairs are close and different products far apart; hard negatives (same category, similar look, different product) teach fine distinctions. Pairs come from purchase and click logs (user uploads followed by a purchase), seller-provided multiple photos and synthetic augmentation (backgrounds, lighting, crops). Category-specific heads or models help where categories differ a lot.
Follow-up: What goes wrong with click-derived pairs? — They are noisy and biased toward what was shown; mix in human-labelled pairs and evaluate on a labelled set built independently of the ranking.
H
You must upgrade the embedding model. Plan it.

Embeddings from the new model are incompatible with the old index, so: re-embed the whole catalogue in a batch job (about 830 GPU-hours at 3 ms per image for 1 billion images, a day on about 35 GPUs), train new PQ codebooks and build a new index version alongside the old one, while also embedding new listings with both models. Evaluate offline on labelled pairs, then A/B test with queries and index switched together by version. Cut over atomically, keep the old version for rollback, then retire it.

Follow-up: Can you avoid a full re-embed? — Backward-compatible training, where the new model is trained so its embeddings stay comparable with the old ones, allows a gradual migration at some cost in quality; it is worth it when re-embedding is very expensive.
H
Recall looks fine offline but users say results are "similar but not the thing I photographed". Debug it.

Separate index fidelity from embedding quality. Check ANN recall against exact search on real queries: if it is high, the index is fine and the embedding is the problem. Then look at the queries: are crops wrong (detector picking the background object), are queries mostly street photos while training data was mostly catalogue-to-catalogue, are certain categories failing? Build a labelled street-to-shop set from these complaints, measure exact-product recall@10 by category, and retrain with more real user-photo pairs and hard negatives.
H
How do you shard and replicate the index for 700 queries a second at peak?

Shard by vector (each shard holds a quarter of the catalogue), so every query fans out to all shards and results are merged; this keeps each shard's scan small and latency low. Each shard probes 64 of its lists, about 16,000 codes, a millisecond or two of CPU. Replicate each shard three times across zones for availability and throughput; a shard replica on a 32-core machine handles well over a thousand such queries a second. Hedge slow shard responses and return partial results if one shard times out rather than failing the query.

Follow-up: Why not shard by category? — Category routing reduces fan-out but makes errors in category prediction fatal (the product is in a shard you did not search) and creates hot shards for popular categories; eBay used predicted categories to limit search but searched the top predictions, not one.
H
What metrics decide whether a new version ships?

Offline: ANN recall@100 against exact search (index fidelity), exact-product recall@10 and similar-product precision@10 on labelled street-to-shop sets by category, latency and memory. Online: an A/B test by user with purchases or add-to-cart per visual search as the primary metric, click-through and zero-click rate, follow-up text searches (a sign of failure), latency p95 and complaints as guardrails. Report by category, because visual search helps visual categories most; Pinterest measured gains of 8.8% in art but 0.2% in fitness planning.
refs: Yang et al., KDD 2017: one ResNet-50 network predicts category and a 4,096-bit binary hash in a single pass; search limited to top predicted categories; 512 bytes per image, under 100 GB for 200 million images; aspect-based re-ranking; built for volatile inventory.

Zhai et al., WWW 2017: Related Pins, Similar Looks, Flashlight and Lens; object detection applied to billions of images; SSD detection at 290 × 290 in 93 ms on a GRID K520; visual features gave +3.2% engagement on 5M query Pins and +4.0% on 100M.
Douze et al., 2024: vector codecs including product quantisation, IVF and graph indexes, refinement with a second index, and guidance on choosing indexes by size and memory.
Faiss wiki: Guidelines to choose an index
Memory per vector for HNSW is (d × 4 + M × 2 × 4) bytes; PQ M-byte codes; IVF1048576_HNSW32 suggested for 100M–1B vectors; IVF list counts and training sizes.
Product quantization for nearest neighbor search
Jégou, Douze and Schmid, IEEE TPAMI 2011: the original product quantisation and asymmetric distance computation, with the inverted-file system (IVFADC) for billion-scale search.
Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)
Radford et al., 2021: a joint image-text embedding trained contrastively on 400 million pairs, the basis of many multimodal (image plus text) retrieval systems.

t: Design a vector database
sum: A multi-tenant vector database for 10 billion vectors: points with metadata, HNSW, IVF-PQ and DiskANN with memory arithmetic, why filtered HNSW recall collapses at 1% selectivity and how planners, ACORN and filter-aware edges fix it, LSM-style segments for writes, deletes and compaction, sharding, hybrid BM25 + vector queries, consistency, recall tuning and cost per million vectors.
prereq: lm10
Embeddings put similar meanings close together; IVF, HNSW and product quantisation trade recall for speed and memory, and recall@k is measured against exact search.
db15

pgvector stores vectors in PostgreSQL with HNSW (m = 16, ef_construction = 64 by default) and IVFFlat indexes; approximate indexes apply WHERE filters after the index scan, so selective filters return too few rows.
rec5
Hybrid search runs lexical (BM25) and dense retrieval and fuses the rankings, usually with reciprocal rank fusion.
hd2
Enterprise RAG stores hundreds of millions of chunk vectors, filters retrieval by user permissions, and needs deletions to propagate in minutes.
hd25
Product quantisation compresses a vector into short codes searched with lookup tables; IVF-PQ fits a billion vectors in tens of gigabytes, and refinement with full vectors restores accuracy.
in3
A distributed system shards data by key, replicates each shard, and chooses how stale a read may be.
why:
A company sells a platform for building AI applications. Each customer uploads documents, product catalogues or support tickets, the platform embeds them, and the customer's application retrieves the most relevant ones for every question (hd2 is one such application). After a year, the platform holds 10 billion vectors for 50,000 customers. The largest customer has 2 billion; the median has 50,000. The vectors sit in an off-the-shelf approximate nearest-neighbour library, one big index per region, with the customer ID stored next to each vector.

The problems arrive together. Memory: an HNSW index over 768-dimensional vectors needs about 3.2 KB per vector, so 10 billion vectors need 32 TB of RAM per replica, and the cloud bill shows it. Filters: a small customer searching only its own 50,000 vectors in a shared index of hundreds of millions gets three results instead of ten, or the right ten after 400 ms, because the index searched everyone's vectors and threw away the ones that were not theirs. Writes: customers upsert documents all day, and the library they chose cannot delete vectors from an HNSW graph, so deleted documents keep appearing in answers until a weekly rebuild. A legal request to erase one customer's data takes a week. And when a node dies, rebuilding its index from scratch takes hours.

These are the problems a vector database exists to solve, and designing one is a favourite senior interview question because it pulls together indexing, storage engines, distributed systems and query planning. The question: design a system that stores billions of vectors with metadata, answers filtered top-k queries in tens of milliseconds at a guaranteed recall, absorbs a stream of upserts and deletes, isolates thousands of tenants, scales out and survives failures, supports hybrid keyword and vector queries, and does it at a cost per million vectors that customers will pay.

The lesson follows the interview: requirements; estimates with memory arithmetic for each index type; the data model and API; the high-level design; deep dives on index choice and cost, filtered search and why its recall collapses, writes, deletes and compaction, sharding and replication, hybrid queries, multi-tenancy and consistency; recall and latency tuning; evaluation; failure modes; and what changes at ten times the scale. The real cases are the HNSW, DiskANN and ACORN papers, the Faiss documentation's memory formulas, and Qdrant's documentation of how a production engine plans filtered queries. The basics of embeddings and approximate search are in lm10 and db15; product quantisation is worked in hd25.
primer:
What a vector database does

A vector database stores points, each an ID, one or more vectors (lists of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers produced by an embedding model) and a payload of metadata such as tenant, document ID, date and tags. Its main query is: given a query vector, return the k points whose vectors are nearest, among those whose payload passes a filter. "Nearest" is by a distance metric fixed per collection: cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. Because exact search over billions of vectors is too slow, it uses approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes that return most of the true nearest points while examining a small fraction, and it measures how many it got right as recall.

The mental model: a library with a map, an index card system, and a returns desk

Imagine a vast library where books are shelved not by title but by what they are about, so that books on similar subjects sit near each other. A reader arrives with a description and wants the ten closest books, but only those in a particular language and published after 2020. The library has three tools. A map of the shelves lets a librarian walk from any shelf toward the right neighbourhood in a few hops: that is a graph index like HNSW. A card catalogue by language and year tells the librarian how many books pass the reader's conditions and where they are: that is a payload index. And a returns desk collects newly arrived books and returned ones until they can be shelved, while a list at the entrance records books that have been withdrawn: that is the mutable segment and the tombstone list.

The hard cases are visible in the analogy. If only one book in a hundred is in the requested language, walking the map and checking each book's language means looking at a hundred books to find one that qualifies; following only qualifying books may lead nowhere, because their neighbours on the map are mostly in other languages. A good librarian checks the card catalogue first: if only 200 books qualify, just look at all 200. That decision, made per query, is the query planner. The analogy breaks in one place: a real library has one copy of each book, while the database keeps several replicas on different machines and must keep them in step as books arrive and leave every second.

Three facts that shape the design

First, memory is the dominant cost, and index choice moves it by a factor of thirty: full-precision graphs in RAM against compressed codes with full vectors on SSD. Second, filters break the indexes' assumptions: ANN structures are built over all vectors, but most real queries ask about a subset (one tenant, recent documents, a category), and a strict filter can wreck recall or latency unless the planner adapts. Third, the data never stops changing: graph indexes are awkward to update and some libraries cannot delete at all, so the engine borrows the log-structured design of modern databases: append to a log, buffer in memory, flush immutable segments, merge them later. A reader who stops here has the shape: a sharded, replicated log-structured store of segments, each with a vector index and payload indexes, searched in parallel and planned per query by filter cardinality.

1 · Requirements

Functional. Namespaces (collections) with a fixed dimension and metric; upsert, delete and fetch points by ID; top-k queries with filters on payload fields (equality, ranges, sets, combinations); multiple named vectors per point and sparse vectors for hybrid search; payload indexes declared per field; batch import; snapshots and restore; per-namespace configuration of index type and recall target. Out of scope, said aloud: computing embeddings (the client or a separate service does that) and general SQL.

Scale. 10 billion vectors across 50,000 namespaces, mostly 768 dimensions; largest namespace 2 billion, median 50,000. 20,000 queries a second in total at peak; 50,000 upserts a second.

Latency and recall targets. In-memory tier: p99 under 50 ms at recall@10 of at least 0.95 for unfiltered and filtered queries. Disk tier: p99 under 150 ms at the same recall. Recall is measured against exact search with the same filter.

Freshness and consistency. Upserts searchable within 1 second at p99 by default; read-your-writes on request. Deletes hidden from results immediately; physically purged within 24 hours, faster on an erasure request.

Durability and availability. No acknowledged write lost; 99.95% availability for queries; a lost node's data back to full replication within 30 minutes.

Cost. A published price per million vectors per month for each tier, which the design must support with margin.

Clarifying questions. "What dimensions and how many vectors per tenant?" "What filters do customers use, and how selective?" "What recall do customers expect, and do they measure it?" "How write-heavy is it, and how fast must deletes disappear?" "Is there a cold tier for rarely queried namespaces?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Memory per vector. For one billion 768-dimensional vectors:

IndexRAM per vectorRAM per 1BSSD per 1B
Raw float32 (flat)768 × 4 = 3,072 B3.07 TB–
HNSW, M = 16, float323,072 + 16 × 2 × 4 = 3,200 B3.2 TB–
HNSW, SQ8 vectors, rescoring from SSD768 + 128 = 896 B0.9 TB3.07 TB
IVF-PQ, 96-byte codes + 8-byte ID104 B104 GB3.07 TB
DiskANN, 64-byte PQ in RAM64 B64 GB≈ 3.33 TB

The HNSW figure uses the Faiss wiki's formula, (d × 4 + M × 2 × 4) bytes per vector: the vector itself plus about 2M links of 4 bytes, because the HNSW paper recommends twice as many links on the bottom layer as on the others (Mmax0 = 2M). DiskANN's SSD figure is the full vector plus up to R = 64 neighbour IDs of 4 bytes per node: 3,072 + 256 = 3,328 bytes. Across 10 billion vectors, HNSW in RAM would be 32 TB per replica; IVF-PQ or DiskANN about 0.6–1 TB of RAM per replica plus SSD.

Cost per million vectors per month. Assume, for illustration, $3 per GB-month for RAM on memory-optimised instances, $0.15 per GB-month for local NVMe SSD, about $0.023 per GB-month for object storage, and two replicas for the hot tiers.

TierPer 1M vectorsMonthly, 2 replicas
HNSW float32 in RAM3.2 GB RAM≈ $19
HNSW SQ8 + SSD rescoring0.9 GB RAM + 3.1 GB SSD≈ $6.30
IVF-PQ96 + SSD rescoring0.10 GB RAM + 3.1 GB SSD≈ $1.54

Compute for queries and index building comes on top, and depends on query rate, but the storage spread is the headline: about fourteen times between all-RAM HNSW and the compressed tiers, and two orders of magnitude more for cold data.

Query compute. 20,000 queries a second, many fanning out to several segments and shards. A filtered HNSW search on one segment computes a few hundred to a few thousand distances; at 768 dimensions a distance is about 1,500 floating-point operations, so a query costs a few million operations per segment, under a millisecond on one core. The fleet is sized by memory first, then by cores for the query rate.

Writes. 50,000 upserts a second at 3 KB of vector plus payload is about 150 MB a second into the logs, replicated three times. Index building is the expensive part of writing: an HNSW insert computes hundreds to thousands of distances. Building segments in the background on separate cores (or separate nodes) keeps writes from stealing query latency.

The insight to say out loud. This is a memory-bound storage engine whose hardest query feature is filtering. Choosing the index per namespace, and the search strategy per query, is where most of the design lives.

Three choices matter. Payload indexes are declared, because the planner needs them both to evaluate filters and to estimate how many points match, and because filter-aware graph structures must be built with knowledge of the indexed fields (Qdrant's documentation recommends creating payload indexes before ingesting data for exactly this reason). Writes return a log position, which a client can pass back for read-your-writes. And the response names the plan chosen, so users and support engineers can see why a query was slow or returned few results.

4 · High-level design

The architecture is the primer diagram. A stateless router maps namespaces to shards using a metadata service (namespace configuration, shard map, replica placement). Each shard is a replicated log: writes go to the leader's write-ahead log (WAL), are replicated to followers by a consensus protocol or a shared durable log service, and are acknowledged once durable on a majority. Each replica applies log entries to its mutable segment, an in-memory buffer of recent points searched by brute force. When the mutable segment reaches its size limit (say 200,000 points) it is sealed, and an index builder creates an immutable segment with its vector index, payload indexes and an empty delete bitmap. Compaction merges small segments and segments with many deletions. Segments are uploaded to object storage as snapshots, so a new replica can download segments and replay only the log tail. On the query path, each replica's planner estimates filter cardinality per segment and picks a strategy; all segments are searched in parallel, results are merged, optionally rescored with full-precision vectors, and returned to the router, which merges across shards.

5 · Deep dive: choosing the index

HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin) builds a multi-layer graph: every vector is in the bottom layer, exponentially fewer in each layer above, and each node links to its nearest neighbours (up to M per layer, 2M on the bottom). Search starts at the top layer, greedily moves toward the query, drops a layer, and repeats; on the bottom layer it keeps a candidate list of size ef_search and returns the best k. It gives the best recall-latency trade-off for in-memory data and supports incremental inserts well. Its costs: full vectors plus links in RAM, slower builds, and awkward deletes (the Faiss wiki notes that its HNSW index does not support removing vectors at all; engines that support deletes mark nodes as deleted and repair or rebuild later).

IVF-PQ clusters vectors into lists, stores product-quantised codes of the residuals, and searches the nprobe nearest lists (the mechanics are worked in hd25). Memory is a small fraction of HNSW's, builds are fast once the codebooks are trained, and appends are easy (add codes to a list). Recall at a given latency is lower, so production systems oversample (fetch, say, 4k candidates) and rescore them with full vectors from SSD. Codebooks fitted to one distribution degrade as data drifts, so they are retrained when segments are rebuilt.

DiskANN (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) builds a graph (its Vamana algorithm) designed for few hops, stores the graph and full-precision vectors on SSD, and keeps only PQ-compressed vectors in RAM to decide which nodes to read next. Its paper reports serving the billion-vector SIFT1B dataset on a workstation with 64 GB of RAM and an inexpensive SSD at more than 5,000 queries a second with under 3 ms mean latency and 95%+ 1-recall@1, and indexing 5–10 times more points per node than in-memory graph indexes in the high-recall regime. The trade-off is SSD reads on every query (a few round trips of a few reads each), so latency depends on SSD performance and on keeping the number of hops small.

Brute force is the right index for small sets. Scanning 50,000 vectors of 768 dimensions is about 150 MB of float32 (or 38 MB at one byte per dimension), a few milliseconds on a modern core with vector instructions, and exact. Most of the 50,000 namespaces are this size, which is why "no index" is a first-class choice.

The policy. The namespace's index type defaults to auto: brute force below about 20,000 points, HNSW for small and medium namespaces where memory is cheap in absolute terms and updates are frequent, IVF-PQ or DiskANN with rescoring for large namespaces on the disk tier, and object storage for namespaces not queried for weeks, loaded into cache on first access. Customers can override per namespace, trading cost for latency.

6 · Deep dive: filtered search and why recall collapses

The problem. Most real queries carry filters: this tenant, this user's permitted documents, the last 30 days, category = shoes. An ANN index is built over all vectors in a segment, without regard to any filter. Three naive strategies each fail at some selectivity (the fraction of points that pass).

Post-filtering searches the index as if there were no filter, then drops results that fail it. With a filter passing 1% of points, the top 100 candidates contain about one that passes. pgvector's documentation, discussed in db15, describes exactly this behaviour for approximate indexes: the WHERE clause is applied after the index scan, so selective filters return too few rows.

In-graph filtering, traversing only passing nodes. Navigate the graph but step only to neighbours that pass the filter. The arithmetic shows why this collapses. On HNSW's bottom layer each node has up to 2M = 32 links. If the filter passes a fraction s of points independently of where they sit in the graph, the expected number of passing neighbours of a passing node is 32s, and the probability that it has none is (1 − s)32:

SelectivityPassing neighbours (of 32)P(no passing neighbour)
50%16≈ 0
20%6.40.1%
10%3.23.4%
5%1.619%
2%0.6452%
1%0.3272%
0.1%0.0397%

Below about 5% selectivity, the subgraph of passing nodes falls apart into islands; a search restricted to it gets stuck in whichever island it entered and misses the true nearest neighbours in other islands. Recall collapses.

In-graph filtering, traversing all nodes. Navigate through every node but add only passing nodes to the result list. Connectivity is fine, but at 1% selectivity the search sees one qualifying node per hundred visited, so filling a result list of ten needs on the order of a thousand or more visits, where an unfiltered search needs a hundred or two. Latency grows roughly as 1/s. Recall holds only if the search is allowed to run that long; with a normal ef budget it stops early and recall collapses anyway.

The fixes, and the planner that chooses between them. The planner uses the payload index to estimate how many points in each segment pass the filter, then picks per segment:

  • Brute force over the matching points when the matching set is small in absolute terms: fetch matching IDs from the payload index and compute exact distances. Qdrant's documentation describes this as full_scan_threshold, measured in kilobytes of vectors (10,000 KB by default, noting that 1 KB is one 256-dimensional vector): when the estimated matching set is below it, the planner uses a full scan instead of HNSW traversal.
  • In-graph filtering when the filter is loose (above roughly 10–20% selectivity), where the passing subgraph stays connected and the extra visits are modest.
  • Filter-aware graph structures in between. ACORN (Patel et al., SIGMOD 2024) builds a denser HNSW-style graph and, at query time, traverses only passing nodes but expands to neighbours of neighbours, so the passing subgraph stays navigable for arbitrary predicates; its paper reports 2–1,000 times higher throughput at fixed recall than prior methods. Qdrant's filterable HNSW adds extra edges based on indexed payload values, so each value's subgraph is connected; its documentation notes that these edges are added per payload index, not for every combination, so combinations of strict filters can still disconnect the graph, which is why it added ACORN-style search (from version 1.16.0) for those cases.
  • Partitioning when one field dominates filters: segments or namespaces split by tenant, by time or by category, so the filter becomes routing or segment pruning and no index sees non-matching points.

Worked plan. A shared namespace holds 50 million points; a query filters tenant = "acme", which matches 500,000 points (1%). Brute force would scan 500,000 × 3 KB = 1.5 GB of float32, around 100 ms of memory bandwidth on one node: too slow for the 50 ms target. Post-filtering or restricted traversal collapses at 1%. Traversing all nodes needs about 100 times the usual visits. The right answers are filter-aware edges on tenant or, better, giving large tenants their own namespace so this query never meets the other 99%. Now the same query with an added doc_date >= last week matches 4,000 points: the planner brute-forces them in under a millisecond, exact. Same namespace, same index, two different plans.

Correlation makes it worse or better. The arithmetic above assumes the filter is unrelated to vector position. If passing points cluster together (a tenant's documents are all about the same topic), the passing subgraph is better connected than the formula says, but the query may be far from that cluster. If they are spread out and the query sits in a region with few passing points, restricted traversal fails even at moderate selectivity. This is why recall must be measured per selectivity bucket on real filters, not inferred.

7 · Deep dive: writes, updates, deletes and compaction

Why log-structured. Graph indexes are expensive to modify in place: inserting a node means finding its neighbours (hundreds of distance computations) and updating their link lists; deleting one means repairing the links of nodes that pointed to it. Doing this synchronously on every write would make writes slow and queries jittery. So the engine borrows the design of log-structured merge (LSM) storage engines: writes are appended to a log and buffered; immutable files are produced in the background; files are merged later.

The write path. An upsert is appended to the shard's WAL and replicated; once a majority has it on durable storage, the client receives the log position. Each replica applies the entry: the point goes into the mutable segment (searched by brute force, so it is visible within milliseconds of being applied), and if the ID existed in an older segment, that segment's delete bitmap marks the old version. Updates are delete plus insert; vector databases rarely update in place.

Sealing and indexing. When the mutable segment reaches its limit, it becomes read-only and an index builder (on separate cores or a separate node) builds its vector and payload indexes. Until the build finishes, the sealed segment is still searched by brute force; at 200,000 points that is about 600 MB of vectors, slower than an index but still tens of milliseconds, which is why segment size and build speed are tuned together.

Deletes. A delete writes a tombstone: the point's bit is set in its segment's delete bitmap, and searches skip it at once. The vector remains in the segment file. Searches waste work on deleted points (a graph search may visit them as stepping stones and then discard them), so a segment with many deletions gets slower and less accurate.

Compaction. A background process picks segments to rewrite: small segments to merge (fewer segments means fewer searches to merge per query) and segments whose deleted fraction exceeds a threshold (say 20%). It builds a new segment containing only live points, indexes it, swaps it in atomically and deletes the old files. Compaction competes with queries for CPU and memory bandwidth, so it is throttled and scheduled; it also needs temporary space for the new segment while the old one still serves.

Erasure deadlines. A customer deleting a document, or a legal erasure request, requires the data to be physically gone within a deadline. The engine tracks the oldest unpurged tombstone per segment and forces compaction of segments whose tombstones approach the deadline; snapshots in object storage that still contain deleted points expire on the same schedule, and the log is truncated past them.

8 · Deep dive: sharding, replication and multi-tenancy

Namespaces first. The cheapest way to make tenant filters fast is to make them unnecessary. Each tenant gets its own namespace, with its own segments, so a query for tenant A never touches tenant B's vectors. Small namespaces are packed many to a shard (thousands of tiny namespaces can share one shard's process), and namespaces under about 20,000 points get no ANN index at all, since brute force is exact and fast. The cost is per-namespace overhead (metadata, open files, a minimum segment), which is why namespaces are cheap but not free, and why very many tiny namespaces are sometimes grouped into one with a partition key the planner treats specially.

Sharding large namespaces. A 2-billion-vector namespace is split into shards by hashing point IDs, for example 16 shards of 125 million. Every query fans out to all 16 and the router merges their top k (each shard returns its own top k, which is sufficient for an exact merge). Hash sharding spreads load evenly; the alternative, sharding by vector region (each shard holds one area of the space, so a query visits only a few), reduces fan-out but creates hot shards for popular regions and complicates rebalancing, so it is used mainly at very large scale with replication of hot regions.

Replication. Each shard's log is replicated, either by a consensus protocol (Raft) among the shard's replicas or by a shared durable log service with replicas as consumers. Replicas serve reads; a write is acknowledged once durable on a majority. Segment snapshots in object storage mean a replacement replica downloads segments in parallel and replays only the log tail instead of rebuilding indexes, which is what makes the 30-minute recovery target achievable: at a few gigabytes per second of download, a shard of tens of gigabytes is back in minutes.

Noisy neighbours. Per-namespace quotas on query rate, write rate and stored vectors; per-query cost accounting in distances computed, so expensive queries (large k, huge ef, unselective filters on big namespaces) are visible and can be limited; fair-share scheduling of index builds and compaction across namespaces on a shard; and the option to move a heavy tenant to dedicated shards, which segment files in object storage make cheap.

Object-storage-backed cold tier. Many namespaces are written once and queried rarely. Keeping their indexes in RAM is waste. In a cold tier, segments live only in object storage; query nodes are stateless with a local SSD cache; the first query to a cold namespace downloads its segments (seconds), later queries hit the cache. Storage cost drops by two orders of magnitude, at the price of slow first queries, which suits archives and batch workloads but not interactive ones.

9 · Deep dive: hybrid queries

Dense vectors capture meaning but miss exact tokens: product codes, names, error messages. Lexical search (BM25, rec2) catches exact terms but misses paraphrases. Hybrid search runs both. Each segment keeps an inverted index over a text field, or a sparse vector per point (term weights from BM25 or a learned sparse model), searched with the same filters as the dense query. Each side returns its top candidates (say 100), and the engine fuses them. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) scores each point by the sum over lists of 1 / (k + rank), with k = 60 the value Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher chose in their 2009 study. Its virtue is that it ignores raw scores, which are on different scales (BM25 is unbounded; cosine lies between −1 and 1). A point ranked 1st lexically and 5th densely scores 1/61 + 1/65 ≈ 0.0318; one ranked 2nd densely and absent lexically scores 1/62 ≈ 0.0161. Weighted score fusion (normalise each list's scores, then α × dense + (1 − α) × lexical) can do better when tuned per workload, but it is brittle across queries. Filters must apply to both sides identically, or a fused result can include points the lexical side would have excluded.

10 · Consistency

The default is eventual consistency: a write is acknowledged when durable in the log, and becomes visible on each replica when that replica applies it, typically within tens of milliseconds and within a second at p99. Applications that write and immediately query (a user uploads a document and asks about it) need read-your-writes: the write returns its log sequence number (LSN), the query carries min_lsn, and the replica waits until it has applied that position (with a short timeout, after which it forwards to the leader). Index building does not affect visibility, because new points sit in the mutable segment, searched by brute force until indexed. What a vector database usually does not offer: multi-point transactions, or atomic updates across the vector store and the application's main database. Applications keep the main database as the source of truth and treat the vector store as an index that can lag and can be rebuilt; a periodic reconciliation job compares IDs and versions between the two.

11 · Recall and latency tuning

Every index has knobs that trade recall for latency: ef_search for HNSW, nprobe for IVF, beam width for DiskANN, plus the rescoring depth (how many candidates to rescore with full vectors) for compressed indexes. Good defaults are a start, but the right values depend on dimension, data distribution, segment size and filters. The engine therefore measures recall continuously: a small share of real queries (say 0.5%) is re-run asynchronously as exact brute-force searches over the same filtered set on spare capacity, and the overlap of the top 10 gives recall@10. Results are broken down by namespace, index type and filter-selectivity bucket. An auto-tuner per namespace raises ef or nprobe when recall falls below the target and lowers it when there is slack, within latency limits. Customers see their measured recall, which turns "approximate" from a vague promise into a reported number.

12 · Evaluation plan

Offline benchmarks before each release: standard datasets plus synthetic filtered workloads at selectivities from 50% to 0.1%, with correlated and uncorrelated filters, measuring recall@10, p50 and p99 latency, throughput, memory and build time per index type. Production metrics: shadow-measured recall per namespace and selectivity bucket; latency percentiles per plan type; freshness (time from write acknowledgement to visibility on replicas); delete visibility and purge lag; compaction backlog; memory per shard; cost per million vectors by tier. Correctness tests: deleted points never returned (a randomised test inserts, deletes and queries continuously); read-your-writes honoured when requested; replica divergence (periodic checksums of segment contents across replicas).
