14 · What changes at 10× scale

At 100 billion vectors, RAM-resident indexes for everything are unaffordable, so the default tier becomes disk-based (DiskANN-style or IVF-PQ with SSD rescoring), with RAM reserved for hot namespaces, and the cold object-storage tier holds most of the data. Fan-out to hundreds of shards for the largest namespaces makes tail latency the main problem, so very large namespaces move to region-partitioned sharding (route each query to the few shards covering its neighbourhood) with replication of hot regions. Index builds become a large compute workload of their own, run on separate GPU or CPU pools. And the planner grows into a cost-based optimiser that weighs strategies by estimated distance computations and I/O, much as relational planners weigh index scans against table scans.
deep:
The bottom layer's 2M links are what make filtering survivable at all

HNSW's paper found that setting the bottom layer's maximum degree to twice the upper layers' (Mmax0 = 2M) markedly improves search at high recall, and it became the standard default. For filtered search this doubling matters directly: the expected number of passing neighbours is degree × selectivity, so 32 links instead of 16 halve the selectivity at which the passing subgraph breaks apart. ACORN generalises the idea: build a denser graph than usual (more candidate edges per node), then at query time consider neighbours and neighbours of neighbours, which raises the effective degree seen by a filtered search by a large factor without storing a separate graph per filter.

Cardinality estimation is the planner's whole job

Every strategy choice hinges on one number: how many points in this segment pass this filter. For a single equality on an indexed keyword, the payload index gives it exactly. For combinations (tenant = A and date in last week and tag in {hr, legal}), the engine must estimate, and the classic database assumption of independence between predicates can be badly wrong: if tenant A's documents are all recent, the true count is far larger than the product of selectivities. Engines estimate by intersecting posting lists when they are small, sampling when they are large, and erring toward the safe plan: if the estimate is near the brute-force threshold, brute force is chosen, because its worst case is bounded and its recall is exact.

Quantisation and rescoring decouple memory from accuracy

Compressed vectors (scalar quantisation to one byte per dimension, product quantisation, binary codes) shrink memory four- to fifty-fold but distort distances. Rescoring separates the two concerns: search with compressed vectors to get, say, four times more candidates than needed, then recompute exact distances for those candidates from full vectors on SSD. If the true top 10 are almost always within the compressed top 40, recall is nearly that of full precision while RAM holds only compressed data. The oversampling factor is the knob: measured recall tells you how deep the true neighbours sit in the compressed ranking, and the factor is set just past that.

Segment size is a three-way trade-off

Small segments index quickly, compact cheaply and keep new data indexed sooner; but every query must search every segment and merge their results, so many small segments multiply per-query overhead and lower recall (each segment's graph is smaller and the top k must be found in each). Large segments search efficiently but take long to build, so new data sits longer in brute-force mode, and compaction rewrites more data each time. Engines settle on a target segment size (hundreds of thousands to a few million points) and a tiered merge policy that combines segments of similar size, the same idea LSM storage engines use for key-value data.

Deletion in graphs is a repair problem

Removing a node from a proximity graph leaves its neighbours with fewer links and can disconnect regions that routed through it. Marking deleted nodes and keeping them as stepping stones preserves connectivity but wastes work and memory; physically removing them requires reconnecting their neighbours, which is expensive. Engines therefore accept a deleted fraction up to a threshold, search through tombstoned nodes without returning them, and rebuild the segment's graph during compaction. FreshDiskANN and similar work studies in-place repair for disk-resident graphs, but rebuild-on-compaction remains the robust default.

Vector search inside an existing database versus a dedicated engine

pgvector and similar extensions (db15) put vectors next to the rest of the data: transactions, joins, one system to operate, and permissions in one place. A dedicated vector database earns its place when the collection is very large, query rates are high, filtered search must work at low selectivity, or memory cost demands disk-based indexes and tiering. The decision is the same as choosing a search engine versus full-text search in a relational database: start inside the database when the scale allows, and move when measured recall, latency or cost says so.

Fan-out turns per-shard tails into query tails

A query that fans out to 16 shards waits for the slowest. If each shard answers within 20 ms 99% of the time, the probability that all 16 do is 0.9916 ≈ 85%, so the query's own p85 already touches the per-shard p99. Large namespaces therefore need per-shard tail control: hedged requests to a second replica after the shard's p95, timeouts with partial results when the application tolerates them, and keeping shards similar in size so none is systematically slow.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The three-result query. A customer moved from separate namespaces to one shared namespace with a tenant payload field to reduce overhead, without declaring a payload index on it. Queries for small tenants started returning two or three results instead of ten, while large tenants were fine. Without the payload index, the planner could not estimate cardinality and defaulted to graph search with post-filtering. Declaring the index (and rebuilding segments so filter-aware edges were created, since they are only built when the payload index exists before indexing) fixed recall; moving the largest tenants back to their own namespaces fixed latency.

The compaction storm. A customer deleted 40% of a large namespace in one batch (re-embedding with a new model by deleting and reinserting). Every segment crossed the deleted-fraction threshold at once, compaction started everywhere, and query p99 rose from 30 ms to 400 ms for every tenant on those shards. Compaction is now throttled per shard with a global concurrency limit, bulk deletions are flagged so compaction is scheduled off-peak, and model migrations are done by building a new namespace and switching, not by in-place churn.

The drifting codebooks. A large namespace on IVF-PQ had its codebooks trained at creation, when the data was mostly English product descriptions. A year later half the data was multilingual, and shadow-measured recall had fallen from 0.96 to 0.89 without anyone noticing, because nobody watched it. Recall alerts per namespace now exist, and segment rebuilds retrain codebooks on a fresh sample.

What to monitor

Per namespace: shadow recall@10 overall and by selectivity bucket, query latency by plan type, results-returned distribution (queries returning fewer than k are a filter symptom), write rate, visibility lag, vectors stored and memory. Per shard: segment count and sizes, deleted fraction, compaction backlog and throughput, index build queue, replica lag in LSN, CPU and memory bandwidth. Fleet: cost per million vectors by tier, cache hit rate for the cold tier, recovery time after node loss.

Knobs people tune

Index type per namespace; HNSW M and ef_construction at build, ef_search at query; IVF list count and nprobe; PQ code size; rescoring oversampling; brute-force threshold; payload indexes and filter-aware edges; segment size and merge policy; deleted-fraction threshold; compaction throttle; replica count; cold-tier eviction age.

The real cases: HNSW, DiskANN, ACORN and Qdrant's planner

The HNSW paper (Malkov and Yashunin) defines the graph, recommends Mmax0 = 2M on the bottom layer and gives M between 5 and 48 as a reasonable range, with efConstruction set high enough that construction recall is close to one. The Faiss wiki gives the memory formula used here, (d × 4 + M × 2 × 4) bytes per vector, and notes that its HNSW index does not support removing vectors. DiskANN (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) shows SSD-resident graph search at billion scale on one machine with 64 GB of RAM: over 5,000 queries a second, under 3 ms mean latency, 95%+ 1-recall@1 on SIFT1B, with PQ-compressed vectors in RAM and full-precision rescoring from SSD. ACORN (Patel et al., SIGMOD 2024) introduces predicate subgraph traversal over a denser HNSW-style graph for arbitrary filters, reporting 2–1,000 times higher throughput at fixed recall. Qdrant's indexing documentation, checked on 10 October 2026, shows how a production engine puts these together: payload indexes that also estimate filter cardinality for query planning, a full_scan_threshold (10,000 KB by default) below which the planner scans rather than traverses, filterable HNSW with extra edges per indexed payload value (requiring payload indexes to exist before data is indexed), and an ACORN search option since version 1.16.0 for combinations of strict filters that the extra edges do not cover. Defaults and features change between versions; the design lesson is that filtered vector search is a planning problem with several strategies, not a single index.
myths: A filter is just a WHERE clause; any vector index supports it.

Graph indexes are navigated through neighbours. If only 1% of vectors pass the filter and each node has 32 neighbours at the bottom layer, the expected number of passing neighbours is 0.32, and 72% of passing nodes have none at all, so a search restricted to passing nodes falls apart, while a search that ignores the filter and checks it afterwards finds one match per hundred visited. Filtered search needs a planner and filter-aware structures.
HNSW is always the best index.

HNSW gives excellent recall and latency but stores full vectors plus links in RAM: about 3.2 KB per 768-dimensional vector, 3.2 TB per billion. IVF-PQ needs about 104 bytes per vector with refinement on SSD, and DiskANN keeps 64-byte compressed vectors in RAM with the graph on SSD. The best index depends on size, recall target, update rate and budget.
Deleting a vector removes it.

In most engines a delete writes a tombstone; the vector stays in the index files until compaction rewrites the segment. That matters for erasure requests, for memory, and for search, since a segment full of tombstones wastes work. Physical deletion is a compaction policy with a deadline.
A vector database is consistent like a relational database.

Most are eventually consistent by default: a write is acknowledged once it is durable in the log, and becomes searchable when a replica applies it, often within a second. Read-your-writes needs a token or a leader read; transactions across vectors and other data usually do not exist. If you need joins and transactions with your vectors, a vector index inside your database (db15) may fit better.
Recall@10 of 0.99 on a public benchmark means my queries get 0.99.

Recall depends on the data distribution, the dimension, the filter mix and the parameters. Benchmarks use unfiltered queries on fixed datasets; production queries carry tenant and metadata filters, data drifts, and segments vary in size. Measure recall continuously on your own traffic by running a small share of queries exactly.
lab:
Goal: reproduce filtered-graph recall collapse on a small graph, and see how expanding to neighbours of neighbours (the ACORN idea) and brute force over the matching set fix it. Python 3.12 with NumPy from the gpt_env environment.

  1. Save as filtered_graph.py and run it with the gpt_env Python. It builds a k-nearest-neighbour graph over 5,000 random vectors (one layer, 32 links per node, like HNSW's bottom layer) and runs a beam search under three strategies at several selectivities.
  2. Read the restricted column: recall@10 when the search may step only through passing nodes. It should fall sharply below about 5% selectivity.
  3. Read the all-nodes column: recall stays higher, but the distance-computation count (cost) grows as selectivity falls, because most visited nodes do not pass.
  4. Read the two-hop column: restricted search that also considers neighbours of non-passing neighbours. Recall should hold much better at low selectivity for a moderate cost.
  5. Note the matching-set size at 1%: 50 points. Brute force over them is exact and costs 50 distances. Compare with every graph strategy.
"""Filtered graph search: recall collapse and fixes. Python 3.12 + NumPy (gpt_env)."""
import heapq
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, D, DEG, EF, K = 5000, 32, 32, 64, 10
X = rng.standard_normal((N, D)).astype(np.float32)
sq = (X ** 2).sum(1)
nbrs = np.empty((N, DEG), dtype=np.int64)
for i in range(0, N, 500):                          # exact kNN graph, built in blocks
    d = sq[i:i + 500, None] - 2 * X[i:i + 500] @ X.T + sq[None, :]
    d[np.arange(d.shape[0]), np.arange(i, i + d.shape[0])] = np.inf
    nbrs[i:i + 500] = np.argpartition(d, DEG, axis=1)[:, :DEG]
adj = [set(r) for r in nbrs.tolist()]
for i, r in enumerate(nbrs.tolist()):               # make links two-way, like HNSW
    for j in r: adj[j].add(i)
adj = [np.fromiter(s, dtype=np.int64) for s in adj]

def search(q, ok, mode):
    """Beam search; returns (top-K ids, number of distance computations)."""
    allowed = np.flatnonzero(ok)
    entry = int(rng.choice(allowed if mode != "all" else N))
    dist = lambda ids: ((X[ids] - q) ** 2).sum(1)
    seen = {entry}; d0 = float(dist([entry])[0]); cost = 1
    cand = [(d0, entry)]; res = [(-d0, entry)] if ok[entry] else []
    while cand:
        dc, c = heapq.heappop(cand)
        if len(res) >= EF and dc > -res[0][0]: break
        nb = adj[c]
        if mode == "restricted": nb = nb[ok[nb]]
        elif mode == "two_hop":                       # passing 1-hop plus passing 2-hop via failing nodes
            hop2 = [adj[x] for x in nb[~ok[nb]]]
            nb = np.concatenate([nb] + hop2) if hop2 else nb
            nb = np.unique(nb[ok[nb]])
        nb = [int(x) for x in nb if int(x) not in seen]
        if not nb: continue
        seen.update(nb); ds = dist(nb); cost += len(nb)
        for x, dx in zip(nb, ds.tolist()):
            if len(res) < EF or dx < -res[0][0]:
                heapq.heappush(cand, (dx, x))
                if ok[x]:
                    heapq.heappush(res, (-dx, x))
                    if len(res) > EF: heapq.heappop(res)
    return [x for _, x in sorted(res, reverse=True)][:K], cost

print(f"{'select.':>7} {'matches':>7} | {'restricted':>14} | {'all-nodes':>14} | {'two-hop':>14}")
for s in (0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01):
    ok = rng.random(N) < s; allowed = np.flatnonzero(ok)
    out = {m: [0.0, 0] for m in ("restricted", "all", "two_hop")}
    for _ in range(100):
        q = rng.standard_normal(D).astype(np.float32)
        truth = set(allowed[np.argsort(((X[allowed] - q) ** 2).sum(1))[:K]].tolist())
        for m in out:
            got, cost = search(q, ok, m)
            out[m][0] += len(truth & set(got)) / len(truth); out[m][1] += cost
    cells = " | ".join(f"{out[m][0]/100:5.2f} r {out[m][1]/100:6.0f} c" for m in out)
    print(f"{s:7.0%} {len(allowed):7} | {cells}")

What to look for: restricted recall falling apart at low selectivity (islands); all-nodes recall holding up only by spending many more distance computations; two-hop recovering most of the recall at moderate cost; and the matching-set size telling you when brute force (cost = matches, recall = 1.0) beats all of them.
recap: A vector database stores points (an ID, one or more vectors and a metadata payload) and answers top-k nearest-neighbour queries with filters, fast enough for interactive use, while absorbing writes and deletes.

For a billion 768-dimensional vectors, raw float32 is 3.07 TB, HNSW about 3.2 TB in RAM, IVF-PQ with 96-byte codes about 104 GB in RAM plus full vectors on SSD, and DiskANN about 64 GB in RAM with about 3.3 TB on SSD.

Under stated assumptions (RAM $3 and SSD $0.15 per GB-month, two replicas), HNSW in RAM costs about $19 per million vectors a month, IVF-PQ and DiskANN about $1.40–1.50, and object-storage-backed cold namespaces a few cents.

Writes go through a replicated log into a mutable segment searched by brute force, which is sealed and indexed in the background; deletes are tombstones; compaction merges segments and purges deleted vectors.
Filtered search collapses on graph indexes at low selectivity: at 1% selectivity a node with 32 neighbours has 0.32 passing neighbours on average and a 72% chance of none.

A query planner estimates filter cardinality from payload indexes and chooses brute force over the matching set when it is small, in-graph filtering when the filter is loose, and filter-aware structures (ACORN's predicate subgraph traversal, Qdrant's extra edges per payload value) in between.
Multi-tenancy is best served by namespaces with their own segments, which turns the tenant filter into routing; tiny namespaces are searched by brute force, large ones get dedicated shards.
Hybrid queries run BM25 or sparse search alongside vector search and fuse rankings with reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), because their scores are not comparable.
Consistency is eventual by default, with read-your-writes available through a log position token; the mutable segment keeps new writes searchable before indexing finishes.
Recall is tuned per workload with ef_search, nprobe and rescoring depth, and measured continuously by running a sample of real queries exactly.
glossary: A filtered-search method for HNSW that builds a denser graph and, at query time, traverses only nodes passing the predicate while expanding to neighbours of neighbours so the passing subgraph stays connected.
A lexical ranking formula that scores documents by how often query terms appear, discounted for common terms and long documents.
Computing the distance from the query to every candidate vector; exact, and fast enough for small sets.
Merging segments into fewer, larger ones and physically removing deleted vectors.
A graph index designed to live on SSD: compressed vectors in RAM guide the search, while the graph and full vectors are read from disk.
The size of the candidate list in an HNSW search; larger values raise recall and cost.
The fraction of vectors that pass a filter; low selectivity (a strict filter) means few pass.
Hierarchical navigable small world: a layered neighbour graph searched greedily from a sparse top layer down to a bottom layer that contains every vector.
An index that clusters vectors into lists (IVF) and stores product-quantised codes of each vector's offset from its list centroid.
A position in the write-ahead log; a replica that has applied up to an LSN has every write before it.
A storage design that buffers writes in memory, flushes them as immutable files and merges files in the background.
The in-memory segment that receives new writes and is searched by brute force until it is sealed and indexed.
A logically separate collection of points, usually one per tenant or use case, with its own segments.
The metadata stored with a vector (tenant, document ID, date, tags) and used for filtering.
A conventional index (keyword, numeric range) over a payload field, used to evaluate filters and estimate how many points match.
Running the vector search first and removing results that fail the filter afterwards; returns too few results when the filter is strict.
Finding the points that pass the filter first and searching only among them, typically by brute force.
Combining ranked lists by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each item across lists, which needs no score normalisation.
Recomputing distances for the top candidates with full-precision vectors after a search on compressed vectors.
Storing each dimension as one byte instead of a 4-byte float, a 4-fold compression with small accuracy loss.
An immutable chunk of a collection with its own vector index, payload indexes and deletion bitmap.
A vector with mostly zero entries, such as term weights from BM25 or a learned sparse model, searched with an inverted index.
A marker recording that a point was deleted, applied at query time until compaction removes the data.
An append-only log where every write is recorded durably before it is applied, used for recovery and replication.
drill:
Estimate it

A customer has 300 million 1,024-dimensional vectors, needs p99 under 80 ms at recall@10 of 0.95, and runs 2,000 queries a second, 80% of them filtered to one of 400 product categories of roughly equal size. Using the lesson's assumptions ($3 per GB-month RAM, $0.15 SSD, two replicas): (a) memory and monthly storage cost for HNSW (M = 16, float32) versus IVF-PQ with 128-byte codes and SSD rescoring; (b) what plan should a category-filtered query use, and why; (c) what would you recommend?

Answer

(a) HNSW: 1,024 × 4 + 16 × 2 × 4 = 4,224 bytes × 300 million ≈ 1.27 TB RAM per replica, about $3,800 a month per replica, $7,600 for two. IVF-PQ: 128 + 8 = 136 bytes × 300 million ≈ 41 GB RAM ($122 per replica) plus 4,096 bytes × 300 million ≈ 1.23 TB of float32 on SSD ($184 per replica), about $610 a month for two replicas, roughly twelve times cheaper.

(b) Each category is 1/400 = 0.25% of the data, 750,000 vectors. That is far below the selectivity where in-graph filtering works (32 × 0.0025 = 0.08 passing neighbours per node) and far too many to brute-force within 80 ms (750,000 × 4 KB = 3 GB). So neither naive plan works on one shared index: partition by category (segments or sub-namespaces per category, each with its own index), or build filter-aware edges on the category field. With partitioning, a category query searches a 750,000-vector index directly.

(c) IVF-PQ with rescoring, partitioned by category, sharded by hash within large categories if needed; measure recall per category with shadow queries and tune nprobe and the rescoring depth to reach 0.95. The unfiltered 20% of queries fan out across category partitions or use a global index; if they matter, keep a global IVF-PQ index too, which at 41 GB is affordable.

Diagnose it

After a weekend batch job deleted and reinserted 30% of a namespace, recall@10 dropped from 0.96 to 0.90 and p99 latency doubled, though query volume was unchanged. What happened and what do you do?

Answer

The deletes became tombstones in existing segments and the reinserts became many new small segments. Searches now traverse graphs where 30% of nodes are deleted (wasted visits, and the live subgraph is less well connected, lowering recall at the same ef), and every query must search and merge many more segments (higher latency). Check the deleted fraction per segment, segment counts and the compaction backlog. Short term: raise ef temporarily to restore recall, and run compaction at a controlled rate off-peak to rebuild affected segments and merge the small ones. Long term: treat bulk replacement as a migration (build a new namespace, switch, drop the old one), flag bulk deletes so compaction is scheduled, and alert on shadow recall and segment count per namespace.
qa: E
What is in a vector database's data model?

Collections or namespaces of points; each point has an ID, one or more dense vectors (sometimes a sparse vector too), and a payload of metadata such as tenant, document ID, date and tags. A collection fixes the dimension and distance metric (cosine, dot product or Euclidean). Payload fields can be indexed for filtering. Queries ask for the top k points nearest a query vector, optionally with filters, and return IDs, scores and payloads.
E
Compare HNSW, IVF-PQ and DiskANN in one sentence each.

HNSW is a layered neighbour graph held in RAM with full vectors: best latency and recall, highest memory (about 3.2 KB per 768-dimensional vector). IVF-PQ clusters vectors and stores short product-quantised codes: tiny memory (about 100 bytes per vector), lower recall unless the top candidates are rescored with full vectors. DiskANN keeps compressed vectors in RAM to guide a graph search whose graph and full vectors are read from SSD: billion-scale on one machine at the cost of SSD reads per query.
E
Why do new writes not have to wait for index building?

Because they land in a small mutable segment that is searched by brute force alongside the indexed segments. When it reaches a size limit it is sealed and an index is built in the background; once built, the indexed segment replaces it in searches. New data is searchable within about a second either way.
M
Explain why filtered HNSW recall collapses with a 1% filter.

HNSW search moves from node to neighbour. If the search may only step through nodes that pass the filter, each passing node has, at 1% selectivity and 32 links on the bottom layer, about 0.32 passing neighbours, and 0.99^32 ≈ 72% of passing nodes have none, so the search gets stuck in tiny islands. If it steps through all nodes and keeps only passing ones, it sees about one passing node per hundred visited, so collecting ten results needs thousands of visits, far beyond a normal ef. Either way recall or latency collapses.

Follow-up: What does the planner do instead? — Estimate the number of matching points from the payload index; if it is small (say under 20,000), brute-force them exactly; if large, use in-graph filtering; in between use ACORN-style expansion or filter-aware edges, or partition the data on that field.
M
Walk through a write, a delete and a compaction.

A write is appended to the shard's replicated write-ahead log and acknowledged; replicas apply it to their mutable segment, where it is immediately searchable by brute force. A delete appends a tombstone, which hides the point from results at once. When the mutable segment fills it is sealed and indexed. Compaction later merges small segments or segments with many tombstones into new ones, rebuilding their indexes without the deleted points, and the old segments are dropped. Erasure deadlines force compaction of affected segments.
M
How do you serve 50,000 tenants of very different sizes?

Give each tenant a namespace with its own segments, so tenant isolation is routing rather than filtering. Pack many small namespaces onto shared shards; search tiny ones (under about 10,000 vectors) by brute force with no index at all; give large tenants dedicated shards and replicas. Apply per-tenant quotas on queries, writes and index-build time, and account cost by vectors scanned, so one tenant cannot degrade others.
M
How does a hybrid BM25 plus vector query work?

Each segment holds an inverted index for text (or sparse vectors) next to the vector index. The query runs both searches with the same filters, takes the top 100 or so from each, and fuses them with reciprocal rank fusion, scoring each point by the sum of 1 / (60 + rank) over the lists it appears in, because BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on different scales. Weighted score fusion is possible but needs per-query normalisation and tuning.

Follow-up: Why k = 60? — Cormack and colleagues found it worked well across collections in their 2009 study; it damps the influence of top ranks so one list cannot dominate. Treat it as a default to tune, not a law.
M
What does read-your-writes mean here and how do you provide it?

A client that has just upserted a point sees it in its next query. Writes return the log position (LSN) at which they were recorded; the client passes it with the query, and the serving replica waits (briefly, with a timeout) until it has applied that position before searching, or the query is routed to the leader. Without the token, queries are eventually consistent, typically within a second.
H
Estimate memory and cost for 1 billion 768-dimensional vectors under three index choices.

Raw float32 is 3,072 bytes per vector, 3.07 TB. HNSW with M = 16 adds 128 bytes of links: 3,200 bytes, 3.2 TB of RAM per replica. IVF-PQ with 96-byte codes plus an 8-byte ID is 104 GB of RAM, with full vectors on SSD for rescoring. DiskANN with 64-byte PQ codes in RAM is 64 GB, with about 3.3 TB of vectors and graph on SSD. At an assumed $3 per GB-month of RAM and $0.15 per GB-month of SSD with two replicas, that is about $19, $1.50 and $1.40 per million vectors a month respectively.

Follow-up: Then why does anyone use HNSW in RAM? — For the lowest latency and highest recall at high query rates, for frequent updates (graph indexes in RAM handle inserts well), and when the collection is small enough that memory cost does not matter.
H
Design sharding and replication for a 2-billion-vector tenant at 5,000 queries a second.

Hash point IDs into, say, 16 shards of 125 million vectors; each query fans out to all 16 and merges their top k. Each shard is a replicated log (a consensus group or a durable log service) with a leader for writes and replicas serving reads; segments are snapshotted to object storage so a new replica bootstraps by downloading segments and replaying the log tail. With IVF-PQ plus SSD rescoring each shard replica is about 13 GB of RAM; three replicas per shard give zone failure tolerance and spread 5,000 queries a second to about 1,700 per replica group. Tail latency comes from the slowest shard, so hedge slow shard requests.
H
How would you continuously measure recall in production?

Shadow a small sample of real queries (say 0.5%) with an exact brute-force search over the same filtered set, run asynchronously on spare capacity, and compare the top 10. Report recall@10 per namespace, per index type and per filter-selectivity bucket, since filtered queries fail differently. Alert when recall drops after a rebuild, a parameter change or data drift, and use the same harness to tune ef_search, nprobe and rescoring depth per namespace.
H
A customer complains that queries with a date filter return only three results instead of ten. Diagnose.

Classic post-filtering: the engine searched the index for the top candidates and then removed those outside the date range, and too few survived. Check the filter's selectivity (perhaps the last 7 days is 0.5% of the namespace) and the query plan. Fixes: make sure the date field has a payload index so the planner can estimate cardinality and switch to pre-filtered brute force for small matching sets; enable filter-aware search (ACORN or extra edges); or, if most queries filter by recent dates, partition segments by time so the filter becomes segment pruning.

Malkov and Yashunin: the HNSW algorithm; parameters M, Mmax0 (2M on the bottom layer is the recommended default), efConstruction; a reasonable range of M is 5 to 48.
DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node

Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019: a billion SIFT vectors on a workstation with 64 GB of RAM and an SSD, over 5,000 queries a second at under 3 ms mean latency and 95%+ 1-recall@1; PQ vectors in RAM, graph and full vectors on SSD.
ACORN: Performant and Predicate-Agnostic Search Over Vector Embeddings and Structured Data
Patel et al., SIGMOD 2024: predicate subgraph traversal over an HNSW-based index, supporting arbitrary filters, with 2–1,000× higher throughput at fixed recall than prior methods.

Payload indexes for filtering and cardinality estimation; filterable HNSW with extra edges per indexed payload value (create payload indexes before ingesting); full_scan_threshold (10,000 KB by default) for switching to full scan; ACORN search since v1.16.0.
Faiss wiki: Guidelines to choose an index
Memory formulas (HNSW uses d × 4 + M × 2 × 4 bytes per vector; HNSW does not support removing vectors), PQ and SQ code sizes, and index choices by dataset size.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods

t: Design a data-labelling and human-feedback platform
sum: The platform that produces SFT demonstrations, preference pairs and eval labels: task design and versioned guidelines, labeller pools and skill routing, gold questions, agreement statistics worked by hand (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha), adjudication, active learning, preference-collection UIs, PII handling, cost per usable label, and feeding results into training and evaluation, with InstructGPT and Llama 2 as cases.
prereq: ev5

Human labelling is a measurement process: guidelines and calibration rounds, Cohen's kappa from a 2×2 table, Krippendorff's alpha for many raters and missing labels, adjudication versus majority vote, gold items and the arithmetic of labelling cost.
ev2
A golden set is a curated, versioned sample of real inputs with verified outputs, sliced so weaknesses are visible and kept fresh as products change.
lm6
A chat model is made by pretraining, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, and preference tuning on comparisons of model responses.
lm23
Reward models and direct preference optimisation learn from pairs of a preferred and a rejected response to the same prompt; noisy or off-distribution pairs limit what they can learn.
hd12
LLM evaluation uses golden sets, validated LLM judges and human review, with release gates on every change.
hd21
A fine-tuning platform consumes versioned datasets, schedules training jobs on shared GPUs and tracks lineage from data to model.
ae5
Personal data spreads into logs and datasets; redact before it leaves your control, minimise and limit retention, and design erasure from the start.
why:
An AI company trains its own chat models. Each training cycle needs three kinds of human data. Supervised fine-tuning needs thousands of demonstrations: prompts with ideal responses written or carefully edited by people. Preference tuning needs tens of thousands of comparisons: two model responses to the same prompt and a judgement of which is better. And evaluation needs labels for golden sets and for checking automated judges. For the first year this ran on spreadsheets and a contractor marketplace: a researcher wrote instructions in a document, exported prompts to a CSV, contractors filled in columns, and someone merged the files.

Then the questions started. Why did the reward model trained on March's comparisons get worse than the one trained on February's? (Half of March's labels came from a new vendor team that had read an older version of the instructions, and nobody could tell which labels were which.) Why do two labellers disagree on 40% of comparisons? (Some pairs are genuinely close, some instructions are ambiguous, and one labeller always picked the longer response.) Why did the legal team find customers' phone numbers in a training dataset? (Prompts were sampled from production logs without scrubbing.) Why did the model's score on the company's main evaluation set jump eight points overnight? (Evaluation prompts had leaked into a preference batch.) And what does a usable label actually cost, now that a third of the budget goes to relabelling?

The senior design question is to build the platform that makes this a reliable production process: task design and versioned guidelines; labeller pools and routing by skill; quality control with gold questions, agreement statistics and adjudication; active learning to decide what is worth labelling; interfaces for collecting preferences well; PII handling; throughput and cost per usable label; and clean, versioned datasets flowing into training and evaluation pipelines. Agreement statistics and labelling operations as a measurement discipline are taught in ev5; preference optimisation in lm23. This case is about the system that runs them at scale.

The lesson follows the interview: requirements with quality, throughput, cost and privacy targets; estimates for labels, hours, people and money; the API and data model; the high-level design; deep dives on task design and guidelines, routing, quality control with worked agreement statistics, active learning, preference-collection interfaces, PII, and cost per usable label; feeding results into training and evaluation; the platform's own evaluation; failure modes; and what changes at ten times the scale. The real cases are the published labelling programmes behind InstructGPT and Llama 2, and a production tool's documentation of how it measures agreement.
primer:
What the platform does

A data-labelling and human-feedback platform takes raw material (prompts, documents, model responses) and produces labelled datasets: demonstrations, preference pairs, safety labels and evaluation labels. Around that core it does what a factory's quality and logistics departments do: defines each task precisely, recruits and qualifies the right workers, sends each item to someone able to do it, checks the work, resolves disagreements, measures quality and cost, protects sensitive material, and delivers versioned, documented output to the teams that use it.

The mental model: a clinical trial's measurement process

Think of how a clinical trial measures outcomes. A protocol defines exactly what counts as "improved", with examples. Assessors are trained and certified before they rate anyone. Some patients are assessed by two people independently, so the trial can report how reliable the ratings are. Known reference cases are slipped in to check that assessors still apply the protocol. Disagreements go to a senior clinician. Every rating is recorded with who made it, when, and under which protocol version, and patient identities are protected throughout.

The platform is that measurement process for model training data. Guidelines are the protocol. Qualification and calibration are assessor training. Overlap labelling and agreement statistics measure reliability. Gold questions are the reference cases. Adjudication is the senior clinician. Lineage is the audit trail, and PII scrubbing is patient confidentiality. The analogy breaks in two places worth noticing. In a trial the outcome usually has a true value; in preference labelling, many comparisons are genuinely matters of judgement, so disagreement is partly signal, not only error. And a trial's protocol is fixed in advance, while the platform's guidelines evolve every few weeks as models and products change, so every label must carry the version it was made under.

Three facts that shape the design

First, labels are measurements with error, and the platform must quantify that error and carry it with the data, because downstream models learn whatever the labels say, including their noise. Second, human time is the expensive, slow resource: every design choice (what to label, how many labellers per item, how much gold and review) is a trade between data quality and human hours. Third, the data is sensitive in two directions: prompts may contain users' personal data, and labelled datasets are crown jewels whose leakage into evaluation, or out of the company, causes real harm. None of these is solved by a better labelling tool alone; they are solved by a process with measurements at every step, which the tool then enforces. A reader who stops here has the shape: select, scrub, build tasks under versioned guidelines, route by skill, label in a secure workspace, check with gold and overlap, adjudicate disagreements, and publish versioned datasets with lineage, in a loop driven by each new model.

1 · Requirements

Functional. Researchers define task types (preference comparison, ranking, SFT demonstration writing or editing, safety classification, evaluation rubric scoring, span or box annotation) with a guideline and an interface; submit batches of items; choose pools, overlap rate and gold share; monitor progress and quality; and export datasets. Labellers see a queue, complete tasks in a secure workspace, see feedback on gold and adjudicated items, and can flag unclear guidelines. Adjudicators resolve disagreements. Administrators manage pools, qualifications, payments and access. Out of scope, said aloud: training the models, and recruiting the vendors' workforce.

Quality targets. Per task type, an agreed reliability floor before data is used: for example Krippendorff's alpha at least 0.67 for categorical safety labels (the threshold Krippendorff suggests for tentative conclusions, with 0.8 for reliable data), gold accuracy at least 90% per active labeller, and for preference pairs a measured agreement reported by strength bucket. Every label traceable to its labeller (pseudonymously), guideline version and quality statistics.

Throughput targets. Weekly: 20,000 usable preference pairs, 3,000 SFT demonstrations, 10,000 evaluation labels and 5,000 safety labels; turnaround for a 2,000-item evaluation batch under 72 hours.

Cost targets. Published cost per usable label per task type, tracked weekly; total spend within budget, with the split between labelling, quality control and adjudication visible.

Privacy and safety targets. No raw personal data visible to labellers; no data leaves the secure workspace; erasure requests applied to every dataset version within 30 days; exposure limits and wellbeing support for labellers handling harmful content.

Clarifying questions. "Which task types, and which matter most?" "In-house labellers, vendors, or both?" "Where do prompts come from, and what consent covers them?" "How fast must data reach training after a model checkpoint?" "Who owns guidelines: researchers or a dedicated data team?"

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Hours per week. A preference comparison of two multi-turn responses of a few hundred words takes about 3 minutes, so 20 an hour. An SFT demonstration takes about 25 minutes (research, writing, self-review). An evaluation label against a rubric about 1.5 minutes; a safety label about 1 minute. Before overheads, the weekly targets need:

TaskUsable per weekMinutes eachRaw hours
Preference pairs20,00031,000
SFT demonstrations3,000251,250
Evaluation labels10,0001.5250
Safety labels5,000183

With overheads (gold, overlap, rejection, unusable items, roughly ×1.4 for preferences as worked below), about 3,000 hours a week, so with labellers productive about 30 hours a week, roughly 100 full-time-equivalent labellers, in practice a pool of 250 part-time generalists, 60 domain experts and a dozen adjudicators and quality leads.

Money. Assume $24 an hour fully loaded for generalists and $60 for domain experts writing demonstrations. Preference pairs: about $2.24 per usable label (worked in section 9), about $45,000 a week. SFT demonstrations: 3,000 × 25 minutes at $60 an hour is $75,000 a week before review, the largest item. Evaluation and safety labels add perhaps $15,000. Roughly $140,000 a week, $7 million a year: a budget line that justifies a platform team, and where a 20% improvement in cost per usable label pays for engineers.

Data volume. Small by infrastructure standards: tens of thousands of tasks a week, each a few kilobytes of text plus metadata. The platform is not a big-data problem; it is a workflow, quality and security problem.

The insight to say out loud. The constraint is human hours and the quality of each hour. Every mechanism in the design either raises the information per labelled item (active learning, good interfaces, clear guidelines) or protects the reliability of each label (qualification, gold, overlap, adjudication), and both are measured in cost per usable label.

3 · API and data model

POST /v1/task-types       { "name": "pref_helpful_v12", "kind": "pairwise_preference",

Core records. Items: prompt and context (scrubbed), responses with the model checkpoint that produced each, source and consent basis. Tasks: an item presented under a task type and guideline version to one labeller, flagged as gold, overlap or normal. Labels: the answer, strength, flags, rationale, edits, time spent, labeller pseudonym, timestamps. Adjudications: final label, reason, adjudicator. Labellers: pools, qualifications, trust score history, exposure counters. Guidelines: versioned documents with change logs and examples. Datasets: immutable snapshots with a manifest listing every record's lineage. Labeller identities are pseudonymous in datasets, so researchers can analyse per-labeller effects without seeing who people are.

4 · High-level design

The pipeline is the primer diagram. Ingestion accepts items from researchers, from sampling jobs that run the latest model checkpoints on prompt sets, and from production logs where consent allows, passing everything through PII scrubbing. The selector applies active-learning policies to choose which items are labelled. The task builder renders items under a task type and guideline version. The router assigns tasks to labellers by pool, skill and trust score, inserting gold questions and overlap duplicates. Labellers work in a secure workspace, a browser application in a locked-down environment with no copy, paste or download, watermarking of screens and full access logs. Quality control runs continuously: gold scoring, agreement on overlap items, speed and pattern checks, a reliability model. Disagreements and flagged items go to adjudication. Accepted labels go to the dataset service, which builds versioned snapshots with lineage and exports them to training (via the fine-tuning platform, hd21) and to evaluation (hd12), with a contamination guard deduplicating training exports against evaluation sets. Dashboards show progress, quality and cost per batch, task type, pool and labeller.

5 · Deep dive: task design and guidelines

A task type is a measurement instrument. Its guideline defines what each answer means, with positive and negative examples, edge cases and tie-breaking rules. For preference comparisons, the guideline says what "better" means: InstructGPT's labellers were asked to prioritise helpfulness to the user while weighing truthfulness and harmlessness, and Llama 2 separated helpfulness and safety into two task types with different guidelines, so each could be specific. A vague guideline ("pick the better response") produces labels that encode each labeller's personal taste.

Calibration before production. A new guideline (or a major revision) starts with a calibration round: 50–100 items labelled by everyone in the pool, agreement computed, disagreements discussed in a session with the guideline owner, the guideline revised, and the round repeated until agreement reaches the target. Only then do production batches start. The calibration items become the first gold questions.

Versioning. Guidelines change as models and products change: a new policy on medical advice, a new definition of "concise". Each change gets a version, and every task records the version it was presented under. Datasets can then be filtered by version, analyses can compare labels across versions, and a bad revision can be rolled back. Without versioning, a mid-month guideline change silently splits a dataset into two incompatible halves, as in the opening story.

Task size and fatigue. Long tasks produce worse labels late in a session. Tasks are sized to a few minutes, sessions are capped, and quality is tracked by time into session, so fatigue shows up as a measurable pattern.

6 · Deep dive: labeller pools and routing

Pools by skill. Generalists by language; domain experts (software engineering, mathematics, medicine, law, finance) for tasks that need expertise to judge correctness; a safety pool trained on harmful-content policies, with wellbeing support; and adjudicators, the most experienced labellers and in-house specialists. InstructGPT's paper describes selecting its roughly 40 contractors with a screening test that measured agreement with researchers on sensitive prompts, which is the same idea: qualify before access.

Qualification and trust. Each pool has a qualification test drawn from gold items; passing grants access to a task type at a probationary trust level. A labeller's trust score is a running estimate from gold accuracy, agreement with peers on overlap items and adjudication outcomes, weighted toward recent work. It drives routing (hard and high-value tasks go to high-trust labellers), the review rate of their work (low trust means more of it is reviewed) and, for vendors, payment bonuses.

The router's rules. Match the task's required skills to qualified pools. Insert gold questions at the configured share, indistinguishable from normal tasks. Assign overlap copies to randomly chosen pairs of qualified labellers, never the same person twice, so agreement estimates are unbiased. Respect exposure limits: a labeller in the safety pool sees at most a set number of graphic items per day. Balance queues across pools and time zones to meet due dates. Prefer giving a labeller a run of tasks of one type (context switching costs time) without letting one labeller dominate a batch (which would bias it toward their judgement).

7 · Deep dive: quality control and agreement statistics

Gold questions. Hidden items with answers agreed by experts, mixed into queues at about 5%. For preference tasks, good gold items are pairs where one response is clearly worse for a reason the guideline names (a factual error, an unsafe instruction, ignoring the question), because close pairs make poor tests. Each labeller's gold accuracy is tracked over a sliding window; a drop below the threshold triggers review of their recent work and reduced routing. Gold items wear out (labellers learn them), so the set is refreshed from adjudicated items.

Overlap and agreement. A fraction of items (20% here) is labelled by two labellers independently. Agreement is computed per task type, per guideline version, per labeller pair and per strength bucket. For two labellers with categorical answers, Cohen's kappa corrects for chance (ev5 derives it). Work an example from overlap data: on 200 preference pairs, labeller 1 chose A 120 times and labeller 2 chose A 110 times; both chose A on 90 and both B on 60, so they agreed on 150. Observed agreement po = 0.75. Chance agreement, from each labeller's base rates, pe = 0.60 × 0.55 + 0.40 × 0.45 = 0.51. Kappa = (0.75 − 0.51) / (1 − 0.51) ≈ 0.49. For comparison, InstructGPT reported raw agreement of 72.6 ± 1.5% among its training labellers and 77.3 ± 1.3% for held-out labellers, and the earlier summarisation work found researchers agreeing with each other 73 ± 4% of the time: preference judgements are genuinely hard to agree on.

Many labellers and missing labels. When items have different numbers of labels (some three, some two, because a labeller skipped or a task expired), Krippendorff's alpha applies: α = 1 − Do / De, observed disagreement over the disagreement expected by chance. A small worked case with nominal labels A and B: eight items, labelled AAA, ABA, BB, AA, BBB, BA, AA and BBA. Count ordered pairs of labels within each item, each weighted by 1 / (labels in the item − 1): this gives AA 8, BB 6, AB 3 and BA 3, a total of 20 pairable values, 11 A and 9 B. Observed disagreement Do = 6 / 20 = 0.30. Expected disagreement from the pooled values De = 2 × 11 × 9 / (20 × 19) = 198 / 380 ≈ 0.52. So α = 1 − 0.30 / 0.52 ≈ 0.42, well below the 0.667 that Krippendorff suggests as the floor for tentative conclusions. The platform computes these statistics continuously; the lab does the same in code.

What the numbers mean for preference data. Low agreement on preferences is partly noise and partly real: some pairs are close, and reasonable people differ. The platform therefore reports agreement by preference strength. If labellers agree strongly on pairs marked "significantly better" and near chance on "negligibly better", the data is behaving as expected, and close pairs can be down-weighted or excluded from training. Llama 2's authors used the strength rating directly, adding a margin to the reward-model loss that is larger for clearly separable pairs, and report that it improved accuracy on separable pairs. If agreement is low even on supposedly clear pairs, the guideline is the problem.

Speed and pattern checks. Tasks completed far faster than reading time allows, labellers who pick the left response 70% of the time when order is randomised, or rationales copied between tasks are flagged automatically for review.

Reliability models. With overlap data, a model such as Dawid–Skene estimates each labeller's confusion pattern and each item's most likely true label jointly, weighting reliable labellers more. It is most useful for categorical tasks (safety labels, rubric scores) and as a diagnostic for preferences.

Adjudication. Disagreements on overlap items go to an adjudicator with more expertise, who records the final label and a reason. A random sample of agreed items is also adjudicated, because two labellers can share a misconception. Adjudicated items feed back as gold questions and as guideline examples. Label Studio's documentation shows how a production tool frames the measurement side: agreement per question and overall, pairwise or consensus methods, exact match for categories, and overlap measures such as IoU for boxes and span overlap for text.

8 · Deep dive: active learning, choosing what to label

Why selection matters. A random sample of prompts with responses from the current model contains many pairs where both responses are fine and nearly identical, and many prompts the model already handles well. Labelling them costs the same as labelling the informative ones. Active learning chooses items expected to teach the model most per label.

Policies, combined. On-policy sampling: generate responses from the latest model checkpoint, since a reward model must score what the current policy produces; Llama 2's authors collected preference data in weekly batches using the latest model for exactly this reason, noting that reward-model accuracy degrades quickly when not exposed to the new distribution. Uncertainty sampling: prefer pairs where the current reward model's predicted preference probability is near 0.5, or where an ensemble of reward models (or a reward model and an LLM judge) disagree. Diversity: cluster prompt embeddings (ml12) and sample across clusters, so the batch is not all one topic. Targeted: prompts from known weaknesses found by evaluation (hd12) and red-teaming. Random slice: keep 20–30% of each batch randomly sampled, so agreement, coverage and reward-model accuracy can be measured without selection bias, and so the training data does not drift entirely toward hard edge cases.

Generating good pairs. Two responses from the same model at the same temperature are often near-identical. Pairs become more informative when responses come from different checkpoints or model variants, different temperatures or different prompts to the model (a concise and a detailed instruction); Llama 2 sampled the two responses from two different model variants with varied temperature to maximise diversity. Rankings of several responses give more comparisons per prompt: InstructGPT presented K = 4 to 9 responses to rank, which yields K(K − 1) / 2 comparisons from one prompt reading, 36 for K = 9.

Deduplication and exclusions. Near-duplicate prompts are removed, and anything within a similarity threshold of an evaluation item is excluded before labelling, not only before export.

9 · Deep dive: throughput and cost per usable label

Raw cost is time per task times the hourly rate: 3 minutes at $24 an hour is $1.20 per preference label. Cost per usable label follows the funnel in the figure. Work it for 1,000 usable labels with these assumptions: 6% of labels rejected by quality checks, 10% of items unusable for pairwise training (ties, or both responses bad), 20% overlap, 5% gold and disagreements on a quarter of overlap items, adjudicated by an expert at $90 an hour taking 5 minutes ($7.50 each).

The levers are visible in the table: clearer guidelines lower rejection and disagreement; better pair generation lowers the unusable share; overlap and gold rates can drop for high-trust labellers once quality is established; and adjudication can be focused on disagreements that matter (clear-strength pairs), since close pairs may be excluded rather than adjudicated. Each lever is measured, because cutting quality control saves money visibly and costs quality invisibly.

Throughput. Queues are planned in labeller-hours by pool. A batch's completion time is its hours divided by the pool's available hours, plus adjudication lag. Bottlenecks are usually expert pools (code, medicine) and adjudicators, so the planner reserves their time for tasks that need them and routes everything else to generalists.

10 · Deep dive: preference-collection interfaces

The interface shapes the data. Its design rules, each with a reason:

  • Randomised order, hidden identity. Left-right position and model names bias choices; order is randomised per task and recorded, so position bias can be measured and corrected.
  • Strength, not just choice. A short scale (Llama 2 used significantly better, better, slightly better, negligibly better or unsure) separates close calls from clear ones, which training and agreement analysis both use.
  • Escape hatches. "Both unsafe", "both bad" and "cannot judge (needs expertise)" options prevent forced choices that pollute the data; Llama 2's safety stage recorded whether the preferred response was safe and the other not (18% of its safety data), both safe (47%) or both unsafe (35%).
  • Per-criterion ratings where needed. Separate ratings for helpfulness, factual accuracy and safety let datasets for different objectives be built from one task, at the cost of time per task.
  • Rationale. A one-line reason helps adjudication, guideline revision and catching careless work, and costs about 20 seconds.
  • Edit to improve. Letting labellers edit the better response turns a comparison into an SFT demonstration, which is often cheaper than writing from scratch.
  • Context and tools. Multi-turn context, the ability to run code (for coding tasks) or search a reference (for factual tasks), keyboard shortcuts and a clear view of long responses, because a labeller who cannot check correctness will judge style.

11 · Deep dive: PII and data protection

Sourcing. Prompts come from researchers, red-teamers, synthetic generation, and production logs only where users consented or the legal basis and contracts allow; enterprise customers' data is typically excluded by contract. The source and consent basis are stored with every item, so a later change (a user withdraws consent) can be enforced.

Scrubbing before humans. Pattern detectors (emails, phone numbers, card numbers, national identifiers, addresses) and a named-entity model replace personal data with consistent typed placeholders ("[PERSON_1] asked [PERSON_2] about [ORDER_ID]") before any task is created. Items the scrubber is unsure about go to a restricted pool or are dropped. Scrubbing recall is measured on a labelled sample, like any classifier.

Secure workspace. Labellers, especially vendor staff, work in a locked-down browser environment: no copy, paste, download or screenshots where the platform can prevent them, visible watermarks with the labeller's pseudonym to deter photographing screens, access only to assigned tasks, and full access logs. Data stays in the company's environment, in the required region.

Retention and erasure. Raw items are kept only as long as needed; datasets keep scrubbed text. Lineage makes erasure possible: an erasure request finds every item derived from the user's data, removes it from future dataset versions and flags past versions (and models trained on them) according to policy.

Labeller wellbeing. Safety tasks expose people to disturbing content. Exposure limits per day, blurred previews by default, opt-in pools, rotation and access to support are part of the design, not an afterthought, and are tracked like any other operational metric.

12 · Feeding training and evaluation

Versioned datasets. An export produces an immutable snapshot with a manifest. Each record carries: item ID, prompt and responses, the model checkpoints that produced the responses, the final label and strength, all individual labels with labeller pseudonyms, the guideline version, agreement statistics for its batch, adjudication outcome, and source and consent basis. Training jobs (hd21) reference a snapshot ID, so every model can be traced to exactly the labels it learned from.

Filters at export. Researchers choose what to train on: exclude negligible-strength pairs, exclude items flagged both bad, require a minimum batch agreement, select guideline versions. These choices are recorded in the manifest.

The contamination guard. Evaluation sets are frozen, hashed and stored separately. Every training export is deduplicated against all evaluation items by exact hash and by embedding similarity above a threshold, and the platform refuses to route evaluation items into training queues. A sudden jump in a model's score on an old evaluation set, with no matching jump on a fresh one, is the alarm that a leak happened anyway.

Closing the loop. Each new checkpoint is sampled for the next round of preference collection; reward-model accuracy on a held-out set of fresh human preferences is measured after every batch, which tells the platform whether its data is still teaching the model something.

13 · Evaluating the platform itself

Label quality: gold accuracy by labeller and pool, agreement by task type, guideline version and strength bucket, adjudication overturn rates (how often adjudicators change agreed labels), scrubbing recall. Throughput: hours completed versus planned by pool, batch turnaround, queue age. Cost: cost per usable label by task type, the share of spend on quality control and adjudication. Downstream value: reward-model accuracy on fresh held-out preferences, and offline evaluation gains of models trained on new batches versus without them; a batch that does not move these is a signal to change selection policies. People: labeller retention, exposure counts for safety pools, and survey feedback on guideline clarity.
