15 · What changes at 10× scale

At 200,000 preference pairs a week, three changes. AI assistance in the loop: an LLM judge pre-labels items, and humans review where the judge is uncertain or disagrees with a second judge, with the judge validated against human labels on a fixed set (hd12); this cuts human hours sharply but makes judge validation part of the platform. Multiple vendors with comparable quality metrics and gold sets, routed by measured cost per usable label and turnaround. Stronger statistics: with millions of labels, labeller-reliability models, per-labeller bias correction and automatic guideline-ambiguity detection (clusters of items with persistent disagreement) become standard tools. The fundamentals stay: versioned guidelines, measured agreement, lineage and the contamination guard.
deep:
Disagreement is data, not just noise

Treating every disagreement as error and forcing a single "true" label throws away information. For subjective judgements, the distribution of labels is itself the most honest answer: if three of five labellers prefer A, the preference is real but weak. Some training methods use soft labels (the proportion preferring each response) or margins proportional to strength, and evaluation can report how often a model agrees with the majority on clear items versus close ones. The platform supports this by keeping every individual label in the dataset, not only the adjudicated one, so downstream teams can choose how to aggregate.

Chance correction depends on prevalence, so report the split

Kappa and alpha subtract chance agreement computed from how often each category is used. When one category dominates (95% of items are "safe"), chance agreement is very high, and even good labellers get low kappa, the so-called prevalence paradox that ev5 works through. The fix is not a different statistic but fuller reporting: raw agreement, the category distribution, and the chance-corrected number together, plus agreement on the rare category specifically, which is usually the one that matters (for safety labels, agreement on what is unsafe).

Gold questions measure attention, not judgement

Gold items must have clear answers, so they test whether a labeller is paying attention and applying the guideline to unambiguous cases. They say little about judgement on hard, close cases, which is where most of the value and most of the disagreement lies. That is why gold accuracy is combined with agreement on overlap items and adjudication outcomes in the trust score, and why adjudicators review a sample of hard agreed items: those are the only signals about quality on difficult cases.

Selection bias is the price of active learning

Choosing uncertain items makes training data more informative, but it makes the labelled set unrepresentative: agreement measured on hard items looks worse than on typical ones, and a reward model trained only on edge cases can become miscalibrated on ordinary responses. Keeping a random slice in every batch solves both: it gives unbiased estimates of agreement and coverage, and it anchors training on the typical distribution. Importance weights can correct estimates computed on the selected items, but the random slice is simpler and more robust.

Reward hacking starts in the data

Reward models learn what labellers reward, including their biases: longer answers, confident tone, lists, flattery. A policy optimised against such a reward model amplifies the bias. The platform can measure these biases directly (preference rate for the longer response on pairs whose content is otherwise equivalent; position bias) and counter them: guidelines that tell labellers to judge content over length, length-controlled pairs, and analysis of strength by length difference. The cheapest place to stop reward hacking is before the label is recorded.

AI-assisted labelling changes what humans are for

As LLM judges improve, the efficient design uses them to pre-label and to flag, with humans concentrating on items where judges are uncertain, disagree with each other or touch high-stakes categories, and on a random sample to keep measuring judge accuracy. This raises the expertise needed from humans (the remaining items are the hard ones) and makes judge validation a first-class platform concern. It also creates a subtle risk: if humans see the judge's label, they anchor on it, so assisted tasks hide the pre-label on the sample used to measure judge quality.

Labeller incentives shape label quality

Paying per task rewards speed; paying per hour rewards nothing in particular; neither rewards care on hard items. Vendors and platforms that tie bonuses to gold accuracy and adjudication outcomes, cap daily task counts and pay more for expert pools get better data, but every incentive can be gamed: labellers learn to recognise gold items (so gold sets rotate), or avoid hard tasks (so routing assigns them rather than letting labellers choose). The platform measures incentive effects like any other change, for example comparing agreement and gold accuracy before and after a payment change, because labelling quality is an outcome of the whole system, including how people are paid and treated, not only of the interface and the guideline. Reporting quality by vendor, pool and payment scheme keeps that visible.
prod:
How it fails in practice

The silent guideline split. Midway through a month, the definition of "concise" in the helpfulness guideline changed. Half the batch was labelled under each version, and the resulting reward model learned contradictory preferences about length, so the next policy's answers became erratic in length. Because tasks recorded only the guideline name, not the version, the two halves could not be separated. Every task now records the version, exports can filter by it, and a guideline change opens a new task type version rather than editing the old one in place.

The left-hand labeller. A vendor labeller chose the left response 78% of the time over two weeks, while order was randomised. Gold accuracy was acceptable because gold pairs were easy. A position-bias check per labeller flagged it; their recent labels were removed and relabelled, and position bias is now part of the trust score.

The leaked evaluation set. An internal evaluation set's prompts were included in a prompt pool used for preference sampling, because both had been imported from the same spreadsheet. The next model jumped eight points on that evaluation set and showed no gain on a fresh one. The contamination guard (deduplication against all evaluation items at selection and export) was built after this, and evaluation sets now live in a separate project that training queues cannot read.

What to monitor

Per batch: progress against plan, agreement by strength and category, gold accuracy, rejection rate, unusable share, adjudication backlog, cost per usable label. Per labeller: gold accuracy, agreement with peers, speed, position bias, trust score trend, exposure counts. Per guideline version: agreement trend and the items with persistent disagreement (candidates for clarification). Pipeline: scrubbing recall on audits, contamination-guard hits, time from checkpoint to labelled data. Downstream: reward-model accuracy on fresh held-out preferences after each batch.

Knobs people tune

Gold share and overlap rate by task type and trust level; trust thresholds for access and review; selection mix (uncertain, diverse, targeted, random); pair generation settings (which checkpoints, temperatures); strength-based export filters; adjudication policy (all disagreements, clear-strength only, sample of agreed items); exposure limits; session length.

The real cases: InstructGPT, Llama 2 and Label Studio

InstructGPT's paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) documents a labelling programme at the scale of a research project: about 40 contractors hired through Upwork and Scale AI, selected by a screening test measuring sensitivity to harmful content and agreement with researchers; an SFT dataset of about 13,000 training prompts, a reward-model dataset of 33,000 and a PPO dataset of 31,000; rankings of K = 4 to 9 responses per prompt to extract many comparisons from one reading; and inter-annotator agreement of 72.6 ± 1.5% among training labellers and 77.3 ± 1.3% for held-out labellers who produced no training data, against 73 ± 4% between researchers in the earlier summarisation work. Llama 2's paper (Touvron et al., 2023) shows the industrial version: binary comparisons with a four-level strength scale, separate helpfulness and safety guidelines, safety bins of 18%, 47% and 35%, weekly batches collected from the latest model to keep the reward model on-distribution (14 batches), over a million comparisons (1,418,091 in its Meta reward-modelling data), and a margin in the reward-model loss driven by the strength rating. Label Studio's agreement documentation, checked on 10 October 2026, shows how a production tool measures label quality per question and overall, with pairwise and consensus methods and task-appropriate similarity measures. The cost figures in this lesson are worked from stated assumptions; the method (funnel the raw label through gold, overlap, rejection, usability and adjudication to a cost per usable label) is what transfers.
myths: Labels are ground truth.

A label is a measurement made by a person following guidelines, with error and disagreement. InstructGPT's trained labellers agreed with each other 72.6% of the time on preference comparisons; a quarter of judgements were contested. The platform's job is to measure that uncertainty (agreement, gold accuracy, adjudication) and carry it with the data, not to pretend it away.
More labels always help.

Labels on easy, redundant or off-distribution examples add cost without teaching the model anything new, and noisy labels can hurt. A reward model trained on last quarter's model outputs drifts from the current model's distribution; Llama 2's authors collected preference data in weekly batches from the latest model for this reason. Choosing what to label is worth as much as labelling more.
Majority vote of three labellers fixes quality.

Majority vote helps when errors are independent, but labellers trained on the same unclear guideline make the same mistakes, and three labels cost three times one. Single labelling with 10–20% overlap to measure agreement, gold questions to catch unreliable labellers, and expert adjudication of disagreements usually gives better data per dollar.
Raw agreement tells you how good the labels are.

Agreement includes agreement by chance: if 90% of items are "acceptable", two careless labellers agree about 82% of the time by chance alone. Chance-corrected statistics (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha) and the category split must be reported together, or a useless labelling process looks excellent.
The cost of a label is the labeller's hourly rate times the time per task.

That is the raw cost. Gold questions, overlap, rejected work, unusable items (ties, both responses bad) and expert adjudication raise it; in the worked example a $1.20 raw preference label becomes about $2.24 per usable label, nearly double. Budgets and vendor comparisons must use cost per usable label.
Production chat logs are free training data.

They contain personal data, confidential business information and content users never agreed to share for training. Using them requires consent or a clear legal basis, PII scrubbing before any human sees them, contractual exclusions (enterprise customers often forbid it), secure labelling environments, and the ability to remove a user's data from every dataset version on request.
lab:
Goal: build the agreement and cost toolkit the platform runs on every batch: Cohen's kappa for two labellers, Krippendorff's alpha (nominal) with missing labels, a bootstrap confidence interval, per-labeller gold accuracy and position bias, and cost per usable label. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Save as agreement.py and run python agreement.py.
  2. Check the kappa block against the lesson: 0.75 observed, 0.51 chance, kappa about 0.49.
  3. Check the alpha block on the eight-item example: about 0.42. Then read alpha on the simulated batch of 400 items with three labellers and missing labels, with its bootstrap interval.
  4. Read the labeller table: the simulated careless labeller should show low gold accuracy and the biased one a high left-choice rate despite reasonable gold accuracy.
  5. Change the assumptions in cost_per_usable (overlap, gold share, rejection) and watch the cost per usable label move from the $2.24 baseline.
"""Agreement and cost toolkit for a labelling platform. Python 3.12, stdlib only."""
import random
from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations
rng = random.Random(3)

def cohen_kappa(a, b):
    n = len(a); po = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / n
    ca, cb = Counter(a), Counter(b)
    pe = sum(ca[k] / n * cb[k] / n for k in set(a) | set(b))
    return po, pe, (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

def kripp_alpha_nominal(units):
    """units: list of label lists; None = missing. Returns alpha."""
    o = Counter()
    for u in units:
        v = [x for x in u if x is not None]
        if len(v) < 2: continue
        for i, j in permutations(range(len(v)), 2):
            o[(v[i], v[j])] += 1 / (len(v) - 1)
    nc = Counter()
    for (c, _), w in o.items(): nc[c] += w
    n = sum(nc.values())
    do = sum(w for (c, k), w in o.items() if c != k) / n
    de = sum(nc[c] * nc[k] for c in nc for k in nc if c != k) / (n * (n - 1))
    return 1 - do / de

a = ["A"] * 90 + ["A"] * 30 + ["B"] * 20 + ["B"] * 60          # labeller 1
b = ["A"] * 90 + ["B"] * 30 + ["A"] * 20 + ["B"] * 60          # labeller 2
po, pe, k = cohen_kappa(a, b)
print(f"Cohen: observed {po:.2f}  chance {pe:.2f}  kappa {k:.2f}")
small = [list("AAA"), list("ABA"), ["B", "B", None], ["A", "A", None], list("BBB"),
         ["B", "A", None], ["A", None, "A"], list("BBA")]
print(f"Krippendorff alpha, 8-item example: {kripp_alpha_nominal(small):.3f}")

# Simulated batch: 400 items, 3 labellers (one careless, one left-biased), some missing
truth = [rng.random() < 0.6 for _ in range(400)]                 # True = A better
gold = set(rng.sample(range(400), 20))
def label(t, kind, left_is_a):
    if kind == "careless" and rng.random() < 0.45: choice_left = rng.random() < 0.5
    elif kind == "biased" and rng.random() < 0.30: choice_left = True
    else:
        correct = rng.random() < 0.85
        a_better = t if correct else not t
        choice_left = a_better == left_is_a
    return "A" if choice_left == left_is_a else "B", choice_left
kinds = {"L1": "good", "L2": "careless", "L3": "biased"}
units, stats = [], {n: Counter() for n in kinds}
for i, t in enumerate(truth):
    row = []
    for name, kind in kinds.items():
        if rng.random() < 0.15: row.append(None); continue        # task expired / skipped
        left_is_a = rng.random() < 0.5
        lab, left = label(t, kind, left_is_a)
        row.append(lab); stats[name]["n"] += 1; stats[name]["left"] += left
        if i in gold: stats[name]["gold"] += 1; stats[name]["gold_ok"] += (lab == "A") == t
    units.append(row)
alpha = kripp_alpha_nominal(units)
boots = sorted(kripp_alpha_nominal([rng.choice(units) for _ in units]) for _ in range(500))
print(f"\nBatch alpha {alpha:.3f}  (95% bootstrap {boots[12]:.3f}-{boots[487]:.3f})")
print(f"{'labeller':8} {'gold acc':>8} {'left %':>7}")
for name, s in stats.items():
    print(f"{name:8} {s['gold_ok'] / max(1, s['gold']):8.2f} {s['left'] / s['n']:7.0%}")

def cost_per_usable(rate=24, minutes=3, reject=0.06, unusable=0.10, overlap=0.2,
                    gold=0.05, disagree=0.25, adj_cost=7.5):
    items = 1000 / ((1 - reject) * (1 - unusable))
    tasks = items * (1 + overlap) / (1 - gold)
    total = tasks * rate * minutes / 60 + items * overlap * disagree * adj_cost
    return total / 1000
print(f"\nCost per usable label: ${cost_per_usable():.2f} (raw ${24 * 3 / 60:.2f})")

What to look for: kappa well below raw agreement; a batch alpha pulled down by the careless labeller, with an interval that shows how uncertain one batch's estimate is; the biased labeller exposed by the left-choice rate rather than by gold accuracy; and a cost per usable label close to double the raw figure.
recap: A labelling and human-feedback platform turns raw prompts and model outputs into SFT demonstrations, preference pairs, safety labels and evaluation labels, with measured quality and full lineage.
Each task type has a versioned guideline and interface; guidelines are piloted in calibration rounds until agreement is acceptable, and every label records the guideline version it was made under.
Labellers are organised into pools by skill (language, domain, safety training), qualified by tests, routed by skill and trust score, and protected by exposure limits on harmful content.
Quality control combines hidden gold questions, overlap labelling to measure agreement, speed and pattern checks, reliability models over labellers, and expert adjudication of disagreements.

In the worked example, two labellers agree on 150 of 200 preference pairs: raw agreement 0.75, chance agreement 0.51, Cohen's kappa 0.49; a three-labeller set with missing labels gives Krippendorff's alpha 0.42.

Low agreement on preferences is partly genuine closeness, so the UI collects preference strength (as Llama 2 did with significantly better, better, slightly better, negligibly better or unsure), and training can weight or filter by it.

Active learning chooses what to label: prompts where the reward model or an ensemble is uncertain, diversity by embedding clusters, fresh responses from the latest model, and a random slice kept for unbiased measurement.
Cost per usable label includes gold, overlap, rejection, unusable items and adjudication: $1.20 raw becomes about $2.24 per usable preference label in the worked example.
PII is handled by consent-based sourcing, scrubbing before tasks, secure labelling environments, minimal retention and lineage that lets an erasure request reach every dataset version.

Outputs are versioned datasets with per-record provenance (prompt, model versions, labeller pseudonyms, guideline version, agreement, adjudication), exported to SFT, reward-model and evaluation pipelines with contamination guards between training and evaluation.
glossary: Choosing which items to label next based on where a model is uncertain or where data is missing, to get more learning per label.
A senior or expert reviewer resolving disagreements between labellers and recording the final label and reason.
A pilot in which all labellers label the same items, disagreements are discussed and the guideline is revised.
Chance-corrected agreement between two labellers: (observed agreement − chance agreement) / (1 − chance agreement).
Total spend (labelling, gold, overlap, rejected work, adjudication) divided by the number of labels that end up in a dataset.
A statistical model that estimates each labeller's error pattern and each item's true label from overlapping labels.
A hidden item with a known correct answer, mixed into a labeller's queue to measure their accuracy.
The written instructions, definitions and examples that define what each label means; versioned like code.
How often different labellers give the same label to the same item, raw or corrected for chance.
A chance-corrected reliability statistic for any number of labellers, missing labels and nominal, ordinal or interval scales: 1 − observed disagreement / expected disagreement.
A group of labellers with shared qualifications (language, domain, safety training) to which matching tasks are routed.
The record linking each dataset record to its sources, labels, labellers, guideline version and the models trained on it.
A language model prompted to grade or compare responses, used to pre-label or check human labels after being validated against them.
Assigning a fraction of items to more than one labeller so agreement can be measured.
Personally identifiable information: data that identifies a person directly, such as a name or email, or in combination with other data.
Proximal policy optimisation: the reinforcement-learning algorithm InstructGPT used to tune the model against the reward model.
Two responses to the same prompt with a label saying which is better, used to train reward models or for direct preference optimisation.
How much better the chosen response is, on a short scale, recorded with the preference.
A model trained on preference pairs to score how good a response is, used to steer reinforcement learning or to rank samples.
A prompt with an ideal response written or edited by a person, used for supervised fine-tuning.
A labeller's running quality estimate from gold accuracy, agreement and review outcomes, used for routing and payment.
drill:
Estimate it

A team needs 5,000 usable code-review preference pairs a week from software-engineering experts at $70 an hour, 6 minutes per pair. Expect 8% rejected labels, 15% unusable items (both responses wrong), 25% overlap, 5% gold, disagreement on 30% of overlap items, and adjudication by a staff engineer at $120 an hour taking 10 minutes. (a) Cost per usable label? (b) Expert hours per week? (c) Which two changes would you test first to cut cost?

Answer

(a) Raw cost: 6 minutes at $70 an hour is $7.00. Items per 1,000 usable: 1,000 / (0.92 × 0.85) ≈ 1,279. Labels with 25% overlap: 1,598. Tasks with 5% gold: 1,598 / 0.95 ≈ 1,683, costing 1,683 × $7.00 ≈ $11,780. Adjudication: 1,279 × 0.25 × 0.30 ≈ 96 items × $20 = $1,920. Total ≈ $13,700 per 1,000, about $13.70 per usable label, nearly twice the raw $7.

(b) For 5,000 usable labels: about 8,415 tasks × 0.1 hours ≈ 840 expert labelling hours, plus about 480 adjudications × 1/6 hour ≈ 80 staff-engineer hours. At 30 productive hours a week, about 28 experts plus part of three senior engineers: the expert pool is the bottleneck.

(c) The unusable share (15%, both responses wrong) suggests the pairs are badly generated: sampling responses from stronger or more varied checkpoints, or filtering out prompts where the model fails completely, would cut wasted expert time. And the 30% disagreement rate suggests guideline ambiguity: a calibration round on the disagreeing items would lower both adjudication cost and rejection. Lowering overlap to 15% for high-trust experts is a third option once agreement is established.

Diagnose it

Reward-model accuracy on fresh held-out preferences has been flat for three weekly batches, although each batch passed its quality checks (gold accuracy 93%, agreement unchanged). What do you investigate?

Answer

Quality checks say the labels are reliable; flat accuracy says they are not informative. Check distribution: are responses being sampled from the latest checkpoint, or from a stale one (a sampling job pinned to an old model is common)? Check selection: has the uncertainty-sampling share dropped, or is the batch dominated by easy pairs where both responses are good (look at the strength distribution: a rising share of "negligibly better" means little signal)? Check coverage: are prompts concentrated in a few clusters the reward model already handles? Check export filters: did a filter change start excluding the informative close-but-clear pairs? Fixes follow the cause: repoint sampling to the current checkpoint, rebalance the selector toward uncertain and under-covered clusters, generate more varied pairs, and add reward-model accuracy on fresh data as a per-batch gate so an uninformative batch is caught the week it happens.
qa: E
What does a human-feedback platform produce, and for whom?

Supervised fine-tuning demonstrations (prompts with ideal responses), preference pairs (which of two responses is better, with strength), safety labels, and evaluation labels for golden sets and judge calibration. Consumers are the training pipelines (SFT, reward models, preference optimisation) and the evaluation platform. Each output is a versioned dataset with quality statistics and provenance.
E
Why use gold questions?

To measure each labeller's accuracy continuously without them knowing which items are tested. Gold items have known answers agreed by experts; a labeller whose gold accuracy drops below a threshold has recent work reviewed or rejected and their routing reduced. They cost labelling time without producing new data, so they are kept to a few per cent of tasks.
E
Why is raw agreement misleading?

Because labellers agree by chance. If 90% of items fall in one category, two people labelling at random with those base rates agree about 82% of the time. Cohen's kappa and Krippendorff's alpha subtract chance agreement; report them with raw agreement and the category split.
M
Compute Cohen's kappa: on 200 overlapping preference pairs, labeller 1 chose A 120 times and labeller 2 chose A 110 times; both chose A on 90 and both chose B on 60.

Observed agreement is (90 + 60) / 200 = 0.75. Chance agreement is 0.60 × 0.55 + 0.40 × 0.45 = 0.33 + 0.18 = 0.51. Kappa = (0.75 − 0.51) / (1 − 0.51) = 0.24 / 0.49 ≈ 0.49, moderate agreement. For preference data this is typical, because many pairs are genuinely close.

Follow-up: What would you do with that number? — Split it by preference strength and task category: if agreement is high on clearly different pairs and low on close ones, the data is fine and close pairs should be down-weighted; if it is low everywhere, the guideline needs a calibration round.
M
Work out the cost per usable preference label.

Raw: 3 minutes at $24 an hour is $1.20. For 1,000 usable labels, with 6% of labels rejected and 10% of items unusable (ties, both bad), you need 1,000 / (0.94 × 0.9) ≈ 1,182 items; 20% overlap makes 1,418 labels; 5% gold makes about 1,493 tasks, costing $1,792. Disagreements on a quarter of overlap items (59 items) go to an expert at $7.50 each, $443. Total about $2,235, so $2.24 per usable label, nearly double the raw figure.
M
How would you route tasks to labellers?

Match required skills (language, domain such as code or medicine, safety training) to qualified pools; within a pool, prefer labellers with high trust scores for hard or high-value tasks; assign overlap items to random pairs so agreement is unbiased; never give the same labeller both copies of an overlap item; respect exposure limits on harmful content; and send disagreements to adjudicators with more expertise than the original labellers. Track throughput per pool so queues stay balanced.
M
Design the preference-collection interface.

Show the prompt and conversation, then two responses side by side with randomised left-right order and no model identity. Ask for a choice plus strength (significantly better, better, slightly better, negligibly better or unsure), optional per-criterion ratings (helpfulness, accuracy, safety), flags for both responses unsafe or both bad, and a short rationale. Offer an edit option that turns the better response into an SFT demonstration. Track time per task and support keyboard shortcuts.

Follow-up: Why ask for strength? — It separates close calls from clear ones; Llama 2 used the four-level strength to add a margin to its reward-model loss, which improved accuracy on clearly separable pairs.
M
How do you choose which prompts to send for preference labelling?

Sample responses from the latest model so data stays on-distribution; prioritise prompts where the reward model's predicted preference is near 50% or an ensemble disagrees; cover the space with diversity sampling over prompt embeddings; add targeted prompts for known weaknesses from evaluation; and keep a random slice (say 20–30%) so quality and coverage can be measured without selection bias. Remove near-duplicates and anything in evaluation sets.
H
Design quality control end to end for a 300-labeller vendor pool.

Qualification tests before access; calibration rounds per guideline version; 5% hidden gold per queue with per-labeller accuracy; 20% overlap with pairwise agreement per labeller and per task type; speed and pattern checks (too fast, always choosing left); a reliability model such as Dawid–Skene over overlapping labels to weight labellers; expert adjudication of disagreements and of a random sample of agreed items; trust scores feeding routing and payment; and dashboards of agreement and gold accuracy by guideline version, task type and labeller. Rejected work is relabelled, and systematic disagreement triggers a guideline revision.
Follow-up: Why audit agreed items? — Two labellers can agree on the same wrong answer when the guideline is unclear or they share a misconception; only expert review of agreed items catches that.
H
How do you keep evaluation data out of training data?

Separate projects and storage for evaluation sets, frozen and hashed by version; deduplicate every training export against all evaluation prompts by exact hash and near-duplicate embedding similarity; never route evaluation items through active-learning queues that feed training; record lineage so any model's training data can be checked against an evaluation set; and rotate fresh evaluation items so a leak is detectable as a sudden jump on old items only.
H
A reward model trained on last month's labels stops improving the policy. What do you suspect, and what does the platform change?

Distribution shift: the policy has improved and now produces responses unlike those the labels were collected on, so the reward model is scoring out-of-distribution inputs, and the policy may be exploiting its errors. The platform should sample fresh responses from the current policy each week (Llama 2 collected in weekly batches for this reason), prioritise pairs where the reward model is uncertain or where it disagrees with judges, and track reward-model accuracy on a held-out set of fresh human preferences after every batch.
H
How do you handle PII in prompts drawn from production?

Source only from users and customers who consented or where the legal basis and contracts allow it; scrub names, emails, phone numbers, addresses and identifiers with patterns and a named-entity model before any human sees the data, replacing them with consistent placeholders; route anything the scrubber flags as uncertain to a restricted pool; run labelling in a secure environment without copy or download, with access logged; keep data minimal and retention limited; and maintain lineage so an erasure request can be applied to every dataset version and flagged for future training runs.
